title: Distributed Architecture for Unmanned Vehicle Services †
abstract: This paper examines distributed architecture for unmanned vehicle services (UVS), an emerging technology that promises to revolutionize public and private transportation. Unmanned vehicles would autonomously navigate passengers from point A to B in a safe, efficient and cost-effective manner. The concept of UVS requires two main components: designing the hardware infrastructure on which such vehicles will run and developing the autonomous software that controls operations in distributed environments. This study focuses on examining enhancements of existing designs for UVS architectures, emphasizing scalability, security, safety compliance and efficiency improvements when applicable. To achieve this task, theoretical models from computer science research were used to create design solutions - applying them through simulations with real-world data in order to evaluate performance. Furthermore, additional experiments were conducted to provide insights into aspects not initially taken into consideration during theory conceptualization phases – such as adaptability/flexibility across different locations or varying levels of traffic volume at different times of day. Finally results are presented here alongside discussion outlining their implications on future implementations of UVS architectures.†Distributed Architecture for Unmanned Vehicle Services

title: A Human Monoclonal Antibody with Neutralizing Activity against Highly Divergent Influenza Subtypes
abstract: This study presents the characterization of a novel human monoclonal antibody (hMAb) with potent, broadly neutralizing activity across common influenza subtypes. Through functional and biochemical characterization of this hMAb, named IG5410, we demonstrate that it can effectively recognize diverse influenza proteins containing variable antigenic regions found in highly divergent cage A subtypes. Fusion-format assays using spike protein receptors revealed that IG5410 is a strong binding epitope with an effective IC50 concentration down to 2 μg/mL against multiple H3N2 and H1N1 isolates collected over 10 years range. Thus, IG5410 may represent an alternative approach for protection against potentially emerging influenza pandemics by providing coverage across different circulating or mutated strains.

title: Graptoloid feeding efficiency, rotation and astogeny
abstract: This paper proposes an investigation into the effects of rotation and astogeny on graptoloid feeding efficiency. Graptolites, or Graptoloidea, are a remarkably successful extinct colony-forming organism believed to have first evolved during Early Ordovician times before finally disappearing in the Late Permian. Of particular interest concerning graptoloids is the interplay between two variables: rotation speed of their bodies and astogeny (i.e., internal division within colonies) - both of which have a significant influence upon feeding efficiency and overall survival strategies. Using ontogenic displacement analysis to measure motion velocity amongst colonies located across different environments, this study determines how changes in rotation speed affect feeding performance under different levels of astogenetic division as well as discusses implications for biophysical models theorizing on habitat ranges for various species housed within those colonies.

title: The Association Between Adverse Child Health, Psychological, Educational and Social Outcomes, and Nondependent Parental Substance: A Rapid Evidence Assessment
abstract: BACKGROUND: Between 5% and 30% of children in high-income countries live with a substance misusing parent, the majority of which is below dependent levels. However, little is understood about the impact of nondependent parental substance misuse upon children. METHODS: We searched the international literature using rigorous systematic methods to identify studies examining parental substance misuse and adverse outcomes in children. The inclusion criteria were cross-sectional, longitudinal, case-control, and cohort studies; of children aged 0–18 years whose parents are high-risk substance misusers; reporting on their health, psychological, substance use, educational, and social outcomes. RESULTS: We identified 36 papers (from 33 unique studies), most of which were assessed as being of medium to high methodological quality (N= 28). Parental nondependent substance misuse was found to be associated with adversity in children, with strong evidence of an association with externalizing difficulties (N = 7 papers, all finding an association) and substance use (N = 23 papers, all finding an association) in adolescents and some evidence of adverse health outcomes in early childhood (N = 6/8 papers finding an association). There is less evidence of an association between parental substance misuse and adverse educational and social outcomes. The body of evidence was largest for parental alcohol misuse, with research examining the impact of parental illicit drug use being limited. CONCLUSION: Methodological limitations restrict our ability to make causal inference. Nonetheless, the prevalence of adverse outcomes in children whose parents are nondependent substance misusers highlights the need for practitioners to intervene with this population before a parent has developed substance dependency.

title: The Role of Microglia in Bacterial Meningitis: Inflammatory Response, Experimental Models and New Neuroprotective Therapeutic Strategies
abstract: Microglia have a pivotal role in the pathophysiology of bacterial meningitis. The goal of this review is to provide an overview on how microglia respond to bacterial pathogens targeting the brain, how the interplay between microglia and bacteria can be studied experimentally, and possible ways to use gained knowledge to identify novel preventive and therapeutic strategies. We discuss the dual role of microglia in disease development, the beneficial functions crucial for bacterial clearing, and the destructive properties through triggering neuroinflammation, characterized by cytokine and chemokine release which leads to leukocyte trafficking through the brain vascular endothelium and breakdown of the blood-brain barrier integrity. Due to intrinsic complexity of microglia and up until recently lack of specific markers, the study of microglial response to bacterial pathogens is challenging. New experimental models and techniques open up possibilities to accelerate progress in the field. We review existing models and discuss possibilities and limitations. Finally, we summarize recent findings where bacterial virulence factors are identified to be important for the microglial response, and how manipulation of evoked responses could be used for therapeutic or preventive purposes. Among promising approaches are: modulations of microglia phenotype switching toward anti-inflammatory and phagocytic functions, the use of non-bacterolytic antimicrobials, preventing release of bacterial components into the neural milieu and consequential amplification of immune activation, and protection of the blood-brain barrier integrity.

title: Basigin drives intracellular accumulation of l-lactate by harvesting protons and substrate anions
abstract: Transmembrane transport of l-lactate by members of the monocarboxylate transporter family, MCT, is vital in human physiology and a malignancy factor in cancer. Interaction with an accessory protein, typically basigin, is required to deliver the MCT to the plasma membrane. It is unknown whether basigin additionally exerts direct effects on the transmembrane l-lactate transport of MCT1. Here, we show that the presence of basigin leads to an intracellular accumulation of l-lactate 4.5-fold above the substrate/proton concentrations provided by the external buffer. Using basigin truncations we localized the effect to arise from the extracellular Ig-I domain. Identification of surface patches of condensed opposite electrostatic potential, and experimental analysis of charge-affecting Ig-I mutants indicated a bivalent harvesting antenna functionality for both, protons and substrate anions. From these data, and determinations of the cytosolic pH with a fluorescent probe, we conclude that the basigin Ig-I domain drives lactate uptake by locally increasing the proton and substrate concentration at the extracellular MCT entry site. The biophysical properties are physiologically relevant as cell growth on lactate media was strongly promoted in the presence of the Ig-I domain. Lack of the domain due to shedding, or misfolding due to breakage of a stabilizing disulfide bridge reversed the effect. Tumor progression according to classical or reverse Warburg effects depends on the transmembrane l-lactate distribution, and this study shows that the basigin Ig-I domain is a pivotal determinant.

title: Diversity of Salmonella spp. serovars isolated from the intestines of water buffalo calves with gastroenteritis
abstract: BACKGROUND: Salmonellosis in water buffalo (Bubalus bubalis) calves is a widespread disease characterized by severe gastrointestinal lesions, profuse diarrhea and severe dehydration, occasionally exhibiting a systemic course. Several Salmonella serovars seem to be able to infect water buffalo, but Salmonella isolates collected from this animal species have been poorly characterized. In the present study, the prevalence of Salmonella spp. in water buffalo calves affected by lethal gastroenteritis was assessed, and a polyphasic characterization of isolated strains of S. Typhimurium was performed. RESULTS: The microbiological analysis of the intestinal contents obtained from 248 water buffalo calves affected by lethal gastroenteritis exhibited a significant prevalence of Salmonella spp. (25%), characterized by different serovars, most frequently Typhimurium (21%), Muenster (11%), and Give (11%). The 13 S. Typhimurium isolates were all associated with enterocolitis characterized by severe damage of the intestine, and only sporadically isolated with another possible causative agent responsible for gastroenteritis, such as Cryptosporidium spp., Rotavirus or Clostridium perfringens. Other Salmonella isolates were mostly isolated from minor intestinal lesions, and often (78% of cases) isolated with other microorganisms, mainly toxinogenic Escherichia coli (35%), Cryptosporidium spp. (20%) and Rotavirus (10%). The S. Typhimurium strains were characterized by phage typing and further genotyped by polymerase chain reaction (PCR) detection of 24 virulence genes. The isolates exhibited nine different phage types and 10 different genetic profiles. Three monophasic S. Typhimurium (B:4,12:i:-) isolates were also found and characterized, displaying three different phage types and three different virulotypes. The molecular characterization was extended to the 7 S. Muenster and 7 S. Give isolates collected, indicating the existence of different virulotypes also within these serovars. Three representative strains of S. Typhimurium were tested in vivo in a mouse model of mixed infection. The most pathogenic strain was characterized by a high number of virulence factors and the presence of the locus agfA, coding for a thin aggregative fimbria. CONCLUSIONS: These results provide evidence that Salmonella is frequently associated with gastroenteritis in water buffalo calves, particularly S. Typhimurium. Moreover, the variety in the number and distribution of different virulence markers among the collected S. Typhimurium strains suggests that within this serovar there are different pathotypes potentially responsible for different clinical syndromes.

title: The Ebola Virus Glycoprotein and HIV-1 Vpu Employ Different Strategies to Counteract the Antiviral Factor Tetherin
abstract: The antiviral protein tetherin/BST2/CD317/HM1.24 restricts cellular egress of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) and of particles mimicking the Ebola virus (EBOV), a hemorrhagic fever virus. The HIV-1 viral protein U (Vpu) and the EBOV-glycoprotein (EBOV-GP) both inhibit tetherin. Here, we compared tetherin counteraction by EBOV-GP and Vpu. We found that EBOV-GP but not Vpu counteracted tetherin from different primate species, indicating that EBOV-GP and Vpu target tetherin differentially. Tetherin interacted with the GP2 subunit of EBOV-GP, which might encode the determinants for tetherin counteraction. Vpu reduced cell surface expression of tetherin while EBOV-GP did not, suggesting that both proteins employ different mechanisms to counteract tetherin. Finally, Marburg virus (MARV)–GP also inhibited tetherin and downregulated tetherin in a cell type–dependent fashion, indicating that tetherin antagonism depends on the cellular source of tetherin. Collectively, our results indicate that EBOV-GP counteracts tetherin by a novel mechanism and that tetherin inhibition is conserved between EBOV-GP and MARV-GP.

title: Development of a measure of stigma towards occupational stress for mental health professionals
abstract: This paper presents the development of a measure to examine occupational stigma towards emotional labor among mental health professionals. A remarkable shift has been seen in recent years toward recognizing occupationally-induced emotional exhaustion and burnout as an area of concern, particularly within the mental health field. This study uses both qualitative and quantitative methodologies to analyze how current professional practice contributes to feelings of inadequacy, isolation, and guilt in workers exposed to emotionally taxing work environments. Findings show that there is significant discrepancy between self-reported levels of stress exposure compared with those reported by supervisors or colleagues. In addition, this disparity partially explains why psychological distress occurs at higher rates among employees who perform emotional labor than those who do not. The newly developed scale can aid employers in identifying workplace conditions which support adequate well-being for their staff members, assisting them in creating better working environments for their employees and ultimately improve service delivery outcomes across the profession.

title: Functional analysis of the SRV-1 RNA frameshifting pseudoknot
abstract: Simian retrovirus type-1 uses programmed ribosomal frameshifting to control expression of the Gag-Pol polyprotein from overlapping gag and pol open-reading frames. The frameshifting signal consists of a heptanucleotide slippery sequence and a downstream-located 12-base pair pseudoknot. The solution structure of this pseudoknot, previously solved by NMR [Michiels,P.J., Versleijen,A.A., Verlaan,P.W., Pleij,C.W., Hilbers,C.W. and Heus,H.A. (2001) Solution structure of the pseudoknot of SRV-1 RNA, involved in ribosomal frameshifting. J. Mol. Biol., 310, 1109–1123] has a classical H-type fold and forms an extended triple helix by interactions between loop 2 and the minor groove of stem 1 involving base–base and base–sugar contacts. A mutational analysis was performed to test the functional importance of the triple helix for −1 frameshifting in vitro. Changing bases in L2 or base pairs in S1 involved in a base triple resulted in a 2- to 5-fold decrease in frameshifting efficiency. Alterations in the length of L2 had adverse effects on frameshifting. The in vitro effects were well reproduced in vivo, although the effect of enlarging L2 was more dramatic in vivo. The putative role of refolding kinetics of frameshifter pseudoknots is discussed. Overall, the data emphasize the role of the triple helix in −1 frameshifting.

title: Oxone(®)-Mediated TEMPO-Oxidized Cellulose Nanomaterial Ultrafiltration and Dialysis Mixed-Matrix Hollow Fiber Membranes
abstract: This paper presents the synthesis, properties and applications of a novel oxone(®)-mediated TEMPO-oxidized cellulose nanomaterial mixed-matrix membrane for ultrafiltration and dialysis. Researchers have recently explored various materials to create membranes that enable efficient filtration with high throughputs while requiring minimal energy input. Cellulosic fibers from plants are believed to be ideal candidates due to their theoretically low cost, renewability and biocompatibility. However, these fibrous raw materials present challenges in terms of controlling pore size and creating uniform sizes which can limit both performance and versatility in applications such as tissue engineering or dialysis support systems. Through a unique approach using an oxidative bleaching technique known as oxidation via 2,2,6,6-Tetramethylpiperidine 1-Oxyl (TEMPO) mediated by Oxone®, this study utilises effectively oxidized microcrystalline cellulose nanomaterials (MCCN) incorporated into hollow fiber membranes achieving desired porosity changes while maintaining strength with both dielectric barrier discharge plasma treatment disinfection ability. The resulting ultrafiltration and dialyses mixed matrix composite modified polymer - based membrane is characterized via Atomic Force Microscopy surface topography analysis plus visual observation through scanning electron microscopy images showing improved permeation rates compared to unmodified counterparts as well as good mechanical stability under extreme conditions including highly acidic solutions along with anti fouling behaviour demonstrated by salt rejection tests carried out over several days’ duration . Finally the overview offers perspectives on potential application areas for this exciting new material combination.

title: Which sample type is better for Xpert MTB/RIF to diagnose adult and pediatric pulmonary tuberculosis?
abstract: This journal article aims to answer the question: ‘Which sample type is better for Xpert MTB/RIF to diagnose adult and pediatric pulmonary tuberculosis?’ Tuberculosis (TB) continues to be a major global public health threat and existing molecular diagnostics are critical for its detection. Xpert MTB/RIF, an automated rapid test that uses sputum samples of suspected TB patients, is regarded as the most frequently used TB diagnostic in many countries. The sample type is one of several variables influencing sensitivity in this test; yet which specimen has been shown to achieve higher performance remains unclear. title: Severe H1N1-infection during pregnancy
abstract: H1N1 is known to induce fulminant courses in youths and young adults. We report the case of a 24-year gravida 4 para 2 with singleton pregnancy admitted to obstetrical unit for fever up to 38°C during the 20th week of a so far uncomplicated pregnancy. Ultrasound examination and urine test was inconspicuous. Throat complaints were initially relieved during antibiotic therapy, but the patient developed dyspnea with progressing signs of cyanosis. Intubation was necessary on the fifth day because of decreasing oxygen saturation. Coincidentally, progressive pancytopenia and increased inflammatory activity was recorded. Echocardiography, blood cultures, and bronchial lavage brought no pathological findings, but CT revealed acute respiratory distress syndrome and hepatomegaly. Recent human immunodeficiency virus, cytomegalic virus, herpes simplex virus, classical influenza and parainfluenza infections were excluded. An H1N1-infection was confirmed by PCR on the sixth day. The antiviral therapy was changed from zanamivir to oseltamivir. Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation was necessary due to insufficient oxygen saturation by mechanical ventilation. Until this time, pregnancy seemed to be unimpaired, but a sudden spontaneous expulsion of the fetus occurred on the seventh day (weight 460 g, no anomalies detectable). Curettage post abortem was not necessary. As a result of the antiviral therapy, H1N1-DNA was not detectable at day 16. Despite all endeavors, the respiratory situation could not be improved significantly; the patient additionally developed multiorgan failure during the time course and died on the 28th day of treatment. The recent case illustrates a very dangerous and imposing course of an H1N1-infection during pregnancy.

title: Control of acute virus diseases of calves in the Federal Republic of Germany
abstract: The most important acute viral diseases of calves in the Federal Republic of Germany (FRG) are: 1. Enzootic bronchopneumonia. 2. Bovine viral diarrhoea — mucosal disease (BVD-MD). 3. Infectious bovine rhinotracheitis — infectious pustular vulvovaginitis (IBR-IPV). 4. Rota- and Coronavirus infections. The incidence, diagnosis and control of these infections in the FRG are discussed. Stomatitis papulosa and malignant catarrhal fever are also briefly mentioned.

title: Innate Immune Responses to Avian Influenza Viruses in Ducks and Chickens
abstract: Avian Influenza (AI) viruses have caused severe disease and mortality in poultry worldwide. In this study, we aimed to explore innate immune responses of ducks and chickens to AI viruses through measuring the expression levels of specific genes associated with immunity. As a result, our findings suggest that chickens posses the strongest innate immune response compared to Ducks when confronted with Level 2 pathogenicity AI viruses. By investigating differences in effective immune responses between two species, future research could be developed to understand why some hosts may not suffer serious impact from Avian Influenza infections while others are severely affected by them. The results of this work can contribute valuable insight into potential outbreaks or spread of avian influenza infections amongst birds as well as potentially improving treatments for farms infected by these types of viruses where they can be implemented on an 'as needed' basis depending on the particular host being exposed to infection.

title: Comprehensive Interactome Analysis Reveals that STT3B Is Required for N-Glycosylation of Lassa Virus Glycoprotein
abstract:
This study seeks to describe the functional role of the STT3B gene in the N-glycosylation of Lassa virus (LASV) glycoprotein, providing insight into how a single factor contributes towards efficient replication and transmission. The interactome mapping technique was used to identify potential interactions between proteins located on or near STT3B as part of a comprehensive analysis. Results from this approach demonstrate that STT3B is inherent for accurate N-glycan maturation thereby contributing to LASV envelope protein surface stability and transmissibility across mucosal surfaces. In all, these findings provide an in-depth understanding of post-translational modifications that are critical for LASV entry mechanisms and represent an important advance in comprehending viral pathogenesis.

title: Use of esophageal balloon manometry in the management of pediatric acute respiratory distress syndrome
abstract: This study aims to analyze the role of esophageal balloon manometry (EBM) in the management and treatment of pediatric acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS). ARDS is an emergent condition that can significantly deteriorate patients’ vital functions, leading to life-threatening complications. The lack of consensus on optimal ventilatory support strategies for critically ill children has raised questions about how best to improve outcomes. With this in mind, we sought to assess if EBM could be used as a reliable resource to help guide clinical decisions regarding providing intensive careventilation. Using patient records derived from a tertiary hospital setting over a two year period, data analysis was conducted on those diagnosed with ARDS who underwent EBM testing during their admission. Results revealed that the use of this tool considerably lowered average hospitalized length-of-stay across affected groups compared to standard care alone, suggesting it could play a positive role in prognostic decision making for pediatric ARDS cases presenting to emergency departments or ICUs where its availability is not necessarily widespread yet established

title: Mass Vaccination and Surveillance/Containment in the Eradication of Smallpox
abstract: This study investigates the effectiveness of mass vaccination and surveillance measures in achieving global eradication of smallpox. Despite its prevalence prior to 1980, a concerted effort involving multilateral advocacy and hundreds of millions of people was made to halt transmission through inoculation programs and infection containment mechanisms. The pursuit culminated with World Health Organization's successful campaign that witnessed only 25 reported cases over 6 decades until it was declared as no longer existent in December 1979. This article seeks to uncover the various quantitative dynamics involved in its successful termination from an epidemiological perspective, including budgetary allocations for immunization campaigns, costs associated with sophisticated surveillance networks established across multiple countries, overall mortality reductions realized upon inoculations and public perceptions about virus-related protocols. By doing so, this research attempts to answer whether a combination of preventive policies can be harnessed towards zeroing-out future outbreaks on better terms than those implemented during mid 20th century for smallpox control resulting into lasting consequences on disease pattern analysis both nationally and globally.

title: Post-mortem volatiles of vertebrate tissue
abstract: Volatile emission during vertebrate decay is a complex process that is understood incompletely. It depends on many factors. The main factor is the metabolism of the microbial species present inside and on the vertebrate. In this review, we combine the results from studies on volatile organic compounds (VOCs) detected during this decay process and those on the biochemical formation of VOCs in order to improve our understanding of the decay process. Micro-organisms are the main producers of VOCs, which are by- or end-products of microbial metabolism. Many microbes are already present inside and on a vertebrate, and these can initiate microbial decay. In addition, micro-organisms from the environment colonize the cadaver. The composition of microbial communities is complex, and communities of different species interact with each other in succession. In comparison to the complexity of the decay process, the resulting volatile pattern does show some consistency. Therefore, the possibility of an existence of a time-dependent core volatile pattern, which could be used for applications in areas such as forensics or food science, is discussed. Possible microbial interactions that might alter the process of decay are highlighted.

title: A Comparative Analysis of Models for West Nile Virus
abstract: This paper presents a detailed comparative analysis of existing models for predicting and responding to outbreaks of the West Nile virus (WNV). Through interviews with experts in public health, epidemiological modeling and prevention planning, key gaps in existing models are identified and assessed. The results provide further insight into how best to improve WNV response strategies, given the dynamics of established outbreak patterns. Additionally this research applies an innovative method requiring inclusion-exclusion principles from set theory as a mathematical tool to characterize fixed points relevant to controlling transmission duration and amplitude of WNV. Findings also suggest that improved predictive capabilities alone may not be sufficient for effective management; policy makers must consider pricing regimes, environmental factors along with economical incentives for comprehensive engagement by both governmental bodies and local citizens.

title: Serum Diamine Oxidase as a Hemorrhagic Shock Biomarker in a Rabbit Model
abstract: BACKGROUND: In prolonged hemorrhagic shock, reductions in intestinal mucosal blood perfusion lead to mucosal barrier damage and systemic inflammation. Gastrointestinal failure in critically ill patients has a poor prognosis, so early assessment of mucosal barrier injury in shock patients is clinically relevant. Unfortunately, there is no serum marker that can accurately assess intestinal ischemia-reperfusion injury. OBJECTIVE: The aim of this study was to assess if serum diamine oxidase levels can reflect intestinal mucosal injury subsequent to prolonged hemorrhagic shock. METHODS: Thirty New Zealand white rabbits were divided into three groups: a control group, a medium blood pressure (BP) group (exsanguinated to a shock BP of 50 to 41 mm Hg), and a low BP group (exsanguinated to a shock blood pressure of 40 to 31 mm Hg), in which the shock BP was sustained for 180 min prior to fluid resuscitation. RESULTS: The severity of hemorrhagic shock in the low BP group was significantly greater than that of the medium BP group according to the post-resuscitation BP, serum tumor necrosis factor (TNF)-α, and arterial lactate. Intestinal damage was significantly more severe in the low BP group according to Chiu’s scoring, claudin-1, intercellular adhesion molecule (ICAM)-1, and myeloperoxidase expression. Serum diamine oxidase was significantly increased in the low BP group compared to the medium BP and control groups and was negatively correlated with shock BP. CONCLUSION: Serum diamine oxidase can be used as a serological marker in evaluating intestinal injury and shows promise as an indicator of hemorrhagic shock severity.

title: TRAF6 is a novel NS3-interacting protein that inhibits classical swine fever virus replication
abstract: The present article investigates TRAF6 as a novel NS3-interacting protein that has the potential to inhibit classical swine fever virus (CSFV) replication. This study is highly significant due to the devastating economic, agricultural and public health effects of CSFV infections in many pig farming communities worldwide. By understanding how TRAF6’s nucleic acid binding activity restricts viral functions, new opportunities can be opened up for developing therapeutic treatments against this considerable threat. After conducting detailed analysis of its structure-function relationship during the invasion process, it was discovered that TRAF6 prevents CSFV replication by interacting with specific residues of NS3. Consequently, these findings enable further studies into other similarly distinct mechanisms behind certain FAM/RING domain proteins' involvement in responding to RNA viruses like CSFV and provide useful insight into antiviral strategies.

title: Evaluating the predictive performance of malaria antibodies and FCGR3B gene polymorphisms on Plasmodium falciparum infection outcome: a prospective cohort study
abstract: BACKGROUND: Malaria antigen-specific antibodies and polymorphisms in host receptors involved in antibody functionality have been associated with different outcomes of Plasmodium falciparum infections. Thus, to identify key prospective malaria antigens for vaccine development, there is the need to evaluate the associations between malaria antibodies and antibody dependent host factors with more rigorous statistical methods. In this study, different statistical models were used to evaluate the predictive performance of malaria-specific antibodies and host gene polymorphisms on P. falciparum infection in a longitudinal cohort study involving Ghanaian children. METHODS: Models with different functional forms were built using known predictors (age, sickle cell status, blood group status, parasite density, and mosquito bed net use) and malaria antigen-specific immunoglobulin (Ig) G and IgG subclasses and FCGR3B polymorphisms shown to mediate antibody-dependent cellular functions. Malaria antigens studied were Merozoite surface proteins (MSP-1 and MSP-3), Glutamate Rich Protein (GLURP)-R0, R2, and the Apical Membrane Antigen (AMA-1). The models were evaluated through visualization and assessment of differences between the Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve and Brier Score estimated by suitable internal cross-validation designs. RESULTS: This study found that the FCGR3B-c.233C>A genotype and IgG against AMA1 were relatively better compared to the other antibodies and FCGR3B genotypes studied in classifying or predicting malaria risk among children. CONCLUSIONS: The data supports the P. falciparum, AMA1 as an important malaria vaccine antigen, while FCGR3B-c.233C>A under the additive and dominant models of inheritance could be an important modifier of the effect of malaria protective antibodies.

title: Hierarchical graphical model reveals HFR1 bridging circadian rhythm and flower development in Arabidopsis thaliana
abstract: This paper presents a hierarchical graphical model of hybridized relationships between HFR1, circadian rhythm and flower development in Arabidopsis thaliana. Drawing on existing models for plant architecture analysis, we propose a novel multi-level modelling approach for evaluating the integrality of multiple components in complicated systems. The proposed approach was applied to elucidate the complex roles of HFR1 as an intermediary hub traversing between rhythmic control elements – termed Circadian Associating Plastic Gears (CAPGs) – and experimental observations that identified key flowering developmental genes associated with clock function at different points of time. Results revealed numerous unexpected effects including surprising interdependent feedback loops within this integrated network between hormone signalling pathways, systemic enlargement capacities and demographical scaling indices to malleable responses influencing cellular redistributions across strict tempos governed by vegetation processes. This paper highlights a computationally rigorous method to uncover emergent mechanisms providing new insights into the dynamic behaviour underlying these systems as they evolve over cycles of life cycle stages.

title: Current Concepts in Community and Ventilator Associated Lower Respiratory Tract Infections in ICU Patients
abstract: It is widely known that pneumonia (either community acquired or hospital acquired, as like ventilator associated pneumonia (VAP)), is the most frequent type of severe infection and continues to pose a significant burden on healthcare services worldwide. Despite new diagnostic developments, most pneumonia cases continue to be difficult to diagnose clinically, partly due to acquired antibiotic resistance and the lack of a ‘gold standard’ method of diagnosis. In other words, the lack of a rapid, accurate diagnostic test, as well as the uncertainty of the initial etiologic diagnosis and the risk stratification, results in empirical antibiotic treatments. There are significant changes in the aetiology of patients with ventilator associated lower respiratory tract infections (VA-LRTI), which are characterised by a higher incidence of multi drug resistant organisms. Evidence suggests that when patients with VA-LRTI develop organ failure, the associated mortality can be exceptionally high with frequent complications, including acute respiratory distress syndrome, acute kidney injury, and septic shock. Appropriate antibiotic treatments must consider that the present cardiovascular failure seen in patients has a different association with the patient’s mortality. Unlike patients with less severe clinical presentations, who have a higher chance of survival when the appropriate antibiotics are administered promptly, for patients with a severe subtype of the disease, the appropriateness of antibiotic treatment will impact the patient’s outcome to a lesser extent. The present review highlights certain factors detectable at the time of admission that could indicate patients who are at a high risk of bacteraemia and who, therefore, merit more intense therapy and stratified care.

title: Keratinocytes contribute to normal cold and heat sensation
abstract: Keratinocytes are the most abundant cell type in the epidermis, the most superficial layer of skin. Historically, epidermal-innervating sensory neurons were thought to be the exclusive detectors and transmitters of environmental stimuli. However, recent work from our lab (Moehring et al., 2018) and others (Baumbauer et al., 2015) has demonstrated that keratinocytes are also critical for normal mechanotransduction and mechanically-evoked behavioral responses in mice. Here, we asked whether keratinocyte activity is also required for normal cold and heat sensation. Using calcium imaging, we determined that keratinocyte cold activity is conserved across mammalian species and requires the release of intracellular calcium through one or more unknown cold-sensitive proteins. Both epidermal cell optogenetic inhibition and interruption of ATP-P2X4 signaling reduced reflexive behavioral responses to cold and heat stimuli. Based on these data and our previous findings, keratinocyte purinergic signaling is a modality-conserved amplification system that is required for normal somatosensation in vivo.

title: Genipin inhibits rotavirus-induced diarrhea by suppressing viral replication and regulating inflammatory responses
abstract: Rotavirus is the leading cause of acute gastroenteritis among young children worldwide. However, agents specifically designed to treat rotavirus infection have not been developed yet. In this study, the anti-rotavirus and anti-inflammatory effects of genipin, a chemical compound found in the fruit of Gardenia jasminoides, were evaluated. Genipin had an antiviral effect against the human rotavirus Wa and SA-11 strains in vitro, and it inhibited two distinct stages of the viral replication cycle: attachment and penetration (early stage) in pre-treatment and assembly and release (late stage) in post-treatment. Additionally, genipin downregulated nitric oxide synthase and pro-inflammatory cytokines in lipopolysaccharide-stimulated RAW264.7 cells and rotavirus-infected Caco-2 cells. Oral administration of genipin before and after viral infection with the murine rotavirus epidemic diarrhea of infant mice strain led to a reduced duration of diarrhea and faecal viral shedding and to decreased destruction of the enteric epithelium. Genipin could have potential as a natural compound with preventive and therapeutic effects against infection and colitis caused by rotavirus.

title: Estimates of global research productivity in using nicotine replacement therapy for tobacco cessation: a bibliometric study
abstract: BACKGROUND: Tobacco use is a major healthcare problem worldwide. Tobacco smoking remains the most important risk factor for both cancer and heart diseases. This study was initiated due to the lack of published data concerning the real progress in research output in the use of nicotine replacement therapy (NRT) for tobacco cessation. This study was aimed to use bibliometric analysis to estimate the NRT literature indexed in Scopus database at global level. METHODS: Core of the search strategy was the documents that contained specific words or phrases regarding NRT as keywords in the title. Publication output of most prolific countries was adjusted to the gross domestic product and population size. All citations analysis were accomplished on December 22, 2017. RESULTS: A total of 2138 references were retrieved and published from 56 countries, which were published between 1970 and 2016. The USA has the most number of published articles accounted to 986, followed by the UK (312 publications) and then Australia (102 publications), and Sweden (102 publications). No data related to NRT were published from 156 countries. No significant correlation was found between the country population size or 2016 gross domestic product values and the number of publications of the top-10 most prolific countries in the field of NRT (r = − 0.156, P = 0.664; and r = − 0.173, P = 0.632, respectively). Furthermore, there is no correlation between prevalence of tobacco smoking and number of publications of the top-10 most prolific countries in the field of NRT (r = − 0.235, P = 0.514). CONCLUSIONS: The present data reveal a solid mass of research activity on NRT. The USA was by far the predominant country in the amount of NRT-based research activity. NRT-based research activities were low or not available in most countries. The results of this study delineate a framework for better understanding the situations of current NRT research and prospective directions of the research in this field which could be applied for managing and prioritizing future research efforts in NRT research.

title: Identifying the Stroke Mimics
abstract: Individuals presenting with sudden and focal neurological findings are usually suspected to have stroke. However, there are other conditions that can simulate stroke, which are often referred to as stroke mimics. Awareness and understanding these stroke-like disorders are of extreme importance as the treatment of each of them might be variable. We hereby briefly discuss these stroke mimics, common differentials, and key features to differentiate amongst the various causes of acute neurological event. Stroke is one of the neurological emergencies that needs urgent intervention to prevent significant mortality and morbidity. At the same time, it is important to realize the importance of other conditions which may mimic to stroke. In this letter, we aim to discuss a few key features that could probably help to distinguish stroke from mimickers thereby helping emergency doctors, neurologists, and hospitalists in streamlining the correct treatment at the earliest.

title: Role of Fly Cleaning Behavior on Carriage of Escherichia coli and Pseudomonas aeruginosa
abstract: This paper discusses the role of fly cleaning behaviour on the carriage rates of Escherichia coli and Pseudomonas aeruginosa, two bacterial species known to cause a variety of human illnesses. The study examines how flies' movements can reduce the presence these bacteria, which can be found in many different environments including homes, hospitals, food production facilities and elsewhere. Through experimental observation in an outdoor setting, changes were noted between fly cleanings that occurred naturally and those where artificial influence was deployed to enhance or force behaviours related to cleaning events. Results demonstrate that fly activity may play a crucial role in reducing pathogenic microbial populations such as E. coli and P. aeruginosa within any given environment through their capacity for mechanical removal via grooming activities.. In summary, this research demonstrates that while conventional hygienic efforts remain essential towards controlling infection sources at public settings; additional interventions do exist with the potential to further lower transmission risks by taking advantage of natural ecosystems -using fly behaviour- thus making them viable components for biosecurity strategies against disease causing organisms.

title: Effects of a School-Based Physical Activity Intervention for Obesity and Health-Related Physical Fitness in Adolescents With Intellectual Disability: Protocol for a Randomized Controlled Trial
abstract: The prevalence of obesity has increased significantly in people with intellectual disability (ID), leading to an alarming increase worldwide in associated health risks. The current study aims to examine the effects of a school-based physical activity intervention for improving the obesity and health-related physical fitness of adolescents with ID through their participation in athletic activities. Participating students will undertake interventions at two different levels, divided according to their abilities; Starter Level and Advanced level. Additionally, various assessments involving self-appointed trainer mentors along with four months post-intervention measures will be used to compare results pre and post program involvement. A total sample size of forty randomized participants from three schools located around X area who are diagnosed with mild intellectual disability by education professionals or medical doctors is planned for this experiment aiming to address one questions: Does a school based physical activity intervention improve the health related physical fitness parameters among adolescents living with Intellectual Disability? This randomized controlled trial will generate valuable insights into innovative approaches that can promote healthy lifestyles necessary in managing the risk factors associated more commonly now than ever before, within this population group.

title: Severe H1N1-infection during pregnancy
abstract: This article explores the underlying biological mechanisms of severe H1N1-infection in pregnant women and discusses the latest developments for managing this condition. Despite significant advancements in viral recall immunity, Immuno-modulation still proved to have a substantial role in extracting expectant mothers from more serious clinical implications, ranging from pneumonias to even fatalities. Although pandemic influenza infections typically cause uncomplicated illnesses with milder symptoms than seasonal flu epidemics due to priming immunologic memory against past exposure, powerful immune responses can still be triggered during pregnancy which can worsen preexisting conditions and damage sensitive organ systems with potentially devastating effects on both mother and unborn child. The major goals of this study is to understand how current respiratory therapies decrease the severity of virus response while also further elucidating gaps that remain within our medical knowledge, so as better optimize treatment protocols moving forward.

title: Spotted fever rickettsioses causing myocarditis and ARDS: a case from Sri Lanka
abstract: "Spotted fever rickettsioses (SFR) are severe diseases endemic in tropicalsettings, with a high morbidity and mortality. Herein, we report the clinical course of one such case from Sri Lanka causing fatal myocarditis and Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS). A 17-year-old male patient presented to our hospital with persistent fever and respiratory symptoms. Clinical examination revealed low saturation level on room air associated with tachyarrhythmia. As part of his investigations, serum samples were collected which subsequently tested positive for specific antibodies against SFG rickettsiae by immunoblotting method. Histopathological analysis of right ventricular biopsy tissue displayed lymphocytic myocyte infiltration and contraction band necrosis. Despite intensive management support the patient succumbed within 48 hours due to septic shock induced multi organ failure along with cardiogenic shock due to massive cardiac dysfunction."

title: Needs, Gaps and Opportunities for Infectious Disease Research in British Columbia: A Perspective from Population and Public Health
abstract: Infectious diseases continue to be a significant burden on individuals, families and communities in British Columbia. It is imperative to gain an understanding of the scientific needs, gaps, and opportunities that exist with respect to infectious disease research in this province in order to effectively address current public health challenges. This article presents perspectives from Population and Public Health professionals on the needs, gaps and opportunities for better promoting evidence-based knowledge translation across population health initiatives for infectious diseases. An analysis of interviewing data collected from twenty Population and Public Health staff revealed that participants identified three main areas where improvements are needed: access to interdisciplinary research networks; resource procurement; and funding sources specific for developing innovative models of care delivery. Recommendations drawn from these critical insights have been made which can provide policymakers guidance on how best to close existing knowledge gaps while optimizing resources already available within British Columbia’s healthcare system so as to strengthen public health engagement related infectious disease prevention efforts.

title: Diagnosis and Management of Tuberculous Pericarditis: What Is New?
abstract: Tuberculous pericarditis, a cardiac complication of tuberculosis caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, presents as an acute or chronic condition in which the pericardial sac around the heart is inflamed. Despite recent advances in antibiotic treatments and chemotherapy for infection control, this disorder carries a high mortality rate. This comprehensive review aims to discuss recent advances in diagnosis and management of tuberculous pericarditis from both an epidemiological perspective and clinical point view. An analysis of available research will be conducted to assess current understanding on etiology and molecular pathogenesis linked to tuberculous pericarditis progression. The latest approach towards medical interventions including drug regimens such as antimycobacterial agents, adjunctive therapy with corticosteroids, surgery and vaccine strategies against Mycobacterium bovis BCG-induced reactivation will also be discussed herein. Finally outcomes related to patient reported symptoms relevant to quality of life are analyzed along with future direction regarding areas most likely requiring further investigation into effective treatment protocols for this debilitating pathology affecting millions worldwide annually.

title: Powerful Sequence Similarity Search Methods and In-Depth Manual Analyses Can Identify Remote Homologs in Many Apparently “Orphan” Viral Proteins
abstract: The advent of large databases of protein sequences has enabled powerful sequence similarity search approaches to identify distant homologs across different taxa. However, the identification of remote homologs in viral proteins remains a difficult task due to their rapid evolutionary divergence and low conservation relative to cellular proteins. This study outlines how two commonly used algorithms, BLAST and PSI-BLAST searches, were used together with manual analysis strategies for assessing the remote relatedness between “orphan” viral peptides with known protein families across different organisms. The combination of these powerful biological mechanisms allowed for reliable identification and classification of new input sequences into pre-existing well established lineages from virus superfamilies or clusters. Furthermore, this report elucidates that many previously uncharacterized orphan viruses can possess novel conserved domains when subjected to proper sequence comparison techniques coupled with detailed manual annotation methodologies. In total, eighteen putative virally encoded orphans matched known archetypal gene product templates both through computing protocols as well as deep conventional analyses revealing relationships not discernable in basic primary structure exploration methods alone. Powerful Sequence Similarity Search Methods and In-Depth Manual Analyses Can Identify Remote Homologs in Many Apparently “Orphan” Viral Proteins highlights how combining several investigative tactics employed together may broaden the horizons of our knowledge surrounding unknown viral molecules while reinforcing previously thought conclusions on their function or functionality within identified predecessor ancestral family memberships..

title: Bacterial insertion sequences: their genomic impact and diversity
abstract: This paper investigates the genomic impact and diversity of bacterial insertion sequences as part of larger viral gene-host dynamics. Insertion sequences (IS) are mobile genetic elements found in bacteria which comprise anywhere from 2% to 10% of their genomes and have been linked to important events such as horizontal gene transfer, chromosomal rearrangements, virulence factor expression and adaptive mutations. Despite decades worth of research on IS families, it has not yet been firmly established how these mobile DNA fragments contribute to genomic diversity or what role they play in evolutionary adaptation within a bacterial population. In this work we analyze data from published reports concerning IS species present in multiple organisms in light of information obtained by genome sequencing studies in order to gain insights into the overall genomic impact and diversity generated by these elements. We further discuss potential implications for host-virus interactions among microbial species which contain them.

title: Conceptualizing LGBT Stigma and Associated HIV Vulnerabilities Among LGBT Persons in Lesotho
abstract: Social marginalization harms lesbian, gay, bisexual, and transgender (LGBT) persons’ wellbeing in Lesotho. Socio-cultural mechanisms linking LGBT stigma, depression, substance use, and HIV among LGBT persons in Lesotho are understudied. We explore associations between LGBT stigma, mental health stressors, and HIV vulnerabilities among LGBT persons in Lesotho. We conducted in-depth, semi-structured interviews with 46 LGBT persons and six key informants (e.g. healthcare providers). Participants described depression, substance use, and HIV as mutually reinforcing and situated in larger social contexts of stigma. Alcohol use was a stigma coping strategy and a way to build LGBT connections. At the same time, alcohol use elevated HIV vulnerabilities by lowering condom use uptake. Pervasive stigma reinforced barriers to healthcare engagement. Community-led support and services were leveraged to navigate stigma, reduce HIV vulnerabilities, and ultimately improve health. Findings emphasize the key role contexts play in shaping sexual and mental health among LGBT persons in Lesotho.

title: Comprehensive Mapping Antigenic Epitopes of NS1 Protein of Japanese Encephalitis Virus with Monoclonal Antibodies
abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive mapping of the antigenic epitopes of the NS1 protein of Japanese Encephalitis Virus with monoclonal antibodies. The NS1 protein is an important component in the envelope structure of JEV and its expression on infected host cells confers protection from antibody neutralization. Using in silico methodologies culminating in phage display experiments, multiple putative epitopes were identified and mapped onto linear peptide fragments derived from analysis of NS1 sequence data. Monoclonal antibodies generated against each peptide fragment-based conjugate were further utilized to determine relative antigenicity rankings for all predicted epitopes. Results demonstrated that most immunogenic sites are located at short distances within candidate regions encompassing residues 16 - 61, 67 - 112 and 121 - 154, although single non-contiguous amino acid substitutions can result in significant variances between independent results. These findings reveal critical insights into mechanisms involved with recognition by anti-JEV monoclonal antibodies which could enable more effective strategies for viral control or development of vaccines against this virus family.

title: Preparing for pandemics
abstract: Pandemics present unique challenges that can put an immense strain on resources, affecting public health and global economies. This article explores the impact of pandemics and how best to prepare for them in terms of prevention and containment measures. By assessing existing knowledge from experts across a variety of disciplines, this paper outlines practical strategies to mitigate risks associated with future pandemics.

title: A Harm Reduction Approach to Treating Opioid Use Disorder in an Independent Primary Care Practice: a Qualitative Study
abstract: BACKGROUND: Stigma is a barrier to the uptake of buprenorphine to treat opioid use disorder. Harm reduction treatment models intend to minimize this stigma by organizing care around non-judgmental interactions with people who use drugs. There are few examples of implementing buprenorphine treatment using a harm reduction approach in a primary care setting in the USA. METHODS: We conducted a qualitative study by interviewing leadership, staff, and external stakeholders at Respectful, Equitable Access to Compassionate Healthcare (REACH) Medical in Ithaca, NY. REACH is a freestanding medical practice that provides buprenorphine treatment for opioid use disorder since 2018. We conducted semi-structured interviews with 17 participants with the objective of describing REACH’s model of care. We selected participants based on their position at REACH or in the community. Interviews were recorded, transcribed, and analyzed for themes using content analysis, guided by the CDC Evaluation Framework. RESULTS: REACH provided buprenorphine, primary care, and mental health services in a low-threshold model. We identified three themes related to delivery of buprenorphine treatment. First, an organizational mission to provide equitable and low-stigma healthcare, which was a key to organizational identity. Second, a low-threshold buprenorphine treatment approach that was critical, but caused concern about over-prescribing and presented logistical challenges. Third, creation and retention of a harm reduction-oriented workforce by offering value-based work and by removing administrative barriers providers may face elsewhere to providing buprenorphine treatment. CONCLUSIONS: A harm reduction primary care model can help reduce stigma for people who use drugs and engage in buprenorphine treatment. Further research is needed to evaluate whether this model leads to improved patient outcomes, can overcome community stakeholder concerns, and is sustainable. title: Interferon Gene Expression in Sputum Cells Correlates with the Asthma Index Score During Virus-Induced Exacerbations
abstract: This paper reviews the current knowledge on the correlation between interferon gene expression and asthma index score in sputum cells during virus-induced exacerbations. Exacerbating viral infections are a common cause of lower airway diseases, such as asthma, in patients worldwide. However, it is still uncertain if increased interferon gene expression gives rise to an increase in asthma index scores (AIS). The goal of this paper therefore was to provide further insight into potential correlations between interferon gene expression levels and AIS observed during virus-induced exacerbations by exploring data from human studies. Using quantitative real-time PCR technology combined with indirect ELISA assays, we analyzed samples collected from asthmatic individuals aged 5–20 years who were enrolled for respiratory symptom monitoring after influenza vaccination. Results showed that Interferon gamma (IFNγ) was significantly correlated with changes in AIS occurring when bronchospasms worsen due to virus-induced inflammation due to higher production of IFNγ induced by either biological or environmental factors associated with severe respiratory tract infection. title: Recent Reports of Solid-Phase Cyclohexapeptide Synthesis and Applications
abstract: Macrocyclic peptides are privileged scaffolds for drug development and constitute a significant portion of macrocyclic drugs on the market today in fields spanning from infectious disease to oncology. Developing orally bioavailable peptide-based drugs remains a challenging task; however, macrocyclization of linear peptides can be an effective strategy to improve membrane permeability, proteolytic stability, oral bioavailability, and overall drug-like characteristics for this class. Significant advances in solid-phase peptide synthesis (SPPS) have enabled the efficient construction of macrocyclic peptide and peptidomimetic libraries with macrolactamization being performed on-resin or in solution phase. The primary goal of this review is to summarize solid-phase cyclohexapeptide synthesis using the on-resin and solution-phase macrocyclization methodologies published since 2013. We also highlight their broad applications ranging from natural product total synthesis, synthetic methodology development, and medicinal chemistry, to drug development and analyses of conformational and physiochemical properties.

title: Tumour necrosis factor, interleukin-6 and interleukin-10 are possibly involved in Plasmodium vivax-associated thrombocytopaenia in southern Pakistani population
abstract: BACKGROUND: In Pakistan, Plasmodium vivax is endemic causing approximately 70% of the malaria cases. A number of haematological changes, especially thrombocytopaenia have been reported for P. vivax. Several host factors including cell-mediated immune cells, such as IL-1, IL-6 and IL-10 have been documented for P. vivax-induced thrombocytopaenia. However, study on correlation of cytokines and thrombocytopaenia in P. vivax, particularly in patients with severe signs and symptoms has not been reported from Pakistan. METHODS: A case control study to correlate TNF, IL-6 and IL-10 in healthy controls and thrombocytopaenic P. vivax-infected patients (both uncomplicated and complicated cases) from southern Pakistan was carried out during January 2009 to December 2011. One Hundred and eighty two patients presenting with microscopy-confirmed asexual P. vivax mono-infection and 100 healthy controls were enrolled in the study at Aga Khan University Hospital, Karachi. Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) was performed for determination of TNF, IL-6 and IL-10 levels. RESULTS: Out of 182 cases, mild thrombocytopaenia (platelet count 100,000-150,000 mm(3)) was observed in ten (5.5%), moderate (50,000-100,000 mm(3)) in 93 (51.1%), and profound thrombocytopaenia (<50,000 mm(3)) was detected in 79 (43.4%) patients. IL-6 and IL-10 levels were found approximately three-fold higher in the mild cases compared to healthy controls. Two-fold increase in TNF and IL-10 (p < 0.0001) was observed in profound thrombocytopaenic when compared with moderate cases, while IL-6 was not found to be significantly elevated. CONCLUSION: Cytokines may have a possible role in P. vivax-induced thrombocytopaenia in Pakistani population. Findings from this study give first insight from Pakistan on the role of cytokines in P.vivax-associated thrombocytopaenia. However, further studies are required to understand the relevance of cytokines in manifestations of thrombocytopaenia in P. vivax malaria.

title: Convergent antibody evolution and clonotype expansion following influenza virus vaccination
abstract: Recent advances in high-throughput single cell sequencing have opened up new avenues into the investigation of B cell receptor (BCR) repertoires. In this study, PBMCs were collected from 17 human participants vaccinated with the split-inactivated influenza virus vaccine during the 2016–2017 influenza season. A combination of Immune Repertoire Capture (IRC(TM)) technology and IgG sequencing was performed on ~7,800 plasmablast (PB) cells and preferential IgG heavy-light chain pairings were investigated. In some participants, a single expanded clonotype accounted for ~22% of their PB BCR repertoire. Approximately 60% (10/17) of participants experienced convergent evolution, possessing public PBs that were elicited independently in multiple participants. Binding profiles of one private and three public PBs confirmed they were all subtype-specific, cross-reactive hemagglutinin (HA) head-directed antibodies. Collectively, this high-resolution antibody repertoire analysis demonstrated the impact evolution can have on BCRs in response to influenza virus vaccination, which can guide future universal influenza prophylactic approaches.

title: Defining the Range of Pathogens Susceptible to Ifitm3 Restriction Using a Knockout Mouse Model
abstract: The interferon-inducible transmembrane (IFITM) family of proteins has been shown to restrict a broad range of viruses in vitro and in vivo by halting progress through the late endosomal pathway. Further, single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in its sequence have been linked with risk of developing severe influenza virus infections in humans. The number of viruses restricted by this host protein has continued to grow since it was first demonstrated as playing an antiviral role; all of which enter cells via the endosomal pathway. We therefore sought to test the limits of antimicrobial restriction by Ifitm3 using a knockout mouse model. We showed that Ifitm3 does not impact on the restriction or pathogenesis of bacterial (Salmonella typhimurium, Citrobacter rodentium, Mycobacterium tuberculosis) or protozoan (Plasmodium berghei) pathogens, despite in vitro evidence. However, Ifitm3 is capable of restricting respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) in vivo either through directly restricting RSV cell infection, or by exerting a previously uncharacterised function controlling disease pathogenesis. This represents the first demonstration of a virus that enters directly through the plasma membrane, without the need for the endosomal pathway, being restricted by the IFITM family; therefore further defining the role of these antiviral proteins.

title: Genomic Fabric Remodeling in Metastatic Clear Cell Renal Cell Carcinoma (ccRCC): A New Paradigm and Proposal for a Personalized Gene Therapy Approach
abstract: Renal cell carcinoma (RCC) is the seventh most common type of cancer and accounts for 2-3% of all adult malignancies. While recent advancements in targeted therapies have improved patient outcomes, ccRCC remains challenging to treat due to its aggressive metastatic behavior. Recent studies suggest that genomic fabric remodeling plays a key role in promoting tumor progression and treatment resistance in RCC tumors. To investigate this phenomenon further, we conducted a comprehensive genomic profiling analysis on 15 high grade metastatic ccRCC surgically resectedtumors and identified areas of altered gene expression concurrent with disease stage transition and proliferation control genes alterations being significantly impacted during advanced stages of cancer development. Our findings revealed patterns associated with hypermutated genomes resulting from repetitive genome rearrangement leading to changes in transcriptional competition between actively transcribed cellular regions and hypomutated patterns evolving towards increased capture by long range promoters, thus presenting proteomic signatures linked to residual functional heterogeneity even at late stage tumorigenesis. Based on our insights into the underlying mechanism driving metabolic plasticity, we propose machineries regulated through epigenetic mediation could be effective targets for therapeutic interventions aimed at reversing metabolic reprogramming associated with clear cell RCC repertoire remodeling. We discuss a personalized gene therapy approach as a potential innovative clinical strategy for treating patients afflicted with advanced ccRCC tumors.

title: Infection and atherosclerosis: TLR-dependent pathways
abstract: Atherosclerotic vascular disease (ASVD) is a chronic process, with a progressive course over many years, but it can cause acute clinical events, including acute coronary syndromes (ACS), myocardial infarction (MI) and stroke. In addition to a series of typical risk factors for atherosclerosis, like hyperlipidemia, hypertension, smoking and obesity, emerging evidence suggests that atherosclerosis is a chronic inflammatory disease, suggesting that chronic infection plays an important role in the development of atherosclerosis. Toll-like receptors (TLRs) are the most characteristic members of pattern recognition receptors (PRRs), which play an important role in innate immune mechanism. TLRs play different roles in different stages of infection of atherosclerosis-related pathogens such as Chlamydia pneumoniae (C. pneumoniae), periodontal pathogens including Porphyromonas gingivalis (P. gingivalis), Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori) and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV). Overall, activation of TLR2 and 4 seems to have a profound impact on infection-related atherosclerosis. title: Jugular Vein Injection of High-Titer Lentiviral Vectors Does Not Transduce the Aorta—Brief Report
abstract: The cardiovascular system is highly susceptible to transduction of gene-based therapies. Recently, jugular vein injection (JVI) of high titer HIV-derived lentiviral vectors has been investigated as an approach to introduce genes into the heart and other areas in the body with potential therapeutic outcomes. Despite these studies showing considerable promise, no reports have yet demonstrated that such a procedure can also target non-cardiac vessels. To address this knowledge gap, we evaluated JVI of concentrated lentiviral vector were tested on two swine models—one designed to measure transduction efficiency and the other to assess safety profiles—in order to monitor efficacy across all cardiovascular sites including both cardiac muscles and vascular walls utilized for vasculogenesis or angiogenesis treatments. The results showed that although there was evidence for efficient atrial wall transducement through JVI delivery, long distal spread towards aortic structures appeared modestly limited; meaning that current approaches must be modified in order compensate for this technical hurdle so as not reduce efficacy when targeting deep seated organs like liver or kidney which may similarly require direct injection access from within their blood supply systems via veins or arteries respectively. This work serves as an important reminder when considering alternative routes for gene editing therapy delivery: organ specific conditions should always be taken into account before any given technique is applied clinically – ultimately determining long-term effectiveness of future treatments depending upon its application suitability.

title: How to Avoid a No-Deal ER Exit
abstract: The Brexit negotiations have been exceedingly complex for both the United Kingdom and European Union. The complexity of no-deal preparations have now reached a critical point, with potential ramifications looming. How to Avoid a No-Deal ER Exit provides an in depth analysis of how policy makers might be able to counterbalance the uncertainty triggered by these negotiations and secure a successful exit from the EU. Drawing upon several socio-economic perspectives, this article examines best practices at avoiding or minimising any deleterious impacts caused by a no-deal outcome while striving towards an orderly and painless process of transition. Strategic assessment is provided on topics such as preparedness levels, trade management and mitigation strategies which must be responsibly initiated prior to any type of 'no deal' scenario arising. With careful planning there is hope that costly economic losses can be avoided in addition to preventing further fragmentation amongst key stakeholders on either side of the English Channel.

title: Polarity of processes with Golgi apparatus in a subpopulation of type I astrocytes
abstract: The Golgi apparatus has a fundamental role in the management of polarized processes in cells, yet its distribution and regulation within subpopulations of astrocytes have not been well researched. This paper describes an investigation into polarity of cellular processes with Regulator Of G Protein Signaling-10 (RGS10) as a key factor among subpopulation Type I Astrocytes(Ast1). We found that varying expression levels of RGS10 led to unique patterns and dynamics across the population, showing how localized regulation at the level of individual cells plays an important role in establishing optimal strategies for functioning within larger populations. Our findings demonstrate evidence that these events are actively regulated by local parameters such as RGS10 expression suggesting potential areas for further research related to this topic. Additionally, these results provide interesting insight regarding the complex organization and control systems put into place by biological machinery when managing polar processes including those associated with cell growth, development and homeostasis.

title: Involvement of microRNAs in physiological and pathological processes in the lung
abstract: To date, at least 900 different microRNA (miRNA) genes have been discovered in the human genome. These short, single-stranded RNA molecules originate from larger precursor molecules that fold to produce hairpin structures, which are subsequently processed by ribonucleases Drosha/Pasha and Dicer to form mature miRNAs. MiRNAs play role in the posttranscriptional regulation of about one third of human genes, mainly via degradation of target mRNAs. Whereas the target mRNAs are often involved in the regulation of diverse physiological processes ranging from developmental timing to apoptosis, miRNAs have a strong potential to regulate fundamental biological processes also in the lung compartment. However, the knowledge of the role of miRNAs in physiological and pathological conditions in the lung is still limited. This review, therefore, summarizes current knowledge of the mechanism, function of miRNAs and their contribution to lung development and homeostasis. Besides the involvement of miRNAs in pulmonary physiological conditions, there is evidence that abnormal miRNA expression may lead to pathological processes and development of various pulmonary diseases. Next, the review describes current state-of-art on the miRNA expression profiles in smoking-related diseases including lung cancerogenesis, in immune system mediated pulmonary diseases and fibrotic processes in the lung. From the current research it is evident that miRNAs may play role in the posttranscriptional regulation of key genes in human pulmonary diseases. Further studies are, therefore, necessary to explore miRNA expression profiles and their association with target mRNAs in human pulmonary diseases.

title: A molecular cell atlas of the human lung from single cell RNA sequencing
abstract: This article reports the optimization and application of single cell RNA sequencing (SCRS) to assemble a molecular cell atlas of the human lung. This comprehensive research is the first to capture key phenotypic states across all cellular compartments within distinct subpopulations throughout the lung anatomy. SCRS works by analyzing gene expression data obtained from individual cells, facilitating an unprecedented level of resolution in anatomical context. Utilizing this cutting-edge technology, researchers were able to map out landmark gene markers as well as identify points in between which highlighted preserved functional relationships amongst clinically relevant tissues. Additionally, they discovered novel transcriptomic features that could potentially lead to improved understanding and identification of various respiratory disorders and therapies targeting specific diseases associated with them. The study contributes significantly towards providing a thorough overview of human pulmonary biology relevant for basic science and clinical applications alike.

title: The EMERALD (Enabling Mobilization, Empowerment, Risk Reduction, and Lasting Dignity) Study: Protocol for the Design, Implementation, and Evaluation of a Community-Based Combination HIV Prevention Intervention for Female Sex Workers in Baltimore, Maryland
abstract: The EMERALD (Enabling Mobilization, Empowerment, Risk Reduction, and Lasting Dignity) study is an innovative community-based program which aims to provide comprehensive prevention services for female sex workers in Baltimore. This paper presents the protocol for the implementation and evaluation of this intervention. The goal of EMERALD is to combat HIV/AIDS among this population through targeting at-risk behaviors associated with vulnerable circumstances including drug use, intimate partner violence and unstable housing. This project employs individualized risk reduction strategies through client education, linkage to sexual health resources and peer mentoring exercises that aim to promote resiliency and self-efficacy among participants enrolled in the study. Specific objectives include assessing cross-sectional knowledge regarding HIV prevention practices; evaluating changes in treatment adherence following completion of educational interventions; surveying physical safety concerns related to gender parity indices amongst female sex workers; and characterizing maternal health risks across reproductive outcomes such as neonatal mortality rate or stillbirths experienced by exposed mothers during pregnancy. Using a mixed methods approach incorporating qualitative surveys as well as quantitative data on participant behaviors prior to, directly after completing interventions outside the scope of social service outreach platforms such rationale policy advocacy programs delivered from non-governmental organizations versus governmental agencies will give validity to these results. The outcome measures obtained can then be utilized for developing tailored targeted approaches towards serving within high burden populations ultimately providing long term sustainable solutions addressing persistent disparities concerning emerging infectious diseases now affecting U.S inhabitants throughout urban settings nationwide

title: Clinical relevance and impact of Corynebacterium isolation in lower respiratory tract of critically ill patients requiring mechanical ventilation
abstract: PURPOSE: Corynebacterium spp. (C. spp.) is commonly considered as a contaminant in respiratory specimens. No study has ever focused on its clinical relevance in the lower respiratory tract of patients admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU) and requiring mechanical ventilation. The aims were to describe the characteristics of ICU patients with a C. spp. positive deep respiratory specimen, to investigate the impact of C. spp. on the occurrence of pneumonia, and to evaluate the outcomes of these pneumonia. METHODS: We retrospectively included all adult patients admitted to ICU in a 1000-bed University Hospital (2007–2017) who had a C. spp. positive lower respiratory tract specimen at a significant quantitative level. We used clinical, radiological, and microbiological criteria to classify the likelihood of such pneumonia. RESULTS: Among the 31 patients included, acute respiratory failure and postoperative care after major surgery were the main reasons of admission. SAPS II was 47 [34–60]. C. spp. pneumonia was considered as probable, possible and unlikely in 10, 14, and 7 patients, respectively. Fifty-two and 94% of C. spp. strains were sensitive to amoxicillin, and vancomycin/linezolid, respectively. Seventeen patients had a complete course of antibiotic against C. spp. The overall ICU mortality was 58%. CONCLUSION: Corynebacterium spp seems to be responsible for authentic pneumonia in mechanically ventilated patients. It should be considered as clinically relevant when predominantly present in respiratory specimen from patients suspected with pneumonia in ICU, and empirically treated.
