title: Expanding Repertoire of Plant Positive-Strand RNA Virus Proteases
abstract: Many plant viruses express their proteins through a polyprotein strategy, requiring the acquisition of protease domains to regulate the release of functional mature proteins and/or intermediate polyproteins. Positive-strand RNA viruses constitute the vast majority of plant viruses and they are diverse in their genomic organization and protein expression strategies. Until recently, proteases encoded by positive-strand RNA viruses were described as belonging to two categories: (1) chymotrypsin-like cysteine and serine proteases and (2) papain-like cysteine protease. However, the functional characterization of plant virus cysteine and serine proteases has highlighted their diversity in terms of biological activities, cleavage site specificities, regulatory mechanisms, and three-dimensional structures. The recent discovery of a plant picorna-like virus glutamic protease with possible structural similarities with fungal and bacterial glutamic proteases also revealed new unexpected sources of protease domains. We discuss the variety of plant positive-strand RNA virus protease domains. We also highlight possible evolution scenarios of these viral proteases, including evidence for the exchange of protease domains amongst unrelated viruses.

title: The Utility of Diaphragm Ultrasound in Reducing Time to Extubation
abstract:
The timely and successful extubation of mechanically ventilated patients is essential for minimising the trauma and gastrointestinal disturbance associated with mechanical ventilation. Inaccurate assessment of a patient’s tolerance to spontaneous breathing can lead to prolonged intubation, possibly resulting in long-term complications or even death. The Utility of Diaphragm Ultrasound in Reducing Time to Extubation addresses this issue by critically evaluating the effectiveness of diaphragm ultrasound (DUS) imaging for predicting positive pressure ventilation (PPV) tolerance during weaning from mechanical ventilation. This review paper aims to provide an understanding of how DUS affords clinicians the ability to diagnose respiratory muscle function quickly and accurately which could aid in providing an optimal ventilator strategy, allowing safeguarding against intubation-associated atrocities while supporting early recovery. 

This systematic review will explore recent studies on predictors of PPV intolerance that use either end expiratory diaphragmatic displacement surface imaging or transabdominal near real-time sonography, literature search strategies and data collection methods employed where available, as well as any potential drawbacks uncovered throughout such research scope. title: Inhibition of Human Cathepsins B and L by Caffeic Acid and Its Derivatives
abstract: Caffeic acid (CA) and its derivatives caffeic acid phenethyl ester (CAPE) and chlorogenic acid (CGA) are phenolic compounds of plant origin with a wide range of biological activities. Here, we identify and characterize their inhibitory properties against human cathepsins B and L, potent, ubiquitously expressed cysteine peptidases involved in protein turnover and homeostasis, as well as pathological conditions, such as cancer. We show that CAPE and CGA inhibit both peptidases, while CA shows a preference for cathepsin B, resulting in the strongest inhibition among these combinations. All compounds are linear (complete) inhibitors acting via mixed or catalytic mechanisms. Cathepsin B is more strongly inhibited at pH 7.4 than at 5.5, and CA inhibits its endopeptidase activity preferentially over its peptidyl-dipeptidase activity. Altogether, the results identify the CA scaffold as a promising candidate for the development of cathepsin B inhibitors, specifically targeting its endopeptidase activity associated with pathological proteolysis of extracellular substrates.

title: Human Respiratory Syncytial Virus: Infection and Pathology
abstract: This article presents the latest scientific research on Human Respiratory Syncytial Virus (HRSV), its infection and resultant pathology. HRSV is one of the major pathogens circulating among young children, often causing severe respiratory illnesses including bronchiolitis, pneumonia and can even lead to death in some cases. However, beyond understanding clinical manifestations it remains important for scientists to investigate etiological factors associated with this complex pathogen. This review outlines available evidence on molecular biology of HRSV as well as highlighting risk factors associated with severity of infection such as young age and pre-existing illnesses like congenital heart conditions or chronic lung diseases. The findings suggest that further interdisciplinary approaches which implement deep-sequencing methods are essential to elucidate the virulence patterns while developing new treatment modalities accordingly.

title: The exon junction complex core factor eIF4A3 is a key regulator of HPV16 gene expression
abstract: This research paper aims to address the role and importance of core factor eIF4A3 in gene expression regulation, specifically focusing on HPV 16. It summarizes findings from experiments conducted in vitro which investigated the relationship between exon junction complex (EJC), core factor eIF4A3, and HPV16 gene expression. The results observed demonstrated that EJC-dependent repression is associated with a diminished level of both the mRNA transcript and protein generated by HPV16-L2 viral transcriptional activities, through the modulation of eIF4A3 activity. These data suggest that eIF4A3 plays an essential role as a key regulator of HPV16 gene expression.

title: Apoptosis in brain-specific autoimmune disease
abstract: Recent neuropathological studies of experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis have focused attention on the high number of cells in the lesions that show typical morphological features of apoptosis. Surprisingly, it has turned out that the vast majority of apoptotic cells are T lymphocytes and that they actually represent the antigen-specific T-cell population responsible for the induction of the disease. Taken together, these data suggest that clearance of autoimmune inflammation in the nervous system is accomplished by the destruction of the antigen-specific T-cell population within the lesions. This may explain the low level of central nervous system specific T-cell memory formation, as well as previously unexplained phenomena of ‘epitope spreading’, in autoimmune inflammation of the nervous system

title: Effect of overground locomotor training on ventilatory kinetics and rate of perceived exertion in persons with cervical motor-incomplete spinal cord injury
abstract: This abstract examines the effect of overground locomotor training on ventilatory kinetics and rate of perceived exertion (RPE) in individuals with cervical motor-incomplete spinal cord injury (SCI). Modern advances in medical rehabilitation are dedicated to the amelioration of mobility, independence, and quality of life (QoL) for people with SCI. However, understanding what factors contribute to successful utility of such treatments above and beyond restoring basic biomechanical functions remains a research priority. This study uses a randomized controlled trial to investigate the effects of an 8-week course of overground locomotor training protocol on ventilatory kinetics as measured by minute ventilation (VE), breathing frequency (f), oxygen uptake efficiency slope (OUES), work rate relative exhaled volume over one breath ratio?1/min (WRV?1/min) and RPE scores among 53 male participants aged between 18–40 years old post-cervical motor incomplete SCI. It is hypothesized that improvements observed during incremental exercise testing can be attributed to changes in ventilatory function brought about by this form of specialized therapeutic intervention. The results will ascertain whether there are differential implications for persons with long-term SCIs looking towards practical recovery solutions that minimize dependence upon assistive external devices while maximizing personal autonomy through active participation in regular physical activities both indoors and outdoors.

title: Broadly resistant HIV-1 against CD4-binding site neutralizing antibodies
abstract: This paper outlines the implications of broadly resistant HIV-1 against CD4-binding site neutralizing antibodies. While mutations in the envelope glycoprotein (Env) have been known to confer resistance for decades, recent advances in sequencing and computational analysis are enabling insights into molecular changes that lead to an overall decrease in antibody efficacy. A database containing numerous sequences of wild type and mutated Envs was used to study these alterations and find new avenues toward therapeutic immunity. Various statistical models were then employed to characterize trends in binding efficiency between species, as well as their respective vaccines or treatments. The results demonstrate how certain deliberate manipulations can lead to multi-level, widespread protection from specific antibodies, implicating an excitingly novel approach towards enhanced global treatment options against HIV infection and providing insight into future possibilities for vaccine development.

title: Decreasing Chronic Lung Disease Associated with Bubble CPAP Technology: Experience at Five Years
abstract: The research article titled, 'Decreasing Chronic Lung Disease Associated with Bubble CPAP Technology: Experience at Five Years' presents a retrospective review of the use of bubble Continuous Positive Airway Pressure (CPAP) technique in reducing chronic lung disease in five-year surveillance. It has been established that Bubble CPAP technology offers impressive noninvasive ventilation for a variety of respiratory dysfunctions including obstructive sleep apnea and bronchopulmonary dysplasia among neonates. The aim of this study was to investigate the long-term outcome of Neonatal Intensive Care Unit Survivors at 5 years follow up period who had received bubble CPAP treatment from birth till discharge. A longitudinal observational study was conducted on 100 participants born between 2012 – 2016 who were monitored for 5 years post discharge and results showed that the group experienced significant reduction in the incidence, severity and duration of respiratory morbidities due to lower dependence on traditional mechanical ventilators as well as optimization techniques employed by staffs such as air modifications, humidity settings etc.. This research adds further evidence towards understanding effectiveness of bubble CPAP technology in improving quality outcomes related to chronic lung diseases.

title: Nanopore Sequencing Is a Credible Alternative to Recover Complete Genomes of Geminiviruses
abstract: Next-generation sequencing (NGS), through the implementation of metagenomic protocols, has led to the discovery of thousands of new viruses in the last decade. Nevertheless, these protocols are still laborious and costly to implement, and the technique has not yet become routine for everyday virus characterization. Within the context of CRESS DNA virus studies, we implemented two alternative long-read NGS protocols, one that is agnostic to the sequence (without a priori knowledge of the viral genome) and the other that use specific primers to target a virus (with a priori). Agnostic and specific long read NGS-based assembled genomes of two capulavirus strains were compared to those obtained using the gold standard technique of Sanger sequencing. Both protocols allowed the detection and accurate full genome characterization of both strains. Globally, the assembled genomes were very similar (99.5–99.7% identity) to the Sanger sequences consensus, but differences in the homopolymeric tracks of these sequences indicated a specific lack of accuracy of the long reads NGS approach that has yet to be improved. Nevertheless, the use of the bench-top sequencer has proven to be a credible alternative in the context of CRESS DNA virus study and could offer a new range of applications not previously accessible.

title: Tracing the source of influenza A virus zoonoses in interconnected circuits of swine exhibitions
abstract: This article introduces a novel approach to better understanding zoonoses diseases by studying them in the context of interconnected circuits of swine exhibitions. By tracing these transmissions, this research sheds light on new pathways for zoonosis disease emergence and spread, particularly influenza A virus (IAV) infections. Previous works have studied the pathogen biology, transmission capacity and epidemiological features of IAV within pig populations; however, their failure to account for intra-species evolutionary dynamics has resulted in an incomplete understanding of disease mechanisms. By integrating information from multiple sources, this study evaluates strain variation patterns across swine exhibition networks to obtain a more comprehensive assessment of rising risks associated with IAV outbreaks among pigs at all levels – population-level exposures and inter-dam connections among individual farms. The findings suggest potential opportunities for reducing risk through enhanced biosecurity measures during veterinary inspection activities as well as linkages between swine operations across national borders that pose high prevalence rates for cross-population contamination events.

title: The S1 glycoprotein but not the N or M proteins of avian infectious bronchitis virus induces protection in vaccinated chickens
abstract: The S1, N and M proteins, obtained from the nephropathogenic N1/62 strain of infectious bronchitis virus (IBV) by immunoaffinity purification with monoclonal antibodies, were used for immunization of chickens. For all three antigens multiple immunizations were necessary for induction of an antibody response. Protection of chickens vaccinated with the S1 glycoprotein against virulent challenge was demonstrated by the complete absence of virus in tracheas and kidneys of vaccinated chickens. Following four immunizations with the S1 glycoprotein 71% and 86% of chickens were protected at the level of tracheas and kidneys, respectively. Three immunizations with the S1 glycoprotein protected 70% and 10% of chickens at the level of kidney and trachea, respectively. Neither the N nor the M antigen induced protection to a virulent challenge with the nephropathogenic N1/62 strain of IBV after four immunizations. Virus neutralizing, haemagglutination inhibiting and ELISA antibodies were detected in chickens immunized with the S1 glycoprotein and inactivated N1/62 virus, however there was no correlation between the presence of any of these antibodies and protection.

title: Detection of infectious bronchitis virus 793B, avian metapneumovirus, Mycoplasma gallisepticum and Mycoplasma synoviae in poultry in Ethiopia
abstract:
Title: Detection of Infectious Bronchitis Virus 793B, Avian Metapneumovirus, Mycoplasma gallisepticum and Mycoplasma synoviae in Poultry in Ethiopia

This study aims to detect the presence of infectious bronchitis virus 793B (793B-IBV), avian metapneumovirus (aMPV), Mycoplasma gallisepticum (MG) and Mycoplasma synoviae (MS) in chickens reared for egg production in four agro-ecological zones of Ethiopia. The country has a long history of poultry keeping but there is limited knowledge on the occurrence and circulation of these pathogens among chicken flocks. Samples from 291 cloacal swabs were collected between November 2019 to February 2020 covering all major types of poultry production systems used in this region. Real Time PCR was used to determine unknown etiologic agents associated with respiratory or related diseases based on a TaqMan probe multiplex assay targeting the specific species/genotypes. This study will provide insight into the putative role played by respiratory viruses and mycoplasmas as causal agents leading to poor health and productivity losses among backyard chickens kept under different management systems across these regions.

title: Endoplasmic Reticulum Stress Contributes to Helicobacter Pylori VacA-Induced Apoptosis
abstract: This study examines the role of endoplasmic reticulum stress in Helicobacter pylori VacA-induced apoptosis. Dysregulation of endoplasmic reticulum (ER) homeostasis has been reported to induce cell death; however, its contribution to VacA-mediated host cell death remains unknown. H. pylori is an important human pathogen and the principal virulence factor for this bacterium is VacA, a protein that induces apoptotic cell death among numerous non-specific effects on host target cells by causing severe damage in subcellular organelles. As such, our research seeks to determine whether ER stress acts synergistically with VacA in determining the fate of infected cells through vacuolar disruption related pathways that would otherwise prevent damage or limit bacterial growth exacerbating existing injury associated with infection. Through this investigation we wish to address questions regarding: What cellular processes involved in proapoptotic pathways are exacerbated due to changes observed in ER function following VacA exposure? How do these reactions interact with other programmed responses triggered inside target tissue upon exposure to various elements secreted by H. pylori? Our results indicate that ER stress contributes substantially towards progression of Apoptosis cascades resulting from Vaca expression and can therefore provide key insight into understanding complex pathogenic states which are difficult or impossible to replicate outside laboratory conditions due to inherent variability between disease cases affecting typical epidemiological studies attempting similar avenues of inquiry

title: Delayed Antibiotic Prescription by General Practitioners in the UK: A Stated-Choice Study
abstract: Delayed antibiotic prescription in primary care has been shown to reduce antibiotic consumption, without increasing risk of complications, yet is not widely used in the UK. We sought to quantify the relative importance of factors affecting the decision to give a delayed prescription, using a stated-choice survey among UK general practitioners. Respondents were asked whether they would provide a delayed or immediate prescription in fifteen hypothetical consultations, described by eight attributes. They were also asked if they would prefer not to prescribe antibiotics. The most important determinants of choice between immediate and delayed prescription were symptoms, duration of illness, and the presence of multiple comorbidities. Respondents were more likely to choose a delayed prescription if the patient preferred not to have antibiotics, but consultation length had little effect. When given the option, respondents chose not to prescribe antibiotics in 51% of cases, with delayed prescription chosen in 21%. Clinical features remained important. Patient preference did not affect the decision to give no antibiotics. We suggest that broader dissemination of the clinical evidence supporting use of delayed prescription for specific presentations may help increase appropriate use. Establishing patient preferences regarding antibiotics may help to overcome concerns about patient acceptance. Increasing consultation length appears unlikely to affect the use of delayed prescription.

title: The Evaluation of a Health-Based Education and Behavioral Change Retreat on Quality of Life, Physical Activity and Psychosocial Health in Adult Cancer Survivors: An Exploratory Analysis
abstract: Knights Cabin Cancer retreats may represent an ideal opportunity and environment to fill the gap in health education and behavioral change. It is unknown, however, whether the program improves quality of life, physical activity, and psychosocial health. Cancer survivors who enrolled in a retreat completed online questionnaires prior to and 3 months post to assess health-related quality of life, physical activity, and psychosocial variables; perceived stress, depression, and self-esteem. Paired t tests were utilized to compare changes pre and 3 months post the retreat. The majority of the 51 cancer survivors were female with a mean age of 53. The mental component summary of health-related quality of life (p < 0.016) and physical activity score (p = 0.048) was significantly improved at follow-up, while the physical component summary of health-related quality of life was not (p = 0.139). In addition, participants showed an improvement in psychosocial variables of self-esteem (p = 0.016) and depression (p = 0.016) after 3 months but did not show a significant improvement in perceived stress (p = 0.054). Improvements were seen following a Knights Cabin Cancer retreat in mental health-related quality of life and physical activity as well as some psychosocial variables. Further research is needed to evaluate the individual program components and the sustainability of the program in the community.

title: Comparative Effectiveness of Caregiver Training in Mindfulness-Based Positive Behavior Support (MBPBS) and Positive Behavior Support (PBS) in a Randomized Controlled Trial
abstract: This randomized controlled trial aims to evaluate the comparative effectiveness of two behavior support strategies, Mindfulness-Based Positive Behavior Support (MBPBS) and Positive Behavior Support (PBS). The study focused on caregivers as it is believed that they play a major role in helping people with identified challenging behaviors. Outcomes were measured by collecting data including self-reported satisfaction levels amongst the program participants. In total, 80 caregivers were recruited and randomly allocated into either MBPBS or PBS intervention groups over a 4 month period. Findings indicated that while caregiver training in both programs showed positive outcomes overall, there was no significant difference observed between the MBPBS group and the PBS group on any outcome measures. These results indicate that both techniques may be appropriate mechanisms for increasing caregiver knowledge about effective approaches for managing problem behaviors associated of people with disabilities; however more research is needed to determine which method might better promote long-term behavior change and optimize health outcomes for those receiving care from others.

title: Influenza A viruses are transmitted via the air from the nasal respiratory epithelium of ferrets
abstract: Human influenza A viruses are known to be transmitted via the air from person to person. It is unknown from which anatomical site of the respiratory tract influenza A virus transmission occurs. Here, pairs of genetically tagged and untagged influenza A/H1N1, A/H3N2 and A/H5N1 viruses that are transmissible via the air are used to co-infect donor ferrets via the intranasal and intratracheal routes to cause an upper and lower respiratory tract infection, respectively. In all transmission cases, we observe that the viruses in the recipient ferrets are of the same genotype as the viruses inoculated intranasally, demonstrating that they are expelled from the upper respiratory tract of ferrets rather than from trachea or the lower airways. Moreover, influenza A viruses that are transmissible via the air preferentially infect ferret and human nasal respiratory epithelium. These results indicate that virus replication in the upper respiratory tract, the nasal respiratory epithelium in particular, of donors is a driver for transmission of influenza A viruses via the air.

title: Generation of inner ear hair cells by direct lineage conversion of primary somatic cells
abstract: The mechanoreceptive sensory hair cells in the inner ear are selectively vulnerable to numerous genetic and environmental insults. In mammals, hair cells lack regenerative capacity, and their death leads to permanent hearing loss and vestibular dysfunction. Their paucity and inaccessibility has limited the search for otoprotective and regenerative strategies. Growing hair cells in vitro would provide a route to overcome this experimental bottleneck. We report a combination of four transcription factors (Six1, Atoh1, Pou4f3, and Gfi1) that can convert mouse embryonic fibroblasts, adult tail-tip fibroblasts and postnatal supporting cells into induced hair cell-like cells (iHCs). iHCs exhibit hair cell-like morphology, transcriptomic and epigenetic profiles, electrophysiological properties, mechanosensory channel expression, and vulnerability to ototoxin in a high-content phenotypic screening system. Thus, direct reprogramming provides a platform to identify causes and treatments for hair cell loss, and may help identify future gene therapy approaches for restoring hearing.

title: The Obesity Paradox in the Trauma Patient: Normal May not Be Better
abstract: The morbidity and mortality associated with being overweight or obese have been well-documented in the medical literature. However, recent studies of trauma patients have suggested that a paradoxical phenomenon, dubbed ‘the obesity paradox’ may exist—namely, a higher preadmission body mass index (BMI) may be protective against adverse outcomes posttrauma hospitalization. The present study seeks to elucidate the veracity of this phenomenon as it pertains to trauma patients by evaluating whether normal BMI is indeed optimal for these individuals. Through an analysis of data collected from 22494 adult trauma admissions over a period of 10 years, various healthcare utilization models were employed to evaluate the influence of patient BMI on operative intervention needs and length of stay in the absence/presence of comorbidities such as diabetes or chronic lung disease. Results will shine further light on how best to optimize care delivery pathways for all levels within the patient population while maximizing resource efficiency during times when they are most needed.

title: Electrochemical Detection of Serum Antibodies Against Mycobacterium avium Subspecies paratuberculosis
abstract: This paper presents a novel electrochemical immunoassay for the rapid and sensitive detection of antibodies against Mycobacterium avium subspecies paratuberculosis in bovine serum. Paratuberculosis (Johne's Disease) is one of the most economically significant diseases in food-producing animals, causing considerable losses to cattle farmers worldwide due to its long incubation period prior to clinical manifestation. Currently available diagnostic approaches are cumbersome, costly and time consuming. To address these challenges, this research focused on establishing an efficient method based on targeting specific antigens using an electrochemical approach that can detect affected animals even before any signs become visible. The results suggest that such a technique could potentially reduce labor costs and speed up diagnosis while maintaining test accuracy comparable with conventional tests.

title: Optogenetic assessment of VIP, PV, SOM and NOS inhibitory neuron activity and cerebral blood flow regulation in mouse somato-sensory cortex
abstract: This study focuses on the optogenetic assessment of key inhibitory neuron populations combined with cerebral blood flow (CBF) analysis in mouse somato-sensory cortex. Despite extensive investigations into how specific cell from these various regions interact, it is not known if their activities overlap and what effect they have on CBF regulation. Using anesthetized mice for in vivo experiments, we discuss our findings wherein individually targeted somatostatin (SOM), vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP), parvalbumin (PV) and nitride oxide synthase expressing neurons can regulate both local field potential and CBF activity while similar VIP+/ SOM+ cells have a global effect by relieving inhibition of excitatory pyramidal neurons within the same area. Our results suggest that functional relationships exist between these distinct classes of inhibitory neurons as well as localized to distributed effects depending upon the pathway being activated - all essential details necessary for understanding cortical activation dynamics due to neuronal stimulus in this anatomical region.

title: Host Single-Nucleotide Polymorphisms and Altered Responses to Inactivated Influenza Vaccine
abstract: This study aims to explore the relationship between host single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) and altered responses to inactivated influenza vaccine. We will seek to determine whether specific SNPs within the human genome may act as predictors of a weak antibody response or increased infection risk following vaccination. In order to investigate this hypothesis, hundreds of samples from multiple cohorts will be genotyped and analyzed for SNP variation, with corresponding vaccination status evaluated through serological assays evaluating immunologic responses post-vaccination. These results will provide important insights on individual variation in immune responses to vaccines, enabling us to identify those at greater risk for inadequate protection against influenza viruses when administered an inactivated vaccine.

title: Schizophrenia is Associated With an Aberrant Immune Response to Epstein–Barr Virus
abstract: BACKGROUND: Epstein–Barr virus (EBV) is a highly prevalent human herpesvirus capable of infecting the central nervous system and establishing persistent infection. METHODS: We employed solid phase immunoassay techniques to measure immunoglobulin G (IgG) class antibodies to EBV virions and defined proteins in 432 individuals with schizophrenia and 311 individuals without a history of a psychiatric disorder. Western blot testing was performed to document reactivity to specific EBV proteins. Polygenic risk for schizophrenia was calculated from genome sequencing arrays. Levels of antibodies between the groups were compared by multivariate analyses incorporating clinical, genetic, and demographic measures. RESULTS: Individuals with schizophrenia had marked elevations in the levels of antibodies to EBV virions as compared to the control population. Further analyses indicated increased levels of reactivity to EBV-viral capsid antibody (VCA) but not to EBV nuclear antigen-1 (EBNA-1) or to other human herpesviruses. Western blot analysis confirmed increased reactivity to VCA proteins in the group of individuals with schizophrenia and documented a lack of increased levels of antibodies to EBNA-1. Genetic analyses indicated an additive effect of increased levels of antibodies to EBV virions and genetic susceptibility to schizophrenia, with individuals with elevated levels of both type of markers having a greater than 8.5-fold odds of a schizophrenia diagnosis. CONCLUSIONS: Individuals with schizophrenia have increased levels of antibodies to some but not all EBV proteins indicating an aberrant response to EBV infection. This aberrant response may contribute to the immunopathology of schizophrenia and related disorders.

This aberrant response may contribute to the immunopathology of schizophrenia and related disorders.

title: CXCR6 regulates localization of tissue-resident memory CD8 T cells to the airways
abstract: Resident memory T cells (T(RM) cells) are an important first-line defense against respiratory pathogens, but the unique contributions of lung T(RM) cell populations to protective immunity and the factors that govern their localization to different compartments of the lung are not well understood. Here, we show that airway and interstitial T(RM) cells have distinct effector functions and that CXCR6 controls the partitioning of T(RM) cells within the lung by recruiting CD8 T(RM) cells to the airways. The absence of CXCR6 significantly decreases airway CD8 T(RM) cells due to altered trafficking of CXCR6(−/−) cells within the lung, and not decreased survival in the airways. CXCL16, the ligand for CXCR6, is localized primarily at the respiratory epithelium, and mice lacking CXCL16 also had decreased CD8 T(RM) cells in the airways. Finally, blocking CXCL16 inhibited the steady-state maintenance of airway T(RM) cells. Thus, the CXCR6/CXCL16 signaling axis controls the localization of T(RM) cells to different compartments of the lung and maintains airway T(RM) cells.

title: Non-HIV Pneumocystis pneumonia: do conventional community-acquired pneumonia guidelines under estimate its severity?
abstract: This paper analyses the empirical evidence of 'Non-HIV Pneumocystis pneumonia' (NHP) and its clinical implications within community-acquired pneumonia guidelines. NHP is a rare fungal infection caused by colonization of the organism Pneumocystis jirovecii, which has become increasingly common in patients who do not have HIV over recent decades. It often presents with severe respiratory symptoms similar to those associated with bacterial infections; however, it can lead to higher morbidity and mortality than many more commonly acquired pneumonias if not correctly identified or treated promptly. This study explores whether current conventional protocols fail to account for this unusual pathogen adequately, potentially leading clinicians to underestimate the severity of NHP cases in their management approaches. The aim of this research therefore is to shed light on any potential deficits in clinical guidance available for non-HIV related pneumocystic pathogens that should be addressed or further considerated in future reviews..

title: Age-Sensitive T Cell Phenotypes Covary in Genetically Heterogeneous Mice and Predict Early Death From Lymphoma
abstract: We have assessed several age-sensitive indicators of immune status in young (i.e., 6 to 11-month-old) mice of a genetically heterogeneous population to see if these varied in parallel and to determine if one or more of the status indices predicted life span or cancer incidence. We report that the number of memory (i.e., CD44(hi)) T cells within the CD8 subset is correlated with number of memory cells in the CD4 population, and inversely correlated with the number of naive (i.e., CD45RB(hi)) CD4 cells at both 6 and 11 months of age, suggesting that the conversion of naive to memory cells may occur at similar rates in both T cell subsets. Mice that ranked high in the proportion of memory T cells (within the CD4 and CD8 pools) at 6 months of age tended to retain their ranking at 11 months, suggesting that the pace or extent of memory cell formation may be a consistent trait that distinguishes mice at least within a genetically heterogeneous population. Mice that at 6 months of age exhibited high levels ofCD4 or CD8 memory T cells, low levels of naive CD4 cells, or low levels of T cells able to proliferate in response to con a and 1l-2 were found to be significantly more likely than their littermates to die within the first 18 months of life. Cases offollicular cell lymphoma, lymphocytic and lymphoblastic lymphoma, and hepatic hemangiosarcoma were seen within the group of mice dying at early ages. Since each of the prognostic immune indices is characteristically seen in aged mice, we suggest that relatively precocious aging of the immune system may predispose a mouse to early death, particularly from lymphoma

title: Corticosteroid treatment in critically ill patients with severe influenza pneumonia: a propensity score matching study
abstract: PURPOSE: To determine clinical predictors associated with corticosteroid administration and its association with ICU mortality in critically ill patients with severe influenza pneumonia. METHODS: Secondary analysis of a prospective cohort study of critically ill patients with confirmed influenza pneumonia admitted to 148 ICUs in Spain between June 2009 and April 2014. Patients who received corticosteroid treatment for causes other than viral pneumonia (e.g., refractory septic shock and asthma or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease [COPD] exacerbation) were excluded. Patients with corticosteroid therapy were compared with those without corticosteroid therapy. We use a propensity score (PS) matching analysis to reduce confounding factors. The primary outcome was ICU mortality. Cox proportional hazards and competing risks analysis was performed to assess the impact of corticosteroids on ICU mortality. RESULTS: A total of 1846 patients with primary influenza pneumonia were enrolled. Corticosteroids were administered in 604 (32.7%) patients, with methylprednisolone the most frequently used corticosteroid (578/604 [95.7%]). The median daily dose was equivalent to 80 mg of methylprednisolone (IQR 60–120) for a median duration of 7 days (IQR 5–10). Asthma, COPD, hematological disease, and the need for mechanical ventilation were independently associated with corticosteroid use. Crude ICU mortality was higher in patients who received corticosteroids (27.5%) than in patients who did not receive corticosteroids (18.8%, p < 0.001). After PS matching, corticosteroid use was associated with ICU mortality in the Cox (HR = 1.32 [95% CI 1.08–1.60], p < 0.006) and competing risks analysis (SHR = 1.37 [95% CI 1.12–1.68], p = 0.001). CONCLUSION: Administration of corticosteroids in patients with severe influenza pneumonia is associated with increased ICU mortality, and these agents should not be used as co-adjuvant therapy. ELECTRONIC SUPPLEMENTARY MATERIAL: The online version of this article (10.1007/s00134-018-5332-4) contains supplementary material, which is available to authorized users.

title: Transcriptome data reveal conserved patterns of fruiting body development and response to heat stress in the mushroom-forming fungus Flammulina filiformis
abstract: This study investigates the transcriptomic profiles of Flammulina filiformis, a mushroom-forming fungus and model organism in fungal biology. Through the developmentally staged isolation and sequencing of polyadenylated mRNA, we report on genome-wide transcriptome data across multiple samples representing disparate stages in early fruiting body formation. In addition to providing insight into age-dependent gene expression profiles that underpin the morphogenetic processes involved in caspule maturation, further analysis revealed evidence for common transcriptional signatures associated with extreme heat stress response. These findings provide new insights into conserved programs of fruiting body formation as well as temperature sensitivity amongst species belonging to the genus Flammulina. Our results contribute towards our understanding of fungal biology at both developmental and physiological levels, particularly within evolutionary and agricultural contexts.

title: n−3 Polyunsaturated fatty acids and inflammation: From molecular biology to the clinic
abstract: The immune system is involved in host defense against infectious agents, tumor cells, and environmental insults. Inflammation is an important component of the early immunologic response. Inappropriate or dysfunctional immune responses underlie acute and chronic inflammatory diseases. The n−6 PUFA arachidonic acid (AA) is the precursor of prostaglandins, leukotrienes, and related compounds that have important roles in inflammation and in the regulation of immunity. Feeding fish oil results in partial replacement of AA in cell membranes by EPA. This leads to decreased production of AA-derived mediators, through several mechanisms, including decreased availability of AA, competition for cyclooxygenase (COX) and lipoxygenase (LOX) enzymes, and decreased expression of COX-2 and 5-LOX. This alone is a potentially beneficial anti-inflammatory effect of n−3 FA. However, n−3 FA have a number of other effects that might occur down-stream of altered eicosanoid production or might be independent of this effect. For example, dietary fish oil results in suppressed production of proinflammatory cytokines and can modulate adhesion molecule expression. These effects occur at the level of altered gene expression. Fish oil feeding has been shown to ameliorate the symptoms of some animal models of autoimmune disease and to protect against the effects of endotoxin. Clinical studies have reported that oral fish oil supplementation has beneficial effects in rheumatoid arthritis and among some asthmatics, supporting the idea that the n−3 FA in fish oil are anti-inflammatory. There are indications that the inclusion of fish oil in enteral and parenteral formulae is beneficial to patients.

title: Alternating pressure (active) air surfaces for preventing pressure ulcers
abstract:
This study focuses on the novel practice of using active alternating pressure (AP) air surfaces for preventing pressure ulcers. Pressure ulcers, or bedsores, are wounds that form when skin and underlying tissues are under prolonged pressure over a bone or bony prominence. They typically develop in hospitalised patients who remain immobilized for long periods of time, as well as among those with altered mental status, limited mobility and indwelling medical devices such as urinary catheters. 

The effects of AP surfaces on the health outcomes of patients with heightened risk of developing pressure ulcers have been studied before, but their efficacy compared to standard static foam mattresses is still unclear. This paper explores how different patient populations respond to an AP surface system compared to usual care methods applied by healthcare providers in community settings nationwide. To measure this phenomenon more concretely, data was gathered from a diverse group of hospitals across four distinct geographic regions: Midwest/Northeast United States; Central Canada; Southwest United States; Southeast Asia.

title: Demographic profile and outcome analysis of a tertiary level pediatric intensive care unit
abstract: This paper aims to analyze the clinical outcomes and demographic profile of patients admitted in a tertiary-level pediatric intensive care unit (PICU). It describes the epidemiological pattern of paediatric critically ill patients, their demographic data, accompanying family information, morbidity profiles etc. To further explore these findings, we used various statistical methods such as chi square analysis to describe patient characteristics and univariate logistic regression for prediction modeling across different sexes, age groups and presence or absence of associated co-morbidities. Patients’ diagnosis at admission was also assessed along with their hospital course variables; length of stay (LOS), number/type of procedures/ interventions received during PICU stay, duration/costs incurred for adjunct therapies if any etc. Our results revealed some interesting trends regarding the association between mortality risk with respect to variable studied such as sex differences for certain diagnosis types like sepsis or obesity related diseases whereas comorbidities had a definite influence on unfavorable prognosis irrespective of patient’s gender or age group. This study is expected to provide insight into possible factors influencing an ICU setting where one can witness most peculiar cases being managed by competent medical professionals aiming at best possible outcomes under a cost effective environment.

title: Nationwide survey on attitudes and perceived barriers toward provision of pharmaceutical care among final year undergraduate pharmacy students in the United Arab Emirates
abstract: Pharmaceutical care (PC) practice is still limited in the United Arab Emirates. It is crucial to understand pharmacy students’ attitudes and their perceived barriers towards PC provision, to evaluate the effectiveness of theoretical and practical curricula in creating positive attitudes toward PC. This study aims to assess attitudes of final year undergraduate pharmacy students in the United Arab Emirates (UAE), and the barriers perceived by them to practice PC. A cross-sectional survey-based study was conducted in February and March, 2020, involving colleges in UAE offering undergraduate pharmacy programs and having students in their final year. Participants filled a questionnaire covering attitudes’ items, based on the Pharmaceutical Care Attitudes Survey (PCAS), and several perceived barriers. A stratified sample of 193 students participated from six universities, 85% were females, 92.2% and 64.8% completed or engaged in community and hospital pharmacy training respectively, at the time of the study. Attitudes’ items receiving the highest agreement were PC will improve patient health (95.3%), all pharmacists should perform PC (93.3%) and PC would benefit pharmacists (92.7%). However, 44.6% agreed PC is not worth the additional workload. Females showed higher attitudes’ total scores, median (IQR): 55 (51–58) and 52 (49–55.5) for females and males respectively, P = 0.032. Having incomplete courses was also associated with lower scores, median (IQR): 55 (51–58) and 52 (48.5–55.5) for “No” and “Yes” respectively, P = 0.048. Poor image of the pharmacist’s role and lack of private counseling area or inappropriate pharmacy layout were the most perceived barriers, with around 78% agreement. In conclusion, final year undergraduate pharmacy students in the UAE have positive attitudes towards pharmaceutical care. The current curricula may be satisfactory in fostering positive attitudes among students. Poor image of the pharmacist’s role and lack of counseling area or inappropriate pharmacy layout were the main barriers identified, among other barriers.

title: 16S ribosomal RNA sequencing reveals a modulation of intestinal microbiome and immune response by dietary L-theanine supplementation in broiler chickens
abstract: Despite the availability of abundant literature on green tea, studies on the use of L-theanine (an amino acid found only in green tea) as a feed additive in poultry especially broiler are limited. So, this study was conducted to explore the effects of L-theanine on the intestinal microbiome and immune response in a broiler. A total of 400-d-old chicks were randomly divided into four treatment groups (A, B, C, and D) using a complete randomized design. Treatments were as follows: A, control (basal diet); B, basal diet + 100 mg L-theanine/kg diet; C, basal diet + 200 mg L-theanine/kg diet; and D, basal diet + 300 mg L-theanine/kg diet. Mucosal samples from ileum and jejunum of broiler chicken were extracted at 21 and 42 d of age. Extraction of genomic DNA was followed by amplification of V3 and V4 hypervariable regions of 16S ribosomal RNA. After Illumina sequencing, results revealed that treatment with L-theanine significantly increased the population of Lactobacillus in ileum and jejunum as compared to a control group, but the higher population was observed in jejunum at both 21 and 42 d of age. The overall diversity of the jejunum microbiome in the treatment group was significantly lower than that of the ileum and control group (P < 0.05). Results of this study revealed that mRNA expression of TLRs (TLR-2 and TLR-4) and cytokines (TNF-α, IFN-γ, and IL-2) was decreased in response to treatment with L-theanine. Moreover, the negative correlation of abundance of Lactobacillus was observed with expression of IL-2 and IFN-γ in the intestine and these effects were highly significant (P < 0.01). In summary, our finding revealed that dietary supplementation of L-theanine exhibited a positive influence on intestinal bacteria by supporting beneficial microbes like Lactobacillus while decreasing harmful microbes like Clostridium.

title: Role of L-type Ca2+ channels in iron transport and iron-overload cardiomyopathy
abstract: This article examines the impact of L-type calcium channels on iron transport, and subsequently its involvement in cardiomyopathy due to iron overload. A growing body of evidence continues to emerge that has shed light into how these ion channels modulate pathways related to cell membrane hyperpolarization and how this relates to cellular movement of essential ions such as iron. By uncovering the biomolecular mechanisms behind L-type Ca2+ exerting its biological effects on cardiac function, researchers can identify crucial drug target molecules for restoring homeostasis, thereby preventing further damage caused by iron-overload cardiomyopathy. This paper aims to overview current research findings associated with these two topics, contextualizing them within a clinical perspective in order to reinforce their importance while discussing potential therapeutic strategies that could potentially be used in attempts at treating this debilitating condition.

title: Discovery and Genomic Characterization of a Novel Ovine Partetravirus and a New Genotype of Bovine Partetravirus
abstract: Partetravirus is a recently described group of animal parvoviruses which include the human partetravirus, bovine partetravirus and porcine partetravirus (previously known as human parvovirus 4, bovine hokovirus and porcine hokovirus respectively). In this report, we describe the discovery and genomic characterization of partetraviruses in bovine and ovine samples from China. These partetraviruses were detected by PCR in 1.8% of bovine liver samples, 66.7% of ovine liver samples and 71.4% of ovine spleen samples. One of the bovine partetraviruses detected in the present samples is phylogenetically distinct from previously reported bovine partetraviruses and likely represents a novel genotype. The ovine partetravirus is a novel partetravirus and phylogenetically most related to the bovine partetraviruses. The genome organization is conserved amongst these viruses, including the presence of a putative transmembrane protein encoded by an overlapping reading frame in ORF2. Results from the present study provide further support to the classification of partetraviruses as a separate genus in Parvovirinae.

abstract: This article examines the increasing occurrence of urbanization, and its consequences on the way people live and work. Through empirical data collection and analysis utilising a unique multi-dimensional framework, it will investigate how these complex factors influence the behaviour of urbanites today.

title: Molecular Drivers of Platelet Activation: Unraveling Novel Targets for Anti-Thrombotic and Anti-Thrombo-Inflammatory Therapy
abstract: Cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) are the leading cause of death globally—partly a consequence of increased population size and ageing—and are major contributors to reduced quality of life. Platelets play a major role in hemostasis and thrombosis. While platelet activation and aggregation are essential for hemostasis at sites of vascular injury, uncontrolled platelet activation leads to pathological thrombus formation and provokes thrombosis leading to myocardial infarction or stroke. Platelet activation and thrombus formation is a multistage process with different signaling pathways involved to trigger platelet shape change, integrin activation, stable platelet adhesion, aggregation, and degranulation. Apart from thrombotic events, thrombo-inflammation contributes to organ damage and dysfunction in CVDs and is mediated by platelets and inflammatory cells. Therefore, in the past, many efforts have been made to investigate specific signaling pathways in platelets to identify innovative and promising approaches for novel antithrombotic and anti-thrombo-inflammatory strategies that do not interfere with hemostasis. In this review, we focus on some of the most recent data reported on different platelet receptors, including GPIb-vWF interactions, GPVI activation, platelet chemokine receptors, regulation of integrin signaling, and channel homeostasis of NMDAR and PANX1.

title: Quiescent stem cell marker genes in glioma gene networks are sufficient to distinguish between normal and glioblastoma (GBM) samples
abstract: The article, titled ‘Quiescent stem cell marker genes in glioma gene networks are sufficient to distinguish between normal and glioblastoma (GBM) samples’ investigates the identification of quiescent genetic markers that differentiate normal from malignant gliomas. Quiescent state has become increasingly important in cancer research due to its correlation with drug resistance and hyposensitivity when used for treatment purposes. Moreover, it is necessary to understand the phenotypic characteristics between different states of tissue or tumors - those developing itself slowly without active proliferation versus a much more aggressive behavior with cells rapidly proliferating and invading neighboring tissues - which can initiate oncogenesis processes leading to advanced malignancy grades such as GBM. This study applies an integrative bioinformatics pipeline using 454 sequencing data generated by exon expression arrays and identified potential quiescence-specific gene networks among non-neoplastic cells comparatively with pathological types related to brain tumors. Our results demonstrate a higher number of targetable candidate biomarkers specific for low-grade gliomas than say GBM, suggesting that this is not just exclusive for these grade IV tumors but rather evolve along the tumor stages providing valuable therapeutic implications for early detection strategies. title: Ghost guns: spookier than you think they are
abstract: The proliferation of 'ghost guns' is an increasingly alarming issue in the U.S., vexing law enforcement agencies through its loosely regulated and untraceable nature. This paper sets out to analyze how the availability of such firearms has raised public safety concerns, and proposes potential policy interventions to adequately address this problem. Understanding the implications of ghost guns as they relate to gun violence prevention will be crucial for policymakers seeking effective regulatory measures on gun control.

title: A conjugated mTOR/MEK bifunctional inhibitor as potential polypharmacological anticancer agent: the prototype compound discovery
abstract: mTOR/MEK bifunctional inhibitors have the potential to surmount the drug resistance aroused from cross talk between PI3K/Akt/mTOR (PAM) and Ras/MEK/ERK pathways. Herein, we report the discovery of a conjugated dual-targeted molecule, compound 13, as the prototype mTOR/MEK bifunctional inhibitor. It exhibited moderately high inhibitory activity against mTOR and MEK1 with IC(50) values of 0.19 μM and 0.98 μM, respectively. In particular, it displayed attractive antiproliferative activity against both A549 (GI(50) = 4.66 μM) and HCT116 (GI(50) = 5.47 μM) cell lines. To our knowledge, it has been the first example of a conjugated mTOR/MEK bifunctional inhibitor. In addition, from this proof-of-principle study, it has become evident that the single-agent dual inhibition of mTOR and MEK can be fulfilled via covalently attaching mTOR kinase inhibitor to an allosteric MEK inhibitor.

title: Utilization of arylaliphatic nitriles by haloalkaliphilic Halomonas nitrilicus sp. nov. isolated from soda soils
abstract: An enrichment culture from saline soda soils, using acetate as carbon and energy source and 2-phenylpropionitrile as nitrogen source (PPN) at pH 10, resulted in the isolation of strain ANL-αCH3. The strain was identified as a representative of the genus Halomonas in the Gammaproteobacteria. The bacterium was capable of PPN utilization as a nitrogen source only, while phenylacetonitrile (PAN) served both as carbon, energy and nitrogen source. This capacity was not described previously for any other haloalkaliphilic bacteria. Apart from the nitriles mentioned above, resting cells of ANL-αCH3 also hydrolyzed mandelonitrile, benzonitrile, acrylonitrile, and phenylglycinonitrile, presumably using nitrilase pathway. Neither nitrile hydratase nor amidase activity was detected. The isolate showed a capacity to grow with benzoate and salicylate as carbon and energy source and demonstrated the ability to completely mineralize PAN. These clearly indicated a potential to catabolize aromatic compounds. On the basis of unique phenotype and distinct phylogeny, strain ANL-αCH3 is proposed as a novel species of the genus Halomonas—Halomonas nitrilicus sp. nov. title: Different Blood Cell-Derived Transcriptome Signatures in Cows Exposed to Vaccination Pre- or Postpartum
abstract: This research study investigates Different Blood Cell-Derived Transcriptome Signatures in Cows Exposed to Vaccination Pre- or Postpartum. It has been established that there are differences in the immunological response of cows dependent on when vaccination is administered, either pre- or postpartum. title: Pulmonary Toxoplasmosis, a Rare but Severe Manifestation of a Common Opportunistic Infection in Late HIV Presenters: Report of Two Cases
abstract: Pulmonary toxoplasmosis is rare, particularly in the era of highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART). Here, we describe two severe cases in patients not known to be HIV-infected. In both patients, early diagnosis and therapy led to a favourable outcome. Pulmonary toxoplasmosis should be considered in the differential diagnosis in potentially HIV-infected patients with respiratory symptoms.

title: Membrane Transporters for Amino Acids as Players of Cancer Metabolic Rewiring
abstract: This article examines the role of membrane transporters for amino acids as players in cancer metabolic rewiring. As difficult-to-treat forms and metastatic stages of cancers develop, these altered cellular environments lead to increased nutrient demands by tumor cells. Recent evidence indicates that membrane transporters involved in the uptake and metabolism of essential nutrients have been observed to be upregulated within tumorigenic contexts. Altered expression profiles, roles and regulation of membrane transporter proteins has broadened our understanding of their involvement within oncogenic pathways. This review will explore how these changes provide vital sources of energy to tumors, as well as focus on potential strategies targeting them as innovative options for anticancer therapy while considering side effects and implications associated with current treatments that target putative biomarkers or metabolic pathways employed by cancer cells.

title: Th17 profile in COPD exacerbations
abstract: COPD is characterized by an ongoing inflammatory process of the airways that leads to obstruction or limitation of airflow. It is mainly associated with exposure to cigarette smoke. In addition, it is considered, at present, a serious public health problem, ranking fourth in mortality worldwide. Many cells participate in the pathophysiology of COPD, the most important are neutrophils, macrophages and CD4+ and CD8+ T cells. Neutrophil migration to the inflammation area could be mediated largely by cytokines related to CD4+ Th17 lymphocytes, because it has been shown that IL-17A, IL-17F and IL-22 act as inducers for CXCL8, CXCL1, CXCL5, G-CSF, and GM-CSF secretion by epithelial cells of the airways. The aims of these molecules are differentiation, proliferation and recruitment of neutrophils. Furthermore, it is believed that CD4+ lymphocytes Th17 may be involved in protection against pathogens for which Th1 and Th2 are not prepared to fight. In COPD exacerbations, there is an increased cellularity in the lung region and respiratory tract. Therefore, the increase in the number of neutrophils and macrophages in the airways and the increase in proinflammatory cytokines are directly related to the severity of exacerbations and that is the importance of the functions of Th17 profile in this entity.

title: Identification of complement-related host genetic risk factors associated with influenza A(H1N1)pdm09 outcome: challenges ahead
abstract: This article presents findings from a study on the identification of host genetic risk factors related to the outcome of influenza A(H1N1)pdm09, and suggests potential solutions to current challenges. During this investigation, data gathered was analysed in order to uncover associations between host factors and severity outcomes associated with infection by Influenza A(H1N1)pdm09. As such, identifying complement-related genetic risk markers could provide a novel approach for predicting propensity towards severe and life threatening infection due to influenza virus subtype pandemics. The implications of these insights are discussed along with current limitations in research on this topic that need further attention for future research initiatives.

title: Protocol for an ‘efficient design’ cluster randomised controlled trial to evaluate a complex intervention to improve antibiotic prescribing for CHIldren presenting to primary care with acute COugh and respiratory tract infection: the CHICO study
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Respiratory tract infections (RTIs) in children are common and present major resource implications for primary care. Unnecessary use of antibiotics is associated with the development and proliferation of antimicrobial resistance. In 2016, the National Institute for Health Research (NIHR)-funded ‘TARGET’ programme developed a prognostic algorithm to identify children with acute cough and RTI at very low risk of 30-day hospitalisation and unlikely to need antibiotics. The intervention includes: (1) explicit elicitation of parental concerns, (2) the results of the prognostic algorithm accompanied by prescribing guidance and (3) provision of a printout for carers including safety netting advice. The CHIldren’s COugh feasibility study suggested differential recruitment of healthier patients in control practices. This phase III ‘efficiently designed’ trial uses routinely collected data at the practice level, thus avoiding individual patient consent. The aim is to assess whether embedding a multifaceted intervention into general practitioner (GP) practice Information Technology (IT) systems will result in reductions of antibiotic prescribing without impacting on hospital attendance for RTI. METHODS AND ANALYSIS: The coprimary outcomes are (1) practice rate of dispensed amoxicillin and macrolide antibiotics, (2) hospital admission rate for RTI using routinely collected data by Clinical Commissioning Groups (CCGs). Data will be collected for children aged 0–9 years registered at 310 practices (155 intervention, 155 usual care) over a 12-month period. Recruitment and randomisation of practices (using the Egton Medical Information Systems web data management system) is conducted via each CCG stratified for children registered and baseline dispensing rates of each practice. Secondary outcomes will explore intervention effect modifiers. Qualitative interviews will explore intervention usage. The economic evaluation will be limited to a between-arm comparison in a cost–consequence analysis. ETHICS AND DISSEMINATION: Research ethics approval was given by London-Camden and Kings Cross Research Ethics Committee (ref:18/LO/0345). This manuscript refers to protocol V.4.0. Results will be disseminated through peer-reviewed journals and international conferences. TRIAL REGISTRATION NUMBER: ISRCTN11405239.

title: The cGAS–STING pathway as a therapeutic target in inflammatory diseases
abstract: The cGAS–STING signalling pathway has emerged as a key mediator of inflammation in the settings of infection, cellular stress and tissue damage. Underlying this broad involvement of the cGAS–STING pathway is its capacity to sense and regulate the cellular response towards microbial and host-derived DNAs, which serve as ubiquitous danger-associated molecules. Insights into the structural and molecular biology of the cGAS–STING pathway have enabled the development of selective small-molecule inhibitors with the potential to target the cGAS–STING axis in a number of inflammatory diseases in humans. Here, we outline the principal elements of the cGAS–STING signalling cascade and discuss the general mechanisms underlying the association of cGAS–STING activity with various autoinflammatory, autoimmune and degenerative diseases. Finally, we outline the chemical nature of recently developed cGAS and STING antagonists and summarize their potential clinical applications.

title: Enhancement of encephalomyeloradiculitis in mice sensitized with spinal cord tissue and infected with lactate dehydrogenase-elevating virus()
abstract: C57BR/cdJ mice develop encephalomyeloradiculitis following peripheral inoculation of the C strain of lactate dehydrogenase-elevating virus (LDV-C). We investigated the effect of subcutaneous administration of syngeneic spinal cord homogenate mixed with phosphate buffered saline or emulsified in complete or incomplete Freund's adjuvant 1 week before or after inoculation of LDV-C on the incidence and severity of central nervous system lesions. C57BR/cdJ mice developed an acute histological allergic encephalomyelitis when given 2 weekly sensitizing injections of homogenate in complete Freund's adjuvant. When peripheral inoculation of LDV-C was substituted for one of the two sensitizing injections, a higher percentage of mice developed lesions, and the lesions were more severe and persisted for much longer periods of time. This same lesion-enhancing effect was not observed if the mice were sensitized with homogenate suspended in buffer or emulsified in incomplete Freund's adjuvant. Interestingly, mice sensitized with complete Freund's adjuvant alone before or after infection with LDV-C also developed intense central nervous system lesions, suggesting that the mycobacterial component of the adjuvant was the critical element in enhancing the lesions.

title: Common Variants in CDKN2B-AS1 Associated with Optic-Nerve Vulnerability of Glaucoma Identified by Genome-Wide Association Studies in Japanese
abstract: This article presents a genome-wide association study to identify common variants in CDKN2B-AS1, an antisense non-coding RNA that maps to the adjacent intron of the cyclin dependent kinase inhibitor 2B (CDKN2B) gene and is associated with optic nerve vulnerability in glaucoma. The comprehensive investigation was conducted among Japanese subjects and included diagnosis of 223 individuals with primary open angle glaucoma (POAG), 620 control participants from Japan Biobank, as well as 300 additional healthy controls from a US cohort. Single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) reported to associate Glaucoma were included for verification of genetic loci for POAG risk. Genotyping revealed significant association between one SNP rs7221196 on chromosome 6p21 and POAG susceptibility compared to both Japanese ethnically matched and ethnically diverse controls; however, other SNPs previously suggested to be involved in Glaucoma exacebration were not confirmed by this study. These results suggest that implications regarding optic nerve vulnerability in POAG may differ depending on ethnic background, which could prove valuable in future clinical applications specifically targeting Asian populations at risk for glaucomatous neovascularization.

title: Role of reactive oxygen species in biological processes
abstract: The article presents an overview of the intricate role reactive oxygen species (ROS) play in biological processes. ROS are a class of ubiquitous, sometimes harmful, molecules that have molecular structures capable of interacting with other cellular components such as nucleic acids, proteins and lipids. This article looks at recent findings suggesting the interconnectivity between multiple pathways generating ROS and its influence on several biological activities like cell growth, development and gene transcription control. Several experiments using antioxidants to counteract ROS activity suggest potential therapeutic applications for disease treatment like cancers or chronic physical disorders linked to oxidative stress. The aim is to gain insight into how cells use oxidative reactions for their own benefit and thus limit deleterious consequences associated with too much ROS formation in order to optimize some cellular functions.

title: Integrating food security into public health and provincial government departments in British Columbia, Canada
abstract: This article explores the advantages of integrating food security into public health and provincial government departments in British Columbia, Canada. Food insecurity is a major problem with many provinces suffering from an increased prevalence of malnutrition, which can cause impaired cognitive development and severe physical illnesses that carry long-term consequences. Extractive industries such aslogging and fishing are two crucial sectors for the province, yet they rarely incorporate sustainable practices or promote social equity such as adequate access to nutritional foods in remote communities. To address this issue, this paper proposes integration of food security into existing public health policies designed by provincial governments across BC and creates recommendations on how it can be implemented at a community level. Drawing from interviews and surveys within select municipalities regarding perceptions on how local economies impact community nutrition initiatives as well as reports about current infrastructure around food supply chains will provide valuable insight for improving legislations targeting these issues in their respective regions. Overall, this investigation strives to complete a mixed method evaluation providing beneficial ideas when incorporating food security programs throughout BC while highlighting existing knowledge gaps so that they may be addressed more effectively overall.

title: Study protocol of the Edinburgh and Lothian Virus Intervention Study in Kids: a randomised controlled trial of hypertonic saline nose drops in children with upper respiratory tract infections (ELVIS Kids)
abstract:
This study protocol outlines the rationale and methodology of the Edinburgh and Lothian Virus Intervention Study in Kids (ELVIS Kids) - a double-blinded randomised controlled trial studying the efficacy of hypertonic saline nose drops in treating acute upper respiratory tract infections in children. The primary objective is to evaluate whether treatment with hypertonic saline solution improves symptom resolution time compared to placebo, as well as related clinical outcomes such as number of additional medical consultations required for recurrent illness, medication use, hospitalisations and adverse events. 

Upper respiratory tract viral infections are very common illnesses among young children experiencing high levels of morbidity worldwide. However, there is limited guidance from current evidence on non-antibiotic interventions that could effectively treat or prevent them and reduce associated healthcare costs. Hypertonic saline nasal drops have shown potential for improving symptoms acutely but remain underinvestigated due to lack of large-scale research studies testing their efficacy within the paediatric population. Therefore, the ELVIS Kids trial aims to fill this gap by collecting enough data through robust methods following Standard Protocol Items: Recommendations for Interventional Trials (SPIRIT) guidelines.

title: The Impact and Control of Emerging and Re-Emerging Viral Diseases in the Environment: An African Perspective
abstract: This paper presents a unique African perspective on the impact and control of emerging and re-emerging viral diseases in the environment. Contextualizing this topical issue, most notably in relation to developments over recent decades, is timely; numerous virus types have emerged as human health threats since 2000 through pathogens such as Ebola, Influenza A (H1N1), Rift Valley Fever and MERS CoV are now present across different continents due to globalization. Moreover, it is well known that environmental conditions can significantly influence disease emergence or re-emergence yet there remains a lack of understanding about how various ecological parameters interact with particular viruses within an environmentally threatened continent. With Africa having suffered from devastating outbreaks such as HIV/AIDS and other long standing health concerns such as Yellow Fever it has been seized upon by many avenues for international collaboration into infectious disease research initiatives around controlling novel epidemics which influence local communities hugely. Thus, this article will examine relevant case studies including risk assessments and evaluate potential control strategies implemented at both local and global levels using multi-disciplinary approaches to better comprehend the component factors involved in safeguarding against acute disease development while preserving biodiversity on the continent.

title: Production, Characterization and Applications for Toxoplasma gondii-Specific Polyclonal Chicken Egg Yolk Immunoglobulins
abstract: BACKGROUND: Toxoplasma gondii may cause abortions, ocular and neurological disorders in warm-blood hosts. Immunized mammals are a wide source of hyperimmune sera used in different approaches, including diagnosis and the study of host-parasite interactions. Unfortunately, mammalian antibodies present limitations for its production, such as the necessity for animal bleeding, low yield, interference with rheumatoid factor, complement activation and affinity to Fc mammalian receptors. IgY antibodies avoid those limitations; therefore they could be an alternative to be applied in T. gondii model. METHODOLOGY/PRINCIPAL FINDINGS: In this study we immunized hens with soluble tachyzoite antigens of T. gondii (STAg) and purified egg yolk antibodies (IgY) by an inexpensive and simple method, with high yield and purity degree. IgY anti-STAg antibodies presented high avidity and were able to recognize a broad range of parasite antigens, although some marked differences were observed in reactivity profile between antibodies produced in immunized hens and mice. Interestingly, IgY antibodies against Neospora caninum and Eimeria spp. did not react to STAg. We also show that IgY antibodies were suitable to detect T. gondii forms in paraffin-embedded sections and culture cell monolayers. CONCLUSIONS/SIGNIFICANCE: Due to its cost-effectiveness, high production yield and varied range of possible applications, polyclonal IgY antibodies are useful tools for studies involving T. gondii.

METHODOLOGY/PRINCIPAL FINDINGS: In this study we immunized hens with soluble tachyzoite antigens of T. gondii (STAg) and purified egg yolk antibodies (IgY) by an inexpensive and simple method, with high yield and purity degree. IgY anti-STAg antibodies presented high avidity and were able to recognize a broad range of parasite antigens, although some marked differences were observed in reactivity profile between antibodies produced in immunized hens and mice. Interestingly, IgY antibodies against Neospora caninum and Eimeria spp. did not react to STAg. We also show that IgY antibodies were suitable to detect T. gondii forms in paraffin-embedded sections and culture cell monolayers. CONCLUSIONS/SIGNIFICANCE: Due to its cost-effectiveness, high production yield and varied range of possible applications, polyclonal IgY antibodies are useful tools for studies involving T. gondii.

title: Incapacitating pain from Tenofovir Induced Hypophosphatemic Osteomalacia in a Hemophilia Patient – A Case Report
abstract: This article is a case study of an uncommon medical phenomenon, focused on the debilitating pain suffered by an individual with hemophilia as a result of Tenofovir-induced hypophosphatemic osteomalacia. A 19-year-old male patient presented to the emergency department with five months of progressively worsening lower back and limb pain, impaired mobility and decreased appetite. Through physical examination and laboratory tests, it was determined that this patient had developed Tenofovir induced hypophosphatemic osteomalacia due to his prophylactic treatment against HIV positive status. This highlights the importance of timely identification in at risk populations such as individuals with coagulopathies like hemophilia who are known to have numerous drug interactions which can lead to upregulation of unrecognized comorbidities such as hypophosphatemia associated bone disease. We discuss management strategies for this rare but serious condition, including calcium supplementation, adjustment in medication dosages or alternative medications when practicable and emphasize the need for close clinical follow ups in these patients to avoid similar issues arising again in future cases.

title: A Neuron-Specific Antiviral Mechanism Prevents Lethal Flaviviral Infection of Mosquitoes
abstract: The flaviviruses – a group of viruses that includes the mosquito-borne Zika, dengue and West Nile virus (WNV) – represent one of the most significant public health threats worldwide. As they endanger both human and animal species, there is an urgent need to identify effective antiviral strategies that can prevent infection. In this study, we investigated a previously unrecognized neuron-specific antipathogenic mechanism in mosquitoes, which successfully prevents WNV replication in vivo and thus limits transmission of the virus. We used immunofluorescence staining techniques and multiple analyses to detect cell development changes at several key stages during WNV infection in mosquitos’ nervous systems. Our research revealed direct evidence for a highly specific pathway involving subsets of neurons that actively restrict Lethal Flaviviral Infection from mosquitos through molecular reorganization to stop further production and spread of variations within their cells' genetic material.  This mechanism was found not only to protect against lethal infections but also demonstrate cross-resistance among different species of flavivirus as demonstrated by our data analysis with such information potentially leading us closer towards developing better targeted antiviral treatments for humans or animals affected by these diseases caused by WNVs.

title: Effects of a Clinical Simulation Course about Basic Life Support on Undergraduate Nursing Students’ Learning
abstract:
This study investigates the efficacy of a clinical simulation course about Basic Life Support (BLS) provided to undergraduate nursing students. The main objective was to assess the impact on learning through a comparison between pre-test and post-test results from participants. A cohort sample of 127 full-time university nursing students was recruited for this study, which took place over three weeks in September 2018 at a public institution in Northern England. Through questionnaires and performance tests, the research team quantitatively assessed any changes experienced by students after receiving BLS training via simulation scenarios - incorporating techniques such as tracheal intubation, chest compression, ventilation with bag valve mask (BVM), correct placement of an automated external defibrillator pad (AED), and other specific practices associated with basic life support interventions. By comparing pre vs post intervention scores on various evaluation measures, results showed that the simulation course was effective in improving student’s knowledge and practical skills related to BLS interventions.
