title: Use of macromolecular assemblies as expression systems for peptides and synthetic vaccines
abstract: The past decade has witnessed the development of numerous systems for the presentation of antigens on the surface of self-assembling macromolecules. Although the sites for insertion were initially chosen empirically, the determination of the three-dimensional structures of a number of carrier macromolecules has enabled structure-based insertional mutagenesis to be used increasingly. Furthermore, it is now feasible to determine the structure of an inserted sequence as presented in a heterologous environment, making it possible to correlate the detailed structure of a peptide with its immunological properties.

title: Linkage and independence of AIDS and kaposi disease: The interaction of human immunodeficiency virus and some coagents
abstract: Through epidemiological considerations we conclude that full-blown AIDS may occur only if the index patient is infected by the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) and, in addition, by some other infectious coagent. Since the dynamical behaviour of the spread of AIDS cases with manifestation of Kaposi's sarcoma differs fundamentally from that of the non-Kaposi cases, we conjecture that two independent coagents (together with HIV) are responsible for the outbreak of full-blown AIDS with or without manifestation of Kaposi's sarcoma, respectively. Our formal epidemiological considerations appear to be supported by recent microbiological findings.

title: Differential and convergent utilization of autophagy components by positive-strand RNA viruses
abstract: Many viruses interface with the autophagy pathway, a highly conserved process for recycling cellular components. For three viral infections in which autophagy constituents are proviral (poliovirus, dengue, and Zika), we developed a panel of knockouts (KOs) of autophagy-related genes to test which components of the canonical pathway are utilized. We discovered that each virus uses a distinct set of initiation components; however, all three viruses utilize autophagy-related gene 9 (ATG9), a lipid scavenging protein, and LC3 (light-chain 3), which is involved in membrane curvature. These results show that viruses use noncanonical routes for membrane sculpting and LC3 recruitment. By measuring viral RNA abundance, we also found that poliovirus utilizes these autophagy components for intracellular growth, while dengue and Zika virus only use autophagy components for post-RNA replication processes. Comparing how RNA viruses manipulate the autophagy pathway reveals new noncanonical autophagy routes, explains the exacerbation of disease by starvation, and uncovers common targets for antiviral drugs.

title: Sepsis-Induced Cardiomyopathy: a Comprehensive Review
abstract: PURPOSE OF REVIEW: To briefly review epidemiology and pathophysiology of SICM and provide a more extensive review of the data on diagnostic and management strategies. RECENT FINDINGS: SICM is likely underdiagnosed and that has mortality implications. Current evidence supports speckle tracking echocardiography to identify decreased contractility irrespective of left ventricular ejection fraction for the diagnosis of SICM. There continues to be a dearth of large clinical trials evaluating the treatment of SICM and current consensus focuses on supportive measures such as vasopressors and inotropes. SUMMARY: Sepsis is a significant cause of mortality, and sepsis-induced cardiomyopathy has both prognostic and management implications for these patients. Individualized work-up and management of these patients is crucial to improving outcomes.

title: Classification of Texas Reservoirs in Relation to Limnology and Fish Community Associations
abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive evaluation of the classification of Texas reservoirs in relation to limnology and fish community associations. Examining eleven bodies of water within six state parks, we assessed the influence of abiotic characteristics on reservoir biotic assemblages. Using predictive species-environment relationships, we explored how morphological patterns influenced habitat partitioning among diverse taxa. Our results indicate that each reservoir is associated with unique limnological profile not easily identified by morphometric measurements alone but supported by an identifiable qualitative connection between biota and specific environmental properties. This study offers new insights into the factors necessary for appropriate management and conservation strategies concerning natural resources as they relate to lasting freshwater quality across Texas reservoirs.

title: Multiple gene mutations identified in patients infected with influenza A (H7N9) virus
abstract: Influenza A (H7N9) virus induced high mortality since 2013. It is important to elucidate the potential genetic variations that contribute to virus infection susceptibilities. In order to identify genetic mutations that might increase host susceptibility to infection, we performed exon sequencing and validated the SNPS by Sanger sequencing on 18 H7N9 patients. Blood samples were collected from 18 confirmed H7N9 patients. The genomic DNA was captured with the Agilent SureSelect Human All Exon kit, sequenced on the Illumina Hiseq 2000, and the resulting data processed and annotated with Genome analysis Tool. SNPs were verified by independent Sanger sequencing. The DAVID database and the DAPPLE database were used to do bioinformatics analysis. Through exon sequencing and Sanger sequencing, we identified 21 genes that were highly associated with H7N9 influenza infection. Protein-protein interaction analysis showed that direct interactions among genetic products were significantly higher than expected (p = 0.004), and DAVID analysis confirmed the defense-related functions of these genes. Gene mutation profiles of survived and non-survived patients were similar, suggesting some of genes identified in this study may be associated with H7N9 influenza susceptibility. Host specific genetic determinants of disease severity identified by this approach may provide new targets for the treatment of H7N9 influenza.

title: The role of the neutral amino acid transporter B(0)AT1 (SLC6A19) in Hartnup disorder and protein nutrition
abstract: Hartnup disorder (OMIM 234500) is an autosomal recessive disorder, which was first described in 1956 as an aminoaciduria of neutral amino acids accompanied by a variety of symptoms, such as a photo‐sensitive skin‐rash and cerebellar ataxia. The disorder is caused by mutations in the neutral amino acid transporter B(0)AT1 (SLC6A19). To date 21 mutations have been identified in more than twenty families. SLC6A19 requires either collectrin or angiotensin‐converting enzyme 2 for surface expression in the kidney and intestine, respectively. This ties SLC6A19 together with more complex functions such as blood‐pressure control, glomerular structure, and exocytosis. © 2009 IUBMB IUBMB Life, 61(6): 591–599, 2009

title: Factors Influencing the Measurement of Plasma/Serum Surfactant Protein D Levels by ELISA
abstract: BACKGROUND: Extensive variations in human surfactant protein D (SP-D) levels in circulation as measured by ELISA exist in the published literature. In order to determine the source of these variations, factors influencing the measurement by ELISA were explored. MATERIALS AND METHODS: Peripheral blood from healthy individuals was collected into various vacutainers during the same blood draw. Recombinant SP-D was diluted into different matrices and used for a standard curve. Samples were analyzed by capture ELISA using one of two distinct detection antibodies. RESULTS: The type of matrix had some effects on detection of recombinant SP-D. The type of anticoagulant used and dilution factor had very little effect, except for in plasma collected in EDTA vacutainers. The extent of variation in published values seemed to be due to the ELISA configuration employed, and, in agreement with this, we found that by switching the detection antibody, there was a 50% decrease in the extrapolated SP-D value of serum and plasma samples. Storage of samples resulted in slight changes in measured SP-D levels. CONCLUSIONS: The ELISA configuration employed to measure circulating levels of SP-D has a significant effect on the extrapolated values. In both configurations tested, the use of EDTA as a coagulant resulted in inconsistent values, and we, therefore, suggest the avoidance of this anticoagulant when assaying for SP-D by ELISA. While the demonstrated effects of several factors on measurement of SP-D may not account for all the disparities amongst the previous studies, they stress that variations in methodologies for measuring the same protein can result in very inconsistent results.

title: The Myeloid LSECtin Is a DAP12-Coupled Receptor That Is Crucial for Inflammatory Response Induced by Ebola Virus Glycoprotein
abstract: Fatal Ebola virus infection is characterized by a systemic inflammatory response similar to septic shock. Ebola glycoprotein (GP) is involved in this process through activating dendritic cells (DCs) and macrophages. However, the mechanism is unclear. Here, we showed that LSECtin (also known as CLEC4G) plays an important role in GP-mediated inflammatory responses in human DCs. Anti-LSECtin mAb engagement induced TNF-α and IL-6 production in DCs, whereas silencing of LSECtin abrogated this effect. Intriguingly, as a pathogen-derived ligand, Ebola GP could trigger TNF-α and IL-6 release by DCs through LSECtin. Mechanistic investigations revealed that LSECtin initiated signaling via association with a 12-kDa DNAX-activating protein (DAP12) and induced Syk activation. Mutation of key tyrosines in the DAP12 immunoreceptor tyrosine-based activation motif abrogated LSECtin-mediated signaling. Furthermore, Syk inhibitors significantly reduced the GP-triggered cytokine production in DCs. Therefore, our results demonstrate that LSECtin is required for the GP-induced inflammatory response, providing new insights into the EBOV-mediated inflammatory response.

title: Improving livestock feed safety and infection prevention: Removal of bacterial contaminants from hay using cold water, bubbles and ultrasound
abstract: This paper presents a novel method of improving the safety, quality and infection prevention of livestock feed by the use of cold water, bubbles and ultrasound. In this current study, hay—which is one of the major sources for animal farming — was contaminated with bacteria in order to determine the effectiveness of decontamination through cold water technique combined with ultrasonic sound waves as an alternate approach compared to using disinfectants alone. Results showed that contamination could be reduced significantly (up to >80%) if ultrasound was used for 5 minutes instead of 15 minutes; moreover adding bubbling action enhanced bacterial reduction efficiency. This knowledge can develop alternative strategies which are both efficient in terms all parameters required along with economically viable alternatives which still guarantee appropriate food-security practices when creating right conditions for livestock nutrition production, hygiene and protection from deadly diseases​.

title: In vitro growth characteristics and heterogeneity of mouse hepatitis virus type 3
abstract: This study attempts to understand the in vitro growth characteristics and heterogeneity of Mouse Hepatitis Virus Type 3 (MHV-3). By using a panel of cell lines for virus replication analysis, this study aims to answer questions about MHV-3 infection in vitro and its capability for further laboratory investigation. The results from this experiment provide new insights into the nature of proliferation and diversification of MHV-3, thus offering vital information regarding viral infectivity in vivo.

title: Multiple probabilistic traveling salesman problem in the coordination of drug transportation—In the context of sustainability goals and Industry 4.0
abstract: This paper addresses the Multiple Probabilistic Traveling Salesman Problem (MPTSP) in the coordination of drug transportation, and examines its implications for sustainability goals in accordance with Industry 4.0. As global health remains an unavoidable concern worldwide, sustainable production and distribution of therapeutic products are essential for their success. Drug delivery logistics offer a powerful tool to bridge gaps between producers and consumers while cutting costs without compromising efficiency and effectiveness. Thus, this paper proposes a specific methodology based on MPTSP to coordinate drug transportation within the scope of sustainability principles that can be implemented by using emerging automation tools such as Industry 4.0 solutions. Experimental test results from simulations demonstrate promising prospects for this method against standard approach applications with respect to cost minimization and reliability increase of medical goods dispatch processes at pharmaceutical factories/companies as well as clinics/hospitals under logistic need uncertainty conditions

title: Influenza epidemics and acute respiratory disease activity are associated with a surge in autopsy-confirmed coronary heart disease death: results from 8 years of autopsies in 34 892 subjects
abstract: AIMS: To determine whether influenza can trigger heart attacks, we investigated the impact of influenza epidemics on autopsy-proven coronary deaths. METHODS AND RESULTS: We studied weekly death due to acute myocardial infarction (AMI) and chronic ischaemic heart disease (IHD) in autopsies conducted in 1993 to 2000 in St Petersburg, Russia. We plotted the weekly acute respiratory disease (ARD) counts and influenza epidemics against AMI and chronic IHD deaths. There were 11 892 subjects dying of AMI and 23 000 subjects dying of chronic IHD. Median age was 75 for women and 65 for men. In every year, a peak of AMI and chronic IHD deaths were present and coincided with the influenza epidemic and peak ARD activity. A similar pattern was seen for each subgroup of men, women, subjects 50 years or older, and subjects 70 years or older. title: Evolution of size and pattern in the social amoebas
abstract: A fundamental goal of biology is to understand how novel phenotypes evolved through changes in existing genes. The Dictyostelia or social amoebas represent a simple form of multicellularity, where starving cells aggregate to build fruiting structures. This review summarizes efforts to provide a framework for investigating the genetic changes that generated novel morphologies in the Dictyostelia. The foundation is a recently constructed molecular phylogeny of the Dictyostelia, which was used to examine trends in the evolution of novel forms and in the divergence of genes that shape these forms. There is a major trend towards the formation of large unbranched fruiting bodies, which is correlated with the use of cyclic AMP (cAMP) as a secreted signal to coordinate cell aggregation. The role of cAMP in aggregation arose through co‐option of a pathway that originally acted to coordinate fruiting body formation. The genotypic changes that caused this innovation and the role of dynamic cAMP signaling in defining fruiting body size and pattern throughout social amoeba evolution are discussed. title: Exploring Lassa Virus Proteome to Design a Multi-epitope Vaccine Through Immunoinformatics and Immune Simulation Analyses
abstract: The Lassa virus has been a major public health concern for many years now. It is estimated to cause nearly 200,000 infections annually around the world, mostly in West Africa. In recent years, there have been serious efforts made to develop effective vaccines against the virus. One promising strategy being developed is that of using multi-epitope vaccines (MEVs). MEVs are built from several conserved peptide sequences derived from different proteins produced by the virus and targeted simultaneously during immunization. The objective of this study was to explore the proteomes of Lassa viruses circulating in West African countries with an aim of designing potential MEV candidates for vaccination through bioinformatics approaches such as immune simulation analyses. We then validated our results using molecular docking simulations and assessment of antibody recognition patterns by means of enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) testing. Our findings will form a basis for better understanding how MEV can protect against wide range genotypes that may emerge due to rapid adaptation capabilities possessed by this RNA based virus causing severe hemorrhagic fever syndrome with high fatality rate associated complications if proper diagnosis treatment measures are not employed timely than intended cases.

title: Novel Approaches to Vaccine Delivery
abstract: Although the currently available vaccines represent an outstanding success story in modern medicine and have had a dramatic effect on morbidity and mortality worldwide, it is clear that improvements are required in the current vaccine delivery technologies. Improvements are required to enable the successful development of vaccines against infectious diseases that have so far proven difficult to control with conventional approaches. Improvements may include the addition of novel injectable adjuvants or the use of novel routes of delivery, including mucosal immunization. Mucosal delivery may be required to provide protection against pathogens that infect at mucosal sites, including sexually transmitted diseases. Alternatively, novel approaches to delivery, including mucosal administration, may be used to improve compliance for existing vaccines. Of particular interest for safer mass immunization campaigns are needle-free delivery devices, which would avoid problems due to needle re-use in many parts of the world and would avoid needle-stick injuries.

title: Characterisation of rotavirus isolates from sub-clinically infected calves by genome profile analysis
abstract: This study presents the characterisation of rotavirus isolates obtained from sub-clinically infected calves using genome profile analysis. Rotaviruses are a major cause of neonatal mortality and morbidity in young ruminants, with severe economic losses. Analysing their genomes provides an understanding of the genetic diversity, pathogenic mechanisms and evolution dynamics among different virus strains. To this aim, 14 calf faecal samples were collected to investigate the presence of type A rotaviruses in healthy animals before sample enrichment and molecular characterization techniques were employed on them. Results showed that 1 isolate demonstrated 99% relatedness to bovine genotype G10P[9], 1 tested positive for Wa genotype associated with gastroenteritis outbreaks in sheep flocks worldwide and 12 were classified into previously unknown rotavirus species from cattle origin into new G/P types combinations: G17P2[11] (n = 5), G14P2[9] (n = 4) or G16P1[7] (n = 2). These findings point out to great variations at genomic level within bovine population so further studies must be addressed to deepen our knowledge about this field.

title: Angiotensin II plasma levels are linked to disease severity and predict fatal outcomes in H7N9-infected patients
abstract: This paper seeks to contribute to the growing body of research investigating whether angiotensin II (Ang-II) plasma levels could be used to predict fatal outcomes in H7N9 avian influenza virus infected patients. Due to its close association with hypertension and cardiovascular disease, patient Ang-II concentrations have been studied extensively. However, few studies have explored how these concentrations might be associated with disease severity or fatality in cases of H7N9. By examining this relationship, we aim to provide vital information that can aid medical practitioners by informing the timing and intensity of intervention strategies in those presenting symptoms due to infection with this deadly pathogen.

title: Haploidentical bone marrow transplant with posttransplant cyclophosphamide for sickle cell disease: An update
abstract: Hematopoietic cell transplant (HCT) can cure both children and adults with sickle cell disease. Outcomes have historically been poor for the vast majority of patients who lack a matched sibling donor. However, the development of haploidentical HCT (haplo-HCT) with high doses of posttransplant cyclophosphamide (PTCy) has allowed for curative long-term potential with favorable transplant-related outcomes, though this has not obviated the potential for graft rejection from human leukocyte antigen mismatch and repeated red blood cell transfusions. Accordingly, multiple strategies have been developed to improve outcomes, the majority of which are based on the Johns Hopkins platform from 2012. Presently, we aim to discuss results from pertinent studies and compare outcomes with the two most recent approaches involving either thiotepa plus 200-cGy total body irradiation or 400-cGy total body irradiation. Direct comparisons are required to determine the optimized curative potential. Transplant-eligible patients must be referred to tertiary medical centers for consideration of haplo-HCT.

title: Five years of non-prescription oseltamivir: effects on resistance, immunization and stockpiling
abstract: OBJECTIVES: In 2007 New Zealand (NZ) became the first country to make oseltamivir (Tamiflu®) available off-prescription. This study investigated the extent of pharmacist supply of oseltamivir over 5 years, including during the influenza A(H1N1) pandemic, and the impact of pharmacist supply of oseltamivir on influenza virus oseltamivir susceptibility, personal stockpiling and influenza vaccine uptake. METHODS: Randomly selected community pharmacies in NZ reported oseltamivir provision by prescription and through pharmacist supply from 1 January 2007 to 15 September 2011. Oseltamivir resistance data on influenza viruses isolated during influenza surveillance from 2008 to 2011 were obtained, along with influenza vaccine uptake data from 2005 to 2011 and influenza detection data. RESULTS: Seventy of 85 eligible pharmacies completed the study (82% response rate). Most supplies of oseltamivir throughout the 5 years were dispensed against a prescription rather than pharmacist supplied, with pharmacist supply responsible for 11% of supplies during the pandemic years (2009–10) versus 27% and 31% during 2007 and 2008, respectively. Pharmacist-supplied oseltamivir did not appear to be associated with the development of resistance, with identified likely stockpiling or with a decline in influenza immunization. Pharmacist supplies largely matched the timing of influenza in the community and peaked in June 2009, as did prescription supplies. CONCLUSIONS: Five years of non-prescription oseltamivir in NZ has resulted in no significant change in the development of resistance or rates of influenza immunization. Supplies remained modest and significant consumer stockpiling through pharmacist supply has not occurred, even during the influenza A(H1N1)pdm09 pandemic in 2009 and 2010. Pharmacists could be better utilized in ensuring fast distribution of antivirals to influenza sufferers during a pandemic.

title: First Evidence for a Role of Siglec-8 in Breast Cancer
abstract: This paper presents the first study to demonstrate a role for Siglec-8, an inhibitory receptor expressed on many types of immune cells, in breast cancer. Using mouse models and human samples from patients with differing levels of expression of Siglec-8, our data reveals that increased expression is associated with significantly improved patient outcomes for estrogen receptor (ER) negative tumors. Further investigation into pathway analysis also displays that elevated Siglec-8 expression is correlated with activation of an antitumorigenic signaling pathway, which suggests a novel immunotherapeutic approach to treating ER negative breast cancer sufferers.

title: Association of transport time with adverse outcome in paediatric trauma
abstract: The title of this study is 'Association of transport time with adverse outcome in paediatric trauma.' This paper aims to assess the impact of increasing prehospital intervals on clinical adversion outcomes and evaluate their relationship. Paediatric trauma is an evolving public health issue with many factors influencing its clinical approach like transportation time, age, anatomical area affected and other environmental variables. Longer distances travelled from medical services have been identified as potential time-related risk factors for poor prognosis particularly among major or organ system traumas; hence prehospital times are a valid indicator for overall health risks likely associated with paediatric trauma. Therefore, timely access and optimisation of intervention can be critical for appropriate management during acute care interventions that might require specialised attention. Thus, it is necessary to investigate the determinants associated to prehospital transport delays which could help reduce morbidity or mortality throughout improved patient care outcomes related to adequate triage tactics when applicable. The objective of this research project was to determine the association between extended ambulance dispatch interval times prior to hospitalisation and adverse consequences both clinically and economically in cases involving severe childhood trauma victims along five academic hospitals affiliated pediatrics units. Results will aid healthcare professionals in addressing current challenges regarding patient’s well-being while collaborating towards publicly funded resources that allow proper attention linked wider availability of emergency aid staff at short notice as well as enable evidence-based policy decisions concerning paediatric acute critical trajectories

title: Inhibition of protein glycosylation is a novel pro-angiogenic strategy that acts via activation of stress pathways
abstract: This study identifies a novel pro-angiogenic strategy to regulate the pathological processes involving aberrant inflammation and dysregulated angiogenesis. Our findings suggest that inhibition of glycosylation in proteins is demonstrated as an efficient approach resulting in upregulation of stress pathways, thus propelling pro-angiogenic mechanism associated with disease developments. We conducted a series of tests on both gene expression and immunofluorescence assays to determine how this strategy works through alteration in multiple signaling cascades leading ultimately to an altered functional status of vessels across diseased conditions among experimental models tested. Our research provides new insights into how manipulation of protein glycosylation can be utilized for designing molecular therapeutics applicable under variety contexts including vascular malformations, tumors or chronic vascular diseases like diabetic retinopathy.

title: Cryptosporidiosis in Perspective
abstract: This chapter focuses on cryptosporidiosis in perspective. The significance of cryptosporidiosis in humans, however, depends on the severity of the disease it produces and the incidence in population, both of which are unknown. The frequency of cryptosporidiosis is highest in children aged between six months and three years. The chapter discusses these epidemiological observations and more accurate information regarding the morphology and the life-cycle of Cryptosporidium. Detailed studies on the life-cycle and the ultrastructure have provided a better understanding of the biology of the parasite and have highlighted its unique characteristics. Of these, the existence of sporulated, thin-walled oocysts, and their independence of reducing conditions for excystation are of major importance and may explain the occurrence of autoinfection and persistent infection. Cryptosporidium has numerous characteristics that set it apart from the rest of that subclass. The parasite's ability to maintain persistent infection in certain individuals and its astonishingly stubborn resistance to chemotherapy are serious medical problems that need to be addressed in the future.

title: The mechanism of the nucleo-sugar selection by multi-subunit RNA polymerases
abstract: RNA polymerases (RNAPs) synthesize RNA from NTPs, whereas DNA polymerases synthesize DNA from 2′dNTPs. DNA polymerases select against NTPs by using steric gates to exclude the 2′OH, but RNAPs have to employ alternative selection strategies. In single-subunit RNAPs, a conserved Tyr residue discriminates against 2′dNTPs, whereas selectivity mechanisms of multi-subunit RNAPs remain hitherto unknown. Here, we show that a conserved Arg residue uses a two-pronged strategy to select against 2′dNTPs in multi-subunit RNAPs. The conserved Arg interacts with the 2′OH group to promote NTP binding, but selectively inhibits incorporation of 2′dNTPs by interacting with their 3′OH group to favor the catalytically-inert 2′-endo conformation of the deoxyribose moiety. This deformative action is an elegant example of an active selection against a substrate that is a substructure of the correct substrate. Our findings provide important insights into the evolutionary origins of biopolymers and the design of selective inhibitors of viral RNAPs.

title: Teaching “Crafty Microbiology”: Safely Teaching Hands-On Microbiology Skills at Home
abstract: This paper proposes a new solution to teaching “Crafty Microbiology”: safely providing learners with an opportunity for hands-on microbiology experience at home. As teachers have shifted to remote education during the COVID pandemic, full in-person engagement has become more difficult. To provide students with adequate activity and learning opportunities that help them gain relevant knowledge and skills, traditional laboratory practicals must be replaced with remote versions. This study evaluates the implementation of Crafty Microbiology—a virtual kit based on ambient microbial sensing methods used for educational activities such as culturing bacteria via agar plates or testing water cleanliness. Results show that this technique helps improve student understanding of essential microbiological principles while ensuring safety in keeping physical distancing protocols through practically making use of local materials related to their everyday life environment. The methodology also allows facilitators outside the field of science to conduct safe experiments at home without compromising issue trends associated with regular lab sessions including contamination and accidental exposure risks; thus helping foster independent and engaged learning habits amongst students.

title: The Historical, Present, and Future Role of Veterinarians in One Health
abstract: The renewed interest in the concept of One Health has occurred as a result of the increased emergence of zoonotic infectious diseases over the past decade. The subsequent impacts of these diseases on human, livestock, and wildlife health, as well as the economic effects, have given international health organizations and national governments a greater appreciation of the importance of collaborative efforts in solving health problems. The One Health concept is not new, but under its umbrella, a new generation of veterinarians, physicians, ecologists, biologists, and social scientists is shaping the concept in novel ways. This has led to increased support for One Health initiatives to control disease by international agencies, national governments, and nongovernmental organizations as well as a growing emphasis on One Health concepts in training the veterinary workforce. Veterinary schools are reorganizing veterinary education to better teach students the precepts of One Health. This chapter explores the evolution and application of the One Health concept from the perspective of the veterinarian. The veterinary profession is positioned to be a strong advocate and leader of One Health. Veterinarians have a long history of involvement with One Health activities, and this involvement has adjusted and shifted with the changing needs of society. A new area of work for veterinarians is ecosystem health, which is becoming more relevant as a result of the impact that the ever-increasing human population is having on the environment that supports them.

title: Spread of different rhinovirus B genotypes in hospitalized children in Spain
abstract: Please cite this paper as: Cuevas et al. (2013) Spread of different rhinovirus B genotypes in hospitalized children in Spain. Influenza and Other Respiratory Viruses 7(5), 623–628. Human Rhinovirus (HRV) classification is an evolving process. New genotypes have been described within HRV‐A and HRV‐C species, but only one has been accepted related to HRV‐B. From 2003 to 2010, a total of 3987 nasopharyngeal aspirate samples were taken from pediatric patients admitted to the Severo Ochoa Hospital in Madrid (Spain). After viral analysis, 949 (23·8%) tested positive to HRV. A random selection of 397 (42%) positive samples showed that 39 (9·8%) were HRV‐B. The sequencing of partial VP4/VP2 coding region revealed the spread of 13 of 25 defined HRV‐B serotypes and three putative new genotypes. Such results remark the high diversity of HRV‐B.

title: Low-temperature laminar flow ward for the treatment of multidrug resistance Acinetobacter baumannii pneumonia
abstract:
The Title: Low-temperature laminar flow ward for the treatment of multidrug resistance Acinetobacter baumannii pneumonia 

This study aimed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of low-temperature laminar flow as an experimental method of treating multidrug resistant (MDR) Acinetobacter baumannii pneumonia in hospitalized children. MDR A. baumamnnii has been increasingly recognized as a leading cause of nosocomial respiratory infections all over the world, with drug regimes proven ineffective against this increasingly prevalent pathogen. Our participants included 19 pediatric patients admitted at the Department of Pediatrics between January 2018 and April 2019 who were suffering from MDR A. baumannii pneumonia upon admission. All subjects underwent lower temperature laminar airflow combined with antibiotic therapy, along with supportive care and monitoring by our team throughout management period; clinical status at follow up was assessed via comparison to baseline values obtained prior to treatment initiation. Results showed significant improvement across participants; fever clearance rate improved by 33%, whereas SpO2 levels fell below 91% on 26 occasions pre-, compared to only 4 post-treatment compliances given overall excellent adherence among participants completing their courseware during follow-up period (19/19). These findings suggest that low temperature laminar flow holds great potential for use against multi-drug resistant cases of A. Baumannii pneumonia, implying enhanced survival rates even in more critical scenarios without exacerbation risk due to possibly harmful implications resulting from elevated temperatures associated with standard techniques employed against such opportunistic pathogens today globally..

title: End-tidal capnography monitoring in infants ventilated on the neonatal intensive care unit
abstract: This paper aims to investigate the impact of end-tidal capnography monitoring in infants that are ventilated on a neonatal intensive care unit. End-tidal capnography (ETCO2) is a relatively new modality within neonatal respiratory care, which offers advantages for both clinicians and patients with regards to continuous real-time assessment of carbon dioxide status and overall ventilation efficacy. The utilization of ETCO2 has been shown to provide improved accuracy for assessing infant oxygenation, airway integrity as well as optimum apneic ventilatory assistance during mechanical ventilation against traditionally used single channel pulse oximetry alone. As such, the purpose of this study is to examine an evidence based approach regarding implementing ETCO2 in managing preterm infants exposed to community hospital level 1 NICUs’ standard pediatric critical care medicine practices.

title: Soluble Form of Canine Transferrin Receptor Inhibits Canine Parvovirus Infection In Vitro and In Vivo
abstract: This study focuses on the potential of using the soluble form of canine transferrin receptor (sTfR) as an inhibitor of canine parvovirus (CPV2) infection both in vitro and in vivo. Using an advanced production method, CPV2-specific sTfR was produced that demonstrated a higher binding capacity and neutralizing antibody activity when compared to its native form. Vaccination with purified recombinant sTfR provided significant protection from CPV2 infection for 84 days in dogs infected with viremia levels exceeding 1:1,200 dilutions; 90% neutralization at different subtypes of CPV2 could also be observed. In vitro studies revealed reduced infectivity by purine inhibition and toxicity assays, suggesting additional functional properties were established due to posttranslational modifications incorporated during protein expression. These results suggest that sTfR is a promising candidate molecule for use as an inhibitor or vaccine platform against CPV2 infection in infectious disease research or veterinary clinical settings.

title: 2002. BioFire® Filmarray® Pneumonia Panel: A Powerful Rapid Diagnostic Test for Antimicrobial Stewardship
abstract: BACKGROUND: BioFire® Filmarray® Pneumonia Panel (BFPP) is a multiplex PCR panel that identifies 33 common bacterial and viral pathogens seen in community- and hospital-acquired pneumonias. It rapidly identifies these pathogens in addition to 7 antibiotic resistance genes on sputum and bronchioalveolar lavage samples in 1 hour. As one of the test centers for this panel, our institution utilized this panel for clinical and laboratory use. We reviewed the impact of BFPP on antimicrobial stewardship, particularly its role in early discontinuation of empiric antibiotics and prompt initiation of optimized targeted therapy. METHODS: We retrospectively reviewed all cases by which BFPP was ordered. We reviewed medical records of each case to identify the results of the panel, culture data, antibiotics used, and subsequent clinical intervention. RESULTS: 43 tests were ordered in total. 17 were for clinical use by an infectious disease specialist and 26 were randomly obtained by the microbiology lab. All 17 clinical cases were intervened upon with the following interventions: discontinuation of anti-pseudomonal antibiotics (8 cases), discontinuation of anti-MRSA antibiotics (5 cases), discontinuation of azithromycin (4 cases), discontinuation of carbapenem (1 case), prevention of inappropriate antibiotic escalation or initiation of inappropriate antibiotics (2 cases), and early IV to PO transition (3 cases). Of the random 26 samples ordered by lab, 13 had opportunities for antibiotic de-escalation if a physician were notified of the results. Viruses were identified in 15 samples with coronavirus being the most common. Virus was the sole pathogen in 9 of the 15 samples. Bacterial pathogens were identified in 20 samples that were reported as normal flora by conventional culture; none of these cases led to or potentially could have led to antibiotic escalation as the sole intervention. CONCLUSION: Clinical use of BFPP had 100% intervention rate with all interventions leading to de-escalation of antibiotics or prevention of inappropriate antibiotics use. Though over-identification of colonizers is a potential limitation, BFPP is a powerful tool for antibiotic stewardship that results in rapid interventions to achieve optimal targeted therapy. DISCLOSURES: All authors: No reported disclosures.

title: Mechanism and role of MCP-1 upregulation upon chikungunya virus infection in human peripheral blood mononuclear cells
abstract:
The study of ‘Mechanism and role of MCP-1 upregulation upon Chikungunya virus infection in human peripheral blood mononuclear cells’ addresses the contribution of cytokines to viral disease pathogenesis. The increasing incidence of this mosquito-borne viral disease is becoming a major public health issue worldwide. Monocyte chemoattractant protein-1 (MCP-1) has been associated with proinflammatory responses but its production after chikungunya virus infections needs further elucidation. In this research, we designed an in vitro experiment using human PBMCs infected with Chikungunya Virus to analyze whether there was any correlation between MCP-1 expression and cell vitality, apoptosis or related pathway signaling molecules after infection. 
Results were compared between infected samples and noninfected controls at different time points postinfection, demonstrating MCP-1 mRNA overexpression by tumor necrosis factor alpha as primary cofactor for stronger induction throughout the observation period. Further analysis also revealed increased tolllike receptor 4 involvement on these processes that could explain why innate response complexes act towards mounting antiviral defence mechanisms against chikungunya infections . These findings provide meaningful insights on how immune system respond quickly to certain pathogens like mosquito borne viruses  hence indicating the potential actions targeting specific signalling pathways during immunomodulation therapies for patients suffering from such diseases.

title: Challenges for Microelectronics in Non-Invasive Medical Diagnostics
abstract: This paper investigates the existing challenges encountered by microelectronics in achieving non-invasive medical diagnostics. In recent decades, modern technologies have provided us with unprecedented opportunities to revolutionize healthcare in ever more efficient ways. As research and design constantly strive to improve patient experience and reduce cost, innovative solutions are needed for incorporating microelectronic advancements into critical non-invasive diagnostic procedures. This study analyzes the current pitfalls that restrain their proper utilization for reliable medical diagnoses—particularly related to amount of required data collection, access accuracy and robustness of algorithms used — suggesting an integrated framework as a potential solution to move forward. The results will finally be discussed from both technological and pricing perspectives with special emphasis on which insights can be harvested along with mainly focusing on how better electronic equipment would ultimately contribute toward improving patient outcomes at decreased costs worldwide.

title: Strategies to Target Specific Components of the Ubiquitin Conjugation/Deconjugation Machinery
abstract: The regulation of ubiquitination status in the cell is controlled by ubiquitin ligases acting in tandem with deubiquitinating enzymes. Ubiquitination controls many key processes in the cell from division to death making its tight regulation key to optimal cell function. Activity based protein profiling has emerged as a powerful technique to study these important enzymes. With around 100 deubiquitinating enzymes and 600 ubiquitin ligases in the human genome targeting a subclass of these enzymes or even a single enzyme is a compelling strategy to unpick this complex system. In this review we will discuss different approaches adopted, including activity-based probes centered around ubiquitin-protein, ubiquitin-peptide and mutated ubiquitin scaffolds. We examine challenges faced and opportunities presented to increase specificity in activity-based protein profiling of the ubiquitin conjugation/deconjugation machinery.

title: Efficient functional screening of a cellular cDNA library to identify severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome virus entry factors
abstract: This article examines the effectiveness of functional screening as a method of identifying cellular entry factors for severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome virus (SFTSV). Through the use of high-throughput assays, we tested cDNA libraries expressing several potential targets in SFTSV infected cells to validate their role as possible viral entry factors. Employing quantitative polymerase chain reaction combined with Western blotting techniques, the efficiency and accuracy of our systematic approach are discussed. This comprehensive study demonstrates that functional screening is an effective method to identify cellular entry points for SFTSV; it also provides additional insight into how this virus interacts with host cells.

title: SUMO fusion system facilitates soluble expression and high production of bioactive human fibroblast growth factor 23 (FGF23)

FGF23, a critical regulator in phosphate metabolism, plays an important role in the etiology and progression of numerous chronic diseases such as cancers, diabetes etc. High-level expression systems have been used to generate recombinant proteins with enhanced solubility in hopes to maximize therapeutic efficiency. Currently existing fusions place tags/modifications after protein synthesis which makes them target for proteases or ligand components and provides no protection from insolubility due to self aggregation or misfolding before their synthesis and does not address oxidation issues with disulfide-linked structures. This study describes how this method was successful towards enabling soluble expression of advanced FGF23 molecules with preserved structure routinely yielding more than 10 mg/L quantity for multiple formulations suitable for forming expected homogenous crystals into single domains allowing detailed structure analysis using X ray crystallography techniques. title: Neurovirulence of herpes simplex virus types 1 and 2 isolates in diseases of the central nervous system
abstract: Herpes simplex virus (HSV) isolates derived from the central nervous system of ten patients with HSV-1-induced encephalitis, one patient with multiple sclerosis, and 14 patients with HSV-2-induced meningitis were investigated for neurovirulence by assaying the LD(50) after nose and intracerebral (i.c.) inoculation of mice. HSV-1 encephalitis strains were significantly more virulent after nose inoculation (i.e. neuroinvasive) when compared with HSV-1 isolates from patients with oral lesions only, whereas HSV-2 meningitis strains were significantly more virulent after i.c. inoculation when compared with HSV-2 isolates from patients with genital lesions only. No correlation between high neurovirulence (defined as low LD(50) for both routes of infection) and replication in cell cultures of neuronal and non-neuronal cell lines was found, but the weakly neurovirulent HSV-1 strain isolated from a patient with multiple sclerosis gave low replication yields. After nose inoculation, a highly neuroinvasive HSV-1 laboratory reference strain replicated to high titers in nose tissue, the trigeminal ganglia and brainstem, while a strain with low neuroinvasiveness but high i.c. virulence replicated less well in the brainstem. Neuroinvasiveness of the virus strain might be one factor of relevance in the pathogenesis of HSV-1 encephalitis in man.

title: Chai Jing: The Power of Vulnerability
abstract: This paper examines the power of vulnerability as exemplified by Chinese journalist Chai Jing in her 2015 environmental documentary, Under The Dome. Through an analysis of Chai’s courage and presentation style, we find that her personal approach enabled her to reach unprecedented levels of viewership in China and worldwide. Our research provides valuable insights into how individuals can inspire social change through courageous acts driven by their commitment to a cause. We further suggest methods for harnessing the power of vulnerability for other civic initiatives with similar objectives. Lastly, we explore what implications people could have when using this model for grassroots campaigns against oppression or injustice. By revealing the potential of vulnerability-driven actions in raising awareness about important causes, our findings will contribute to broader discussions on how inclusionary language contributes to positive social changes.

title: Identification of a novel base J binding protein complex involved in RNA polymerase II transcription termination in trypanosomes
abstract: The identification of genetic regulators capable of modulating the expression levels of various genes is a central theme in molecular biology. In this study, we present the identification and characterization of a novel base-J binding protein complex in Trypanosomes which plays an important role in RNA polymerase II transcription termination. We characterized this complex by purifying its components using pulldown assays and antibodies against specific epitopes found in each component. Moreover, our analysis revealed that these constituents interact with excess strength to form an integral part of a regulatory structure linked to both gene expression control and mechanistic aspects required for proper function. Furthermore, biochemical assays confirmed the regulation activity seen via mRNA transcript level changes when targeting key components within this new protein complex as compared to control conditions or treatment with other negative controls. Ultimately, our results reveal a novel method for RNA polymerase II transcription termination involving noncoding regions known as base J sequences readily found among diverse phylogenetic lineages suggesting conservation between organisms beyond prokaryotes and eukaryotes.

title: 1083 DIFFUSION OF MOXALACTAM INTO CSF OF CHILDREN WITH BACTERIAL MENINGITIS
abstract: This paper presents the findings of a study on the diffusion of Moxalactam into Cerebrospinal Fluid (CSF) when administered to children suffering from Bacterial Meningitis. The purpose of this research was to investigate and gain knowledge regarding drug susceptibility, efficacy, resistance levels and pharmacokinetics in such cases. Clinical trials were conducted with a sample size of 20 patients between six months and 15 years old, who received a single dose by direct CSF injection. Study results revealed that Moxalactam could be safely and effectively diffused through the CSF barrier across all age groups studied, regardless of existing bacterial characteristics or strain profiles present at time-of-injection. title: Global dynamics for discrete-time analog of viral infection model with nonlinear incidence and CTL immune response
abstract: This paper presents the development of an analytical methodology to investigate the global dynamics of a discrete-time analog model for viral infections. The novel mathematical model features nonlinear incidence and CTL immune response, capturing details on both pathogen growth and reproductive number during different stages in its life cycle. We conduct extensive numerical analysis using parameter bifurcation methods that allow us to map out the behaviour for different scenarios as well as characterize local dynamical regimes under given immunity conditions. By deploying rigorous stability theory and Lyapunov functions, our work provides conclusive evidence into how infection control can be regulated at scale under immunological management. Results are discussed with respect to existing reported cases coupled with implications for virus COVID-19 pandemics worldwide.

title: Saturated Five-Membered Thiazolidines and Their Derivatives: From Synthesis to Biological Applications
abstract: This paper reviews the synthesis and biological applications of saturated five-membered thiazolidines and their natural derivatives, a neglected class of heterocyclic scaffolds. In recent years, there has been substantial progress in chemical preparations as well as improved understanding of the associated reaction processes. These advances offer plentiful opportunities for further exploration into this family's potential uses due to its beneficial features such as minimal substrate reactivity and expressive synthetic capability for chemical diversity. Concomitantly, potential biological activities have been highlighted including antifungal activity among others which enable these components to be effective therapeutic agents or useful intermediates in drug discovery programs. By reviewing recent literature specific to the synthesis techniques and content regarding medicinal design with these structural entities, this paper provides an updated overview of both then present usages while illustrating future perspectives involving them.

title: How I See Me—A Meta-Analysis Investigating the Association Between Identities and Pro-environmental Behaviour
abstract: Prolific research suggests identity associates with pro-environmental behaviours (PEBs) that are individual and/or group focused. Individual PEB is personally driven, self-reliant, and are conducted on one's own (e.g., home recycling). Group focused PEB is other people-reliant and completed as part of a group (e.g., attending meetings of an environmental organisation). A wide range of identities have been related to PEBs. For example, a recent systematic qualitative review revealed 99 different types of identities studied in a PEB context. Most studies were correlational, few had an experimental design. However, the relationships between all these identities and PEBs have so far not been tested quantitatively with meta-analytical techniques. As such, a clear overview of this field is currently lacking. Due to the diverse nature of the field, a priori hypotheses were not possible and relatively broad definitions of identity had to be used to encompass all types of identities and the diverse meanings of identity that have been included in PEB research. What prior theory did allow for was to assess the distinction between two main types of identity, namely how people label, describe, and recognise oneself individually (individual identity), or as part of a group (group identity). Our overall goal was thus to assess the current state of knowledge on identities and PEBs. In 104 studies using a meta-regression following the preferred reporting items for systematic reviews and meta-analyses guidelines, our random-effects meta-analysis showed that the overall concept of identity associated with PEB with a medium Pearson's r (Aim 1). Furthermore, we found that individual identities associated more strongly with PEBs than group identities (Aim 2). The associations between individual and group identities were stronger when the identity and PEB were from the same category (e.g., when both were group-focused; Aim 3). Methodologically, the findings revealed that group identities and group PEBs were most strongly associated for self-reported rather than observed PEBs (Aim 4). Overall identity associated most strongly with group PEBs in the field rather than in the lab (Aim 5) and in student- rather than non-student samples (Aim 6). We discuss the theoretical and practical implications.

title: Intratumoural administration and tumour tissue targeting of cancer immunotherapies
abstract: This article examines the effects of direct intratumoral administration and cellular targets within the tumour tissue to effectively deliver cancer immunotherapies. Through recent technological advances, an array of promising treatment strategies are being developed in order to activate an immune response towards malignant cells and therefore explore alternative methods for solid tumours that cannot be addressed through traditional systemic treatments such as chemotherapy or radiation therapy. By injecting therapeutics directly into the tumour with precise techniques, immunotherapeutic agents can optimally reach specific cells within a complexly composed microenvironment including but not limited to epithelium, stromal fibroblasts, inflammatory cells, vascularized structures and extracellular matrix components. We have conducted experiments using animal models demonstrating enhanced specificity by redirecting therapy from immune-affine regions outside of the tumor area to represent a major challenge which needs further investigation: To effectively induce anti-tumor immunity while minimizing detrimental side-effects associated with current concepts used in clinical practice. This study will thus potentially provide new means of target-specific delivery strategy leading to improved outcomes for solid tumors refractory to existing therapeutic regimens when combined with appropriate conventional therapies.

title: Novel atmospheric pressure plasma device releasing atomic hydrogen: reduction of microbial-contaminants and OH radicals in the air
abstract: This study presents a novel atmospheric pressure plasma device designed to release atomic hydrogen and deliver results for decreasing the presence of microorganism contaminants, as well as OH radicals in the atmosphere. This new approach utilizes technology consisting of multiple electrodes powered by high frequency signals with energies contained within a confined space generating an intense glow discharge plasma that forms ozone gas while releasing reactive hydrogens known as antimicrobials. The method reveals its bactericidal properties when destructing vegetative cells of Gram-positive bacteria like Streptococcus mutans, indicating potential clinical applications in reducing oral microorganism growth inside human bodies but also outside as part of air purification systems. The focus here is to evaluate how effective this newly constructed device truly is at achieving brand-new levels of microbial reduction and oxidation capability previously unknown amongst more traditional ionization methods. It is hypothesized that such action has great potential to become one part among many components dedicated to creating ambient atmospheres free from harmful contamination caused uncontrolled airborne bacterial colonies incursions present nowadays.

title: CApecitabine plus Radium-223 (Xofigo™) in breast cancer patients with BONe metastases (CARBON): study protocol for a phase IB/IIA randomised controlled trial
abstract: BACKGROUND: A substantial proportion of breast cancer patients develop metastatic disease, with over 450,000 deaths globally per year. Bone is the most common first site of metastatic disease accounting for 40% of all first recurrence and 70% of patients with advanced disease develop skeletal involvement. Treatment of bone metastases currently focusses on symptom relief and prevention and treatment of skeletal complications. However, there remains a need for further treatment options for patients with bone metastases. Combining systemic therapy with a bone-targeted agent, such as radium-223, may provide an effective treatment with minimal additional side effects. METHODS/DESIGN: CARBON is a UK-based, open-label, multi-centre study which comprises an initial safety phase to establish the feasibility and safety of combining radium-223 given on a 6-weekly schedule in combination with orally administered capecitabine followed by a randomised extension phase to further characterise the safety profile and provide preliminary estimation of efficacy. DISCUSSION: The CARBON study is important as the results will be the first to assess radium-223 with chemotherapy in advanced breast cancer. If the results find acceptable rates of toxicity with a decrease in bone turnover markers, further work will be necessary in a phase II/III setting to assess the efficacy and clinical benefit. TRIAL REGISTRATION: ISRCTN, ISRCTN92755158, Registered on 17 February 2016. ELECTRONIC SUPPLEMENTARY MATERIAL: The online version of this article (10.1186/s13063-019-3643-6) contains supplementary material, which is available to authorized users.

title: Functionalized magnetic microparticle-based colorimetric platform for influenza A virus detection
abstract: This paper investigates the utility of a novel colorimetric platform based on functionalized magnetic microparticles for the detection of influenza A virus (IAV). The system utilizes an aptamer-immobilized and streptavidin-coated monodispersed magnetic silica microparticulate matrix. Our proposed method was able to detect IAV accurately with high sensitivity and specificity within a one hour time frame without any pretreatment or complicated instrumentation. Furthermore, it has potential applications in rapid screening in public health surveillance, clinical laboratories and epidemiological studies, among others. Its low cost, easy operation and environmental friendliness highly positions our approach as an attractive alternative to existing nucleoprotein detection schemes using real-time PCR technology. In summary, this study provides a reliable platform which may provide insight into further advancement in IAV diagnosis with minimal requirement for specialized personnel or technical training.

title: Host susceptibility to severe influenza A virus infection
abstract: Most people exposed to a new flu virus do not notice any symptoms. A small minority develops critical illness. Some of this extremely broad variation in susceptibility is explained by the size of the initial inoculum or the influenza exposure history of the individual; some is explained by generic host factors, such as frailty, that decrease resilience following any systemic insult. Some demographic factors (pregnancy, obesity, and advanced age) appear to confer a more specific susceptibility to severe illness following infection with influenza viruses. As with other infectious diseases, a substantial component of susceptibility is determined by host genetics. Several genetic susceptibility variants have now been reported with varying levels of evidence. Susceptible hosts may have impaired intracellular controls of viral replication (e.g. IFITM3, TMPRS22 variants), defective interferon responses (e.g. GLDC, IRF7/9 variants), or defects in cell-mediated immunity with increased baseline levels of systemic inflammation (obesity, pregnancy, advanced age). These mechanisms may explain the prolonged viral replication reported in critically ill patients with influenza: patients with life-threatening disease are, by definition, abnormal hosts. Understanding these molecular mechanisms of susceptibility may in the future enable the design of host-directed therapies to promote resilience.

title: Avian Infectious Bronchitis Virus
abstract:
Avian Infectious Bronchitis Virus (IBV): An Overview
The avian infectious bronchitis virus (IBV) has caused significant economic losses and is one of the most common pathogens associated with respiratory diseases in chickens over the past century. As IBV belongs to the family Coronaviridae, it is able to spread rapidly across large populations and poses a great challenge for poultry production worldwide due to its highly contagious nature. Despite efforts from scientists all over the world, this virus remains poorly characterized due to its genetic diversity, rapid mutations and lack of effective vaccines available. This review aims at examining current literature on IBV prevalence, epidemiology, pathology, clinical signs, diagnosis and control measures used in several countries against this pathogen. By doing so, we hope to provide an overall overview of existing knowledge concerning this serious problem in order to stimulate future research with goal of better understanding how best contain or eliminate it altogether.

title: Growth hormone does not affect albumin synthesis in the critically ill
abstract:
Title: Growth hormone does not affect albumin synthesis in the critically ill
A myriad of life-threatening conditions contribute to critical illness, including trauma, infection and cancer. The underlying etiology can lead to inflammation as well as metabolic complications, making it difficult for affected patients to survive without adequate medical attention. One possible measure by which to treat these severely ill patients is through growth hormone (GH) replacement therapy due its potential anti-inflammatory effects; however, there has been no direct evidence surrounding how GH may affect albumin production during times of critical illness. In order to investigate this topic thoroughly the authors conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of trials looking at if GH treatment was associated with increased serum albumin levels among critically ill adult humans compared with placebo or no treatment/standard care control groups. Results indicated that 2 randomized controlled trials involving 393 participants found no differences between those receiving GH and those who did not when looking at increases inalbumin levels. This brings forth an important message – while growth hormone might have therapeutic benefits in some classesof disease it appears ineffective at promoting protein synthesis during chronic states like acute illnesses or other physiological stresses brought on by injury or systemic inflammation

title: Yeast display platform technology to prepare oral vaccine against lethal H7N9 virus challenge in mice
abstract: BACKGROUND: Existing methods for preparing influenza vaccines pose the greatest challenge against highly pandemic avian influenza H7N9 outbreak in the poultry and humans. Exploring a new strategy for manufacturing and delivering a safe and effective H7N9 vaccine is needed urgently. RESULTS: An alternative approach is to develop an influenza H7N9 oral vaccine based on yeast display technology in a timely manner. Hemagglutinin (HA) of A/Anhui/1/2013 (AH-H7N9) is used as a model antigen and characterized its expression on the surface of Saccharomyces cerevisiae (S.cerevisiae) EBY 100. Mice administrated orally with S.cerevisiae EBY100/pYD5-HA produced significant titers of IgG antibody as well as significant amounts of cytokines IFN-γ and IL-4. Importantly, S.cerevisiae EBY100/pYD5-HA could provide effective immune protection against homologous A/Anhui/1/2013 (AH-H7N9) virus challenge. CONCLUSIONS: Our findings suggest that platform based on yeast surface technology provides an alternative approach to prepare a promising influenza H7N9 oral vaccine candidate that can significantly shorten the preparedness period and result in effective protection against influenza A pandemic.

title: Bird flu 2005: the ongoing story
abstract: The ongoing story of bird flu in 2005 is a complex and ever evolving narrative. This paper seeks to explore the social, cultural and economic ramifications of this global epidemic, beginning with its initial emergence in Southeast Asia, before progressing through its impact on human populations around the world. It further investigates how preventive measures have been implemented worldwide as well as their effectiveness in averting or ameliorating future outbreaks. Finally, current innovations are discussed which incorporate technological solutions into controlling avian influenza viruses (AIVs). Using analysis and normative approaches incorporating both research-based data and individual perspectives, this article provides insight into understanding AIV for prevention of potential future events like that of 2005.

title: New Insight Into Avian Papillomavirus Ecology and Evolution From Characterization of Novel Wild Bird Papillomaviruses
abstract: This paper presents new insights into the ecology and evolution of avian papillomaviruses (APVs) from the characterization of novel APVs in wild birds. In recent years, the importance of understanding all aspects of APV infection has been increasingly highlighted due to their ability to induce persistent infections in numerous species worldwide, including humans. Using molecular diagnostics such as PCR and next generation sequencing technologies, our study identified unique strains within four different orders of wild birds that have not previously been associated with APVs. Through comparative genomics, phylogenetic analysis and amino acid prediction we discovered significant genetic diversity within these distinct viral lineages. Our results suggest a correlation between virus strain variation and host dietary habits; indicating potential factors driving evolutionary divergence among diverse hosts. Furthermore, this research offers deeper biological insight into temporal aspects impacting viral trends amongst certain populations over time such as migration patterns or environmental fluctuations. This is critical for better elucidating true public health implications related to any form of wildlife-origin virus transmission in wildlife-human interface areas worldwide which may be pertinent for similar viruses affecting other animals including livestock species or even companion animals like dogs and cats.

title: Mechanisms of synergy in polymicrobial infections
abstract: This study explores the mechanisms of synergy between pathogenic and nonpathogenic microorganisms in polymicrobial infections. To understand the parameters that contribute to increased virulence associated with infection, a comprehensive investigation was conducted on multiple species in diverse conditions. In order to determine any enhanced rates of disease progression due to synergistic actions, it is essential to identify key components involved in microbial interactions which further influence the nature of such cooperative relationships. Through an array of experiments encompassing various organisms within different environments and controlled simulations, this research outlines a periodic overview distinguishing factors that bring about phenotype changes contributing to heightened infectiousness across multiple microbial constituents during polymicrobial infection events.

title: Prognosis-Based Early Intervention Strategies to Resolve Exacerbation and Progressive Lung Function Decline in Cystic Fibrosis
abstract: This paper presents a novel prognosis-based early intervention strategy to address the exacerbation and progressive lung function decline of cystic fibrosis (CF). Patients with CF experience episodes of lung infection, in turn resulting in decreased pulmonary functions that require corrective medical intervention. However, the ability to predict when these exacerbations are likely to happen is not well understood, leading to suboptimal treatment strategies. This poses an urgent clinical instability and highlights the need for new therapeutic approaches. Through analyzing patient data both retrospectively and prospectively, this study seeks to identify potential prognostic biomarkers associated with an increased risk of recurrent infectious morbidity events in patients with advanced forms of CF. Additionally, this project proposes proactive interventions designed specifically for this distinct group by providing timely access to preventive care measures that can help manage the progression and reduce symptoms intensity over time. Ultimately it should be possible through integration of such strategies into clinical practice guidelines create a more effective treatment approach than current methods available today.

title: Nogo-B protects mice against lipopolysaccharide-induced acute lung injury
abstract: Nogo-B, a member of the reticulon 4 protein family, plays a critical role in tissue repair and acute inflammation. Its role in acute lung injury (ALI) remains unclear. Here, we assessed the function of Nogo-B during tissue injury in a lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-induced ALI mouse model. We found that pulmonary Nogo-B was significantly repressed after LPS instillation in C57BL/6 mice. Over-expression of pulmonary Nogo-B using an adenovirus vector carrying the Nogo-B-RFP-3flag gene (Ad-Nogo-B) significantly prolonged the survival of mice challenged with a lethal dose of LPS. The Ad-Nogo-B-treated mice also had less severe lung injury, less alveolar protein exudation, and a higher number of macrophages but less neutrophil infiltration compared with Ad-RFP-treated mice. Interestingly, microarray analysis showed that the Ad-Nogo-B-treated mice had different gene expression profiles compared with the controls and the prominent expression of genes related to wound healing and the humoral immune response after LPS induction. Of the 49 differently expressed genes, we found that the expression of PTX3 was significantly up-regulated following Nogo-B over-expression as observed in lung tissues and RAW264.7 cells. In conclusion, Nogo-B plays a protective role against LPS-induced ALI, and this effect might be exerted through the modulation of alveolar macrophage recruitment and PTX3 production.

title: Trafficking of activated cytotoxic T lymphocytes into the central nervous system: Use of a transgenic model
abstract: We have used cell or tissue-specific promoters to express lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus (LCMV) proteins in selected cells in independent lines of transgenic mice. Upon adoptive transfers into these mice, MHC-restricted LCMV-specific cytotoxic T lymphocytes homed specifically to either the choroid plexus (SV40 promoter) or β cells of the islets of Langerhans (rat insulin promoter). The availability of promoters specific for neurons, oligodendrocytes and astrocytes makes this approach compelling for evaluating T cell trafficking into the CNS and for analyzing antigen presentation in vivo in the CNS.

title: RNA structure prediction using positive and negative evolutionary information
abstract: Knowing the structure of conserved structural RNAs is important to elucidate their function and mechanism of action. However, predicting a conserved RNA structure remains unreliable, even when using a combination of thermodynamic stability and evolutionary covariation information. Here we present a method to predict a conserved RNA structure that combines the following three features. First, it uses significant covariation due to RNA structure and removes spurious covariation due to phylogeny. Second, it uses negative evolutionary information: basepairs that have variation but no significant covariation are prevented from occurring. Lastly, it uses a battery of probabilistic folding algorithms that incorporate all positive covariation into one structure. The method, named CaCoFold (Cascade variation/covariation Constrained Folding algorithm), predicts a nested structure guided by a maximal subset of positive basepairs, and recursively incorporates all remaining positive basepairs into alternative helices. The alternative helices can be compatible with the nested structure such as pseudoknots, or overlapping such as competing structures, base triplets, or other 3D non-antiparallel interactions. We present evidence that CaCoFold predictions are consistent with structures modeled from crystallography.

title: Host and Viral Factors Affecting the Decreased Immunogenicity of Sabin Type 3 Vaccine after Administration of Trivalent Oral Polio Vaccine to Rural Mayan Children
abstract: This paper examines host and viral factors impacting the immunogenicity of Sabin Type 3 vaccine administered via trivalent oral polio vaccine (tOPV) to rural Mayan children in Central America. Recent epidemiological studies have suggested an alarming drop in the immune response against Sabin Type 3 after tOPV administration, which could have serious implications for public health policies as this population is at a greater risk of developing paralysis associated with poliovirus infection. To better understand protective immunity following tOPV vaccination among these vulnerable children, we analyzed serum neutralizing antibody titers and genetic characteristics of wild-type circulation strains of Sabin Type 3 from pre-vaccination surveys collected during recent outbreaks in Guatemala and Belize. Our results provide insights into how environmental exposure discrepancies may influence pathogen communities along with varying human immune responses hence highlighting the need for more individualized management strategies that are scientifically informed.

title: High-flux isobutanol production using engineered Escherichia coli: a bioreactor study with in situ product removal
abstract: Promising approaches to produce higher alcohols, e.g., isobutanol, using Escherichia coli have been developed with successful results. Here, we translated the isobutanol process from shake flasks to a 1-L bioreactor in order to characterize three E. coli strains. With in situ isobutanol removal from the bioreactor using gas stripping, the engineered E. coli strain (JCL260) produced more than 50 g/L in 72 h. In addition, the isobutanol production by the parental strain (JCL16) and the high isobutanol-tolerant mutant (SA481) were compared with JCL260. Interestingly, we found that the isobutanol-tolerant strain in fact produced worse than either JCL16 or JCL260. This result suggests that in situ product removal can properly overcome isobutanol toxicity in E. coli cultures. The isobutanol productivity was approximately twofold and the titer was 9% higher than n-butanol produced by Clostridium in a similar integrated system.

title: The approximately universal shapes of epidemic curves in the Susceptible-Exposed-Infectious-Recovered (SEIR) model
abstract: This paper presents an analysis of the shapes and features of epidemic curves modeled in a Susceptible-Exposed-Infectious-Recovered (SEIR) framework. Epidemiological models have long been studied to better understand how disease spreads through populations, with SEIR being the most commonly used model for infectious diseases due to its detailed representation of epidemics. This work seeks to provide insight into some universal patterns that emerge regardless of the specifics related to the specific pathogen and population dynamics when epidemics are put in this form. The results obtained show evidence on why these models can be customized easily by altering only two parameters, leading us closer towards understanding management measures applicable globally irrespective of other geographical or demographical differences.

title: Spatial and Temporal Characteristics of the 2009 A/H1N1 Influenza Pandemic in Peru
abstract: This paper outlines the spatial and temporal characteristics of the 2009 A/H1N1 influenza pandemic in Peru. At a global level, seasonal influenza is highly prevalent and causes substantial morbidity and mortality, especially among low-income countries with inadequate healthcare services including Peru. In this study we investigate the spatial extent, distribution and timing of the 2009 Influenza A/H1N1 Pandemic in Peru to allow for evidence-based planning of control activities such as vaccination programs or public health measures such as social distancing protocols. By analyzing surveillance data from 1 January 2005 to 31December2009 on 1056 confirmed cases, we compare five disease indicators: age group affected; month of initial onset; origin (geographical location); spread (disease clusters) spread over time; and severity by comparing proportions admitted to hospitals compared with outpatient treatment. The results demonstrate that approximately 70% of all reported cases were focused within two geographical regions which coincided with high population density zones along coastal areas containing three Peruvian cities : Lima, Arequipa y Piura . Furthermore ,we found an increase in infections during December 2008 where 76% patients were younger than 19 years old closely followed by April–May potentially related to school holidays coinciding emergence in Brazil . The findings suggest widespread transmission between these geographically contiguous areas following distinct patterns linked to demographic changes across Peru allowing us timely implementation preventive strategies thus reducing significant diseases burden observed particularly amongst children below 4 years old
