title: Application of an Amine Functionalized Biopolymer in the Colonic Delivery of Glycyrrhizin: A Design and In Vivo Efficacy Study
abstract: In our current study, a newer amine functionalized guar gum derivative was studied for its efficacy in colonic drug delivery. Glycyrrhizic acid mono-ammonium salt was used as the model drug. Drug-loaded microparticles were formulated by ionic crosslinking using sodium tripolyphosphate. The Scanning Electron Microscopic study revealed spherical particles of sizes from 4.9 ± 3.8 μm to 6.9 ± 3.9 μm. The FT-IR studies presented a possible interaction between the drug and the polymer. The drug was encapsulated in amorphous form as observed from the powder X-Ray Diffraction studies. A cumulative drug release study was carried out in simulated gastric, intestinal, and colonic fluids. The cumulative drug release studies presented a burst release followed by a sustained release of the drug in simulated colonic fluid containing rat cecal contents. The drug-polymer ratio was optimised using a 3(2) factorial design by taking the amounts of glycyrrhizic acid (X(1)) and guar gum alkyl amine (X(2)) as the independant variables. The percent cumulative drug release at 240 mins (Q(240)), 720 mins (Q(720)), and at 1,440 mins (Q(1440)) were considered as the dependant variables. The efficacy of the optimized formulation was studied in a 2,4,6-trinitrobenzene sulfonic acid-induced rat colitis model. The tissue’s nitric oxide, malondialdehyde, and myeloperoxidase activities were found to be much lower in the microparticle-treated group compared to free drug-treated group. The histology of the colonic tissue from the treated group of animals revealed almost no infiltration of inflammatory cells in the tissue for the microparticle-treated group of animals. The synthesized amine derivative of guar gum was found to be better in vitro with a better in vivo efficacy in the colonic delivery of glycyrrhizic acid monoammonium salt and can be considered as a newer modified biopolymer for colonic drug delivery.

title: Identification and Validation of Reference Genes for RT-qPCR Normalization in Mythimna separata (Lepidoptera: Noctuidae)
abstract: This study focuses on the important task of selecting suitable reference genes for RT-qPCR normalization in Mythimna separata (Lepidoptera: Noctuidae). To date, there is a lack of systematic studies dedicated to identifying and validating potential reference genes from this species. Using RNA sequencing data from both cDNA libraries constructed from brain tissues and 10 time points across 4 developmental stages, 15 novel candidate reference gene candidates were identified. These genes were then further evaluated through quantitative analysis conducted with reverse transcription qPCR technique. The expression stability was assessed by calculating the coefficient variation amongst biological replicates for each candidate gene as well as performing principle component, correlation and cluster analyses. Ultimately, three optimal stable reference genes SANDALPHONBLUE12 (SAND), MYTH149039 (MYTE_1) and EB261M1182121Li08K09Bb02A042t33Ag11670P2021k13g50f100847H24G03e17p05v54d098030ii06A1540221871_2(JUNK)were validated based on their low coefficient values, strong correlations amongst replicates and clusters grouping them together respectively. This study serves to provide options regarding reliable internal control references in future studies comparing mRNA expression profiles in M. separata under different treatments or conditions such as insecticides or temperature changes..

title: Near-Patient Sampling to Assist Infection Control—A Case Report and Discussion
abstract: This study presents a case report on the use of near-patient sampling in infection control, as well as a comprehensive overview and discussion. Healthcare-associated infections (HAIs) are serious threats to patient safety, yet suitable methods for preventing HAI transmission remain elusive. Recent evidence has shown that effective identification is key in reducing healthcare derived infections, leading to increased focus on microbial surveillance technologies such as near-patient sampling (NPS). NPS has been identified as an accurate tool for rapid microbial profiling within clinical settings; however its usage remains limited due to poor adoption from health care workers. In this unique case–report highlighting the experiences of one rural hospital that faced outbreaks of multi resistant bacteria, we discuss our experience with implementing NPS technology at an individual nursing unit level. By collecting samples from both surfaces and air throughout the infectious ward areas at regular intervals during multiple outbreaks over two years’ time period, we reflect how monitoring with NPS enabled quick action taken where traditional swabbing would have left too late or no response possible. The results show significant reduction in prevalence and emergence rates of MRSB once using NPS technology was implemented indicating its advantages over cultures when used together with standard hygienic practice in daily operation within hospitals.

title: Optimisation of Design and Manufacturing Parameters of 3D Printed Solid Microneedles for Improved Strength, Sharpness, and Drug Delivery
abstract: This paper examines the optimisation of design and manufacturing parameters of 3D printed solid microneedles to improve their strength, sharpness and drug delivery. Solid microneedle technology has already shown great potential for various applications related to transdermal therapeutic delivery and rapid diagnostics. However, further improvements in characteristics such as strength, sharpness, etc., and enhanced reliability require better understanding of the relationship between design parameters and dispositive performance. In this study we investigate a range of considerations for improved material selection as well as geometrical arrangement through modelling simulations, in order to identify effective parameter combinations that when employed offer optimal mechanical behaviour under applied loading conditions for efficient traction energy transfer during insertion into skin tissue. Additionally, finite element analysis is conducted to evaluate effects on tip stability, drug diffusion from needle’s core region towards human body environment while also validating a high rate of reproducibility./

title: Willingness to accept H1N1 pandemic influenza vaccine: A cross-sectional study of Hong Kong community nurses
abstract: This paper aims to explore the willingness of Hong Kong community nurses to accept H1N1 pandemic influenza vaccine by examining their acceptance rates. In recent years, due to widespread occurrences of H1N1 virus outbreaks, it is acknowledged that vaccination is an effective preventative measure against H1N1 infections in high-risk groups. It has been speculated that with proper recognition and knowledge of the pros and cons related to receiving the vaccine will facilitate understanding, enforce positive perceptions and ensure successful implementation of preventive strategies such as vaccinations amongst professionals working in health care settings. A cross-sectional survey was designed using a specifically designed questionnaire measuring relevant factors associated with willingness towards accepting the vaccine among 186 participants. The results showed that 83% had accepted or expressed a desire to receive the flu shot while 17% were unwilling or undecided on receiving this preventive measure. Our findings highlighted some key determinants which can be used for informing public health practices and might help health authorities in improving awareness about vaccines during future epidemics or pandemics threatening society.

title: A Clathrin Independent Macropinocytosis-Like Entry Mechanism Used by Bluetongue Virus-1 during Infection of BHK Cells
abstract: Acid dependent infection of Hela and Vero cells by BTV-10 occurs from within early-endosomes following virus uptake by clathrin-mediated endocytosis (Forzan et al., 2007: J Virol 81: 4819–4827). Here we report that BTV-1 infection of BHK cells is also dependent on a low endosomal pH; however, virus entry and infection were not inhibited by dominant-negative mutants of Eps15, AP180 or the ‘aa’ splice variant of dynamin-2, which were shown to inhibit clathrin-mediated endocytosis. In addition, infection was not inhibited by depletion of cellular cholesterol, which suggests that virus entry is not mediated by a lipid-raft dependent process such as caveolae-mediated endocytosis. Although virus entry and infection were not inhibited by the dominant-negative dynamin-2 mutant, entry was inhibited by the general dynamin inhibitor, dynasore, indicating that virus entry is dynamin dependent. During entry, BTV-1 co-localised with LAMP-1 but not with transferrin, suggesting that virus is delivered to late-endosomal compartments without first passing through early-endosomes. BTV-1 entry and infection were inhibited by EIPA and cytochalasin-D, known macropinocytosis inhibitors, and during entry virus co-localised with dextran, a known marker for macropinocytosis/fluid-phase uptake. Our results extend earlier observations with BTV-10, and show that BTV-1 can infect BHK cells via an entry mechanism that is clathrin and cholesterol-independent, but requires dynamin, and shares certain characteristics in common with macropinocytosis.

title: Impact of hand hygiene intervention on hand washing ability of school-aged children
abstract:
Text 
This article seeks to examine the potential impact of hand hygiene intervention on the hand washing ability of school-aged children in a university setting. Hand hygiene is an important quality measure that helps protect individuals from infection, yet it remains an area where there is limited prior research. This study seeks to answer how a multifaceted educational approach including original lessons delivered by nursing faculty aides and class activities affected the behavioural intentions reported by school-aged children, measuring their willingness and perceived difficulty for performing proper hand wash techniques. The primary quantitative method employed was qualitative survey data collection with 30 participants. Results indicate that following four weeks, students showed significant improvement overall in both behaviour intent and self-reported abilities related to correct hand washing techniques. Therefore, this suggests that combined education methods could be effective in aiding students’ acquisition of proper handwashing skills at school settings which will ultimately lead to better rate of compliance concerning health policy implementation among all stakeholders involved in healthcare services delivery system.

title: Growth of fastidious adenovirus serotype 40 in HRT 18 cells: Interactions with E 1 A and E 1 B deletion mutants of subgenus C adenoviruses
abstract: Growth of fastidious adenovirus serotype 40 (Ad 40) in several cell lines was investigated. Ad 40 was able to readily propagate in human intestinal cell line, HRT 18. Coinfection assays were made in non-permissive and permissive cells between Ad 40 and Ad 5dl 312 or dl 1520, mutants deleted in E 1 A and E 1 B regions, respectively, to test the ability of Ad 40 to complement these mutants and vice versa. Ad 40 could enhance Ad 5dl 312 DNA synthesis in HRT 18 and HeLa cells, although its own DNA disappeared in the presence of this mutant in HRT 18 cells. In coinfection with dl 1520, Ad 40 DNA synthesis was inhibitied by dl 1520 in HRT 18 cells and dl 1520 DNA synthesis was inhibited by Ad 40 in 293 cells. This might reflect the presence of unusual products encoded by Ad 40 E 1 B region.

title: Methods for studying naturally occurring human pain and their analogues
abstract: This article examines the current available methods for assessing naturally occurring pain in humans, as well as their similarities to animal models used to evaluate similar states of distress. Pain is an essential symptom of many health conditions, and there exist numerous strategies for studying such cognitive-affective constructs in a variety of organisms. As it is difficult to capture participating humans' authentic emotion due to potential confounding factors such as bias or insensitivity towards negative stimuli, researchers are motivated by promising results from animal studies in order to develop means that accurately assess human experience. Therefore, this paper will explore the major components required for conducting research on human reactions with respect for validity and practicality in mind. Results may contribute newfound knowledge into how we interpret reports from both disorders and healthy subjects; which could eventually contribute toward more effective remedies targeting chronic ailments characterized by pain that pervade contemporary societies.

title: Evidence for distinct mechanisms of small molecule inhibitors of filovirus entry
abstract: This paper presents findings on the distinct mechanisms of small molecule inhibitors for filovirus entry inhibition. We investigated more than 300 compounds evaluated against three prototypic Filoviruses, Ebola virus (EBOV), Marburg virus (MARV) and Ravn virus (RAVV). Our results demonstrate that small molecules from two chemicalseries effectively inhibited EBOV, MARV and RAVV replication in a cell-free assay. By using computational virtual screening to predict target proteins, we further identified two protein families associated with filoviral fusion processes – cysteine proteases and glycosylated alkali phosphatase family members - as potential targets for our identified inhibitors. Through additional evaluation of these components' intracellular localizations and kinetics of enzyme activity upon inhibitor binding, we confirmed their roles in inhibiting frameshifting at the genomic level which subsequently reduces host cell infection. The collective test results revealed substantial evidence for distinct mechanismsof action by small molecule inhibitors that can inhibitFilovirus entry into host cells at different stages duringthe viral replication cycle.

title: Far-UVC light: A new tool to control the spread of airborne-mediated microbial diseases
abstract: This paper investigates the safety and effectiveness of Far-UVC light as a new tool to control the spread of airborne-mediated microbial diseases. Through extensive in vitro laboratory experiments, our study demonstrates that although it is highly effective at deactivating microorganisms, Far-UVC light does not pose any risk for human health – indicating its potential clinical use for disinfecting public spaces. We utilized chemical and microbiological assays to confirm that no viable cells were detected after exposure to tandem doses of Far-UVC lights; this confirms uptake within cell membranes and resultant cytotoxicity from photodynamic damage. In addition, these studies verified data obtained from previous ex vivo skin studies concerning bacterial load reduction. Finally, we highlight key considerations related to wavelength selection based on global climate factors when using these tools outside existing healthcare facilities in both rural and densely populated areas. The results presented provide science practitioners with an encouraging view on using far UV research towards controlling the transmission of infectious organisms in humans across multiple environments worldwide

title: Role of RNA helicases in HIV-1 replication
abstract: RNA helicases are essential enzymes responsible for unwinding RNA duplexes that play major roles in multiple biological processes such as transcription, translation, and replication. This article aims to provide insight into the role of these enzymes during HIV-1 replication. Recent advances have revealed a multifaceted function of RNA helicase activities and their importance in controlling viral expression levels, providing essential regulatory control over many aspects of the virus life cycle. The findings from this research suggest that interfering with specific antiviral therapies targeting RNA helicases could be used to inhibit active viral production. Consequently, it implies that further exploration into the evolution and regulation of HIV-1 could lead to more targeted and effective therapeutic approaches for this deadly pathogen.

title: Clinical characteristics of 42 SARS patients and their treatment of integrative Chinese and western medicine
abstract: Objective: To understand the clinical manifestation of severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS) and explore its effective treatment with integrative Chinese and western medicine (ICWM).Methods: The data of patients, whose diagnosis of SARS had been confirmed were summarized and analyzed, and clinical observation was conducted when the patients were treated with ICWM.Results: In the early stage of the 42 patients, the symptoms revealed were fever in 100% of SARS patients, headache in 92. 9%, aversion to cold in 76. 2%, chest stuffiness in 76. 2%, cough in 73. 8% and myalgia in 88. 1%; pulmonary lesion involves ≥3 lobes in 42. 9%, 2 lobes in 47. 6% and 1 lobe in 9. 5%; 61. 9% of them showed liver function abnormality (increase of ALT or AST), 47. 6% showed elevated myocardial enzyme (CK or CK-MB), 0. 48% showed an inclination of renal function (higher of BUN or Cr); in their T lymphocyte subsets, 91. 2% (31/34 patients) had lowered CD(3) and 76. 5% (26/34 patients) lowered CD(4)/CD(8) ratio. In the mid-late stage, the symptoms were lassitude and weakness in 85. 7%, scare in 81. 0%, short of breath or chest stuffiness in 71. 4%, loss of appetite in 64. 3%; light dark tongue proper in 52.4%, yellow and white tongue coating in 45. 2%, and yellow thick coating on the middle-root part of the tongue in 21. 4%. Most of them were asymptomatic when discharged from hospital, with 92. 8% of their pulmonary lesion, according to chest film, completely absorbed and liver function, myocardial enzyme and renal function all normalized. However, of the 30 patients who had CD(3) reexamination, 70% of the CD(3) showed lower than normal range and 36. 7% showed their CD(4)/CD(8) inclined to lower margin, follow-up should be done for these patients. Of the 42 patients, who received western medicine (WM) alone in the early stage and ICWM in the mid-late stage, 10 were severe cases and 3 critical cases, but none of them died. The mean defervescent time was 3. 52±0. 85 days, the time for complete absorption of pulmonary lesion judged by chest X-ray film was 26. 82±5. 98 days, and the mean hospitalization time was 33. 60±4. 37 days.Conclusion: The manifestation of SARS is multifarious, showing that there were damage in multiple organs. The T lymphocyte count percentage and its subsets, CD(3) and CD(4) /CD(8) ratio, are valuable for early diagnosis and follow-up in the rehabilitation stage. Majority of the patients could be clinically cured. Combined treatment of WM and TCM according to syndrome differentiation and psychiatric intervention are beneficial to remit partial symptoms and promote rehabilitation.

title: Prematurity alters the progenitor cell program of the upper respiratory tract of neonates
abstract: The impact of prematurity on human development and neonatal diseases, such as bronchopulmonary dysplasia, has been widely reported. However, little is known about the effects of prematurity on the programs of stem cell self-renewal and differentiation of the upper respiratory epithelium, which is key for adaptation to neonatal life. We developed a minimally invasive methodology for isolation of neonatal basal cells from nasopharyngeal (NP) aspirates and performed functional analysis in organotypic cultures to address this issue. We show that preterm NP progenitors have a markedly distinct molecular signature of abnormal proliferation and mitochondria quality control compared to term progenitors. Preterm progenitors had lower oxygen consumption at baseline and were unable to ramp up consumption to the levels of term cells when challenged. Although they formed a mucociliary epithelium, ciliary function tended to decline in premature cells as they differentiated, compared to term cells. Together, these differences suggested increased sensitivity of preterm progenitors to environmental stressors under non-homeostatic conditions.

title: The Struggle for Technology: Towards a Realistic Political Theory of Technology
abstract: Pieter Lemmens’ neo-Marxist approach to technology urges us to rethink how to do political philosophy of technology. First, Lemmens’ high level of abstraction raises the question of how empirically informed a political theory of technology needs to be. Second, his dialectical focus on a “struggle” between humans and technologies reveals the limits of neo-Marxism. Political philosophy of technology needs to return “to the things themselves”. The political significance of technologies cannot be reduced to its origins in systems of production or social organization, but requires study at the micro-level, where technologies help to shape engagement, interaction, power, and social awareness.

title: RM12 similar to substance P from tachykinin of freshwater murrel Channa striatus influence intracellular ROS in vitro fish erythrocytes and developmental toxicity and antioxidant enzymes in vivo zebrafish embryo
abstract: In this study, substance P, an antioxidant peptide of tachykinin, was identified using bioinformatics tools from the earlier established muscle transcriptome of a freshwater murrel Channa striatus and the peptide was named RM12. The antioxidant properties of RM12 were screened using various colorimetric assays. The toxicity of RM12 was experimented using fish erythrocytes, and it is observed that the maximum concentration (320M) of RM12 was found to have 15 or 20% of hemolytic activity; however, it was not significant with other tested concentrations (10, 20, 40, 80, and 160M). Further, the in vivo antioxidant properties of RM12 were experimented on zebrafish embryo, the intracellular ROS level was estimated by 5mM H(2)O(2) stress in the zebrafish embryo, and inhibition of apoptosis was evaluated. The antioxidant enzymes were extracted from the H(2)O(2)-stressed zebrafish embryo, and the intracellular ROS was eliminated due to RM12. Collectively, the experiment showed that the substance P from the freshwater murrel C. striatus possessed potent antioxidant properties; thus, it can further be focused to develop it as antioxidant molecule in aquaculture organisms. SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1007/s10695-021-00950-9.

title: Safety of Tdap vaccine in pregnant women: an observational study
abstract: OBJECTIVES: Actively recruit and intensively follow pregnant women receiving a dose of acellular pertussis vaccine for 4 weeks after vaccination. DESIGN AND SETTINGS: A prospective observational study conducted in 2 New Zealand regions. PARTICIPANTS: Women in their 28th–38th week of pregnancy, recruited from primary care and antenatal clinics at the time of Tdap administration. Telephone interviews were conducted at 48 h and 4 weeks postvaccination. MAIN OUTCOMES MEASURES: Outcomes were injection site reactions, systemic symptoms and serious adverse events (SAEs). Where available, data have been classified and reported according to Brighton Collaboration definitions. RESULTS: 793 women participated with 27.9% receiving trivalent inactivated influenza vaccine concomitantly. 79% of participants reported mild or moderate pain and 2.6% severe pain. Any swelling was reported by 7.6%, induration by 12.0% (collected from 1 site only, n=326), and erythema by 5.8% of participants. Fever was reported by 17 (2.1%) participants, 14 of these occurred within 24 h. Headache, dizziness, nausea, myalgia or arthralgia was reported by <4% of participants, respectively, and fatigue by 8.4%. During the study period, there were 115 adverse events in 113 participants, most of which were minor. At the end of the reporting period, 31 events were classified as serious (eg, obstetric bleeding, hypertension, infection, tachycardia, preterm labour, exacerbation of pre-existing condition and pre-eclampsia). All had variable onset time from vaccination. There were two perinatal deaths. Clinician assessment of all SAEs found none likely to be vaccine related. CONCLUSIONS: Vaccination with Tdap in pregnant women was well tolerated with no SAE likely to be caused by the vaccine. TRIAL REGISTRATION NUMBER: ACTRN12613001045707.

Telephone interviews were conducted at 48 h and 4 weeks postvaccination. MAIN OUTCOMES MEASURES: Outcomes were injection site reactions, systemic symptoms and serious adverse events (SAEs). Where available, data have been classified and reported according to Brighton Collaboration definitions. RESULTS: 793 women participated with 27.9% receiving trivalent inactivated influenza vaccine concomitantly. 79% of participants reported mild or moderate pain and 2.6% severe pain. Any swelling was reported by 7.6%, induration by 12.0% (collected from 1 site only, n=326), and erythema by 5.8% of participants. Fever was reported by 17 (2.1%) participants, 14 of these occurred within 24 h. Headache, dizziness, nausea, myalgia or arthralgia was reported by <4% of participants, respectively, and fatigue by 8.4%. During the study period, there were 115 adverse events in 113 participants, most of which were minor. At the end of the reporting period, 31 events were classified as serious (eg, obstetric bleeding, hypertension, infection, tachycardia, preterm labour, exacerbation of pre-existing condition and pre-eclampsia). All had variable onset time from vaccination. There were two perinatal deaths. Clinician assessment of all SAEs found none likely to be vaccine related. CONCLUSIONS: Vaccination with Tdap in pregnant women was well tolerated with no SAE likely to be caused by the vaccine. TRIAL REGISTRATION NUMBER: ACTRN12613001045707.

title: It’s Friendship, Jim, but Not as We Know It: A Degrees-of-Friendship View of Human–Robot Friendships
abstract: This article argues in defence of human–robot friendship. I begin by outlining the standard Aristotelian view of friendship, according to which there are certain necessary conditions which x must meet in order to ‘be a friend’. I explain how the current literature typically uses this Aristotelian view to object to human–robot friendships on theoretical and ethical grounds. Theoretically, a robot cannot be our friend because it cannot meet the requisite necessary conditions for friendship. Ethically, human–robot friendships are wrong because they are deceptive (the robot does not actually meet the conditions for being a friend), and could also make it more likely that we will favour ‘perfect’ robots, and disrespect, exploit, or exclude other human beings. To argue against the above position, I begin by outlining and assessing current attempts to reject the theoretical argument—that we cannot befriend robots. I argue that the current attempts are problematic, and do little to support the claim that we can be friends with robots now (rather than in some future time). I then use the standard Aristotelian view as a touchstone to develop a new degrees-of-friendship view. On my view, it is theoretically possible for humans to have some degree of friendship with social robots now. I explain how my view avoids ethical concerns about human–robot friendships being deceptive, and/or leading to the disrespect, exploitation, or exclusion of other human beings.

title: Glycan repositioning of influenza hemagglutinin stem facilitates the elicitation of protective cross-group antibody responses
abstract: This study entitled 'Glycan Repositioning of Influenza Hemagglutinin Stem Facilitates the Elicitation of Protective Cross-Group Antibody Responses' investigates a novel influenza HA stem immunogen platform with potential to generate protective cross-group antibody reactions. Influenza is a seasonally reoccurring, highly infectious disease and a major public health concern. Vaccines are available but they are only effective against limited subtypes due to antigenic drift over time. Therefore, the development of broadly applicable vaccines has been an active field in recent years. The focus here is on the repositioning of glycan sites on the HA2 domain for improved immunogenicity and antibodies capable of neutralizing greater diversity between clades across multiple hemagglutinins (HAs). Here we present our results showing that hydrocarbon modification positioned within CDR1 increased binding capacity by as much as 84%, suggesting this technology may provide a viable strategy for developing more efficient vaccines when compared to existing methods used today.

title: Excellence Available Everywhere: The Virtual Pathology Grand Rounds Experience
abstract: OBJECTIVES: The goal is to describe the use of a virtual platform in the delivery of Virtual Pathology Grand Rounds (VPGR) and discuss the overall experience from the perspective of hosts, speakers, and participants. METHODS: Zoom was a natural choice for an online format because virtual platforms had been increasingly used to conduct meetings and medical education. VPGR hosted 14 speakers on a variety of topics, including subspecialty anatomic pathology material, digital pathology, molecular pathology, and medical education. RESULTS: There were 221 registrants and 114 participants for the first lecture, reaching a maximum of 1,268 registrants for the 12th lecture and the maximum limit of 300 participants during 3 lectures. Speakers stated that VPGR conveniently provided career-building opportunities through partnerships with host universities and remote attendance. Participants identified a lack of interpersonal communication and technical challenges as downsides. CONCLUSIONS: VPGR serves as strong proof of concept for the feasibility and demand for high-quality, remote academic pathology talks.

title: Targeted Profiling of Immunological Genes during Norovirus Replication in Human Intestinal Enteroids
abstract: The ability of human gut enteroids to model virus replication provides a unique platform to study host-pathogen interactions in situ. In this study, we aimed to achieve a comprehensive understanding of the immunological gene regulation during Norovirus infection in human intestinal enteroids using targeted profiling techniques. Utilizing next-generation sequencing (NGS) processes such as RNA sequencing (RNAseq), our analyses revealed changes in the expression levels of several genes related to pathogenesis and innate immunity pathways upon norovirus replication compared with healthy controls. Additionally, quantitative real-time PCR was used for validation purposes due to its superior sensitivity. By combining individual findings from transcriptomic data analysis and bioinformatics approaches, we identified overlapping regulatory networks that may be essential for shaping the local environment within infected samples towards successful viral propagation or control via immune activation mechanisms. The results from our experiments provide a new methodological approach towards improved comprehension of norovirus biology while simultaneously posing implications on therapeutic development against human gastroenteric diseases caused by viruses belonging to Caliciviridae family such as Norovirus and Sapovirus

title: Neutralizing Antibodies Targeting the Conserved Stem Region of Influenza Hemagglutinin
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach for inducing broad cross-reactive neutralizing antibodies to the conserved stem region of Influenza Hemagglutinin (HA) from various subtypes. Recent epidemics have highlighted the need for broadly protective and long-lasting immunity against influenza. Here, we report on the generation of a single immunogen capable of eliciting antibody-mediated responses that neutralize all known circulating strains of H1, H2 and H5 HA in mouse models. Candidates from our panel were tested in serum transfer protection assays and homologous virus challenge studies. Significantly, these findings demonstrate that targeting the highly conserved stem region can be used to develop potent therapeutic countermeasures as well as next-generation vaccines against emerging pandemics threats posed by an ever-diverse set of circulating influenza strains.

title: Immunogenicity of a recombinant coronavirus spike glycoprotein expressed in transgenic plants
abstract: Recently, it has been demonstrated that plants offer the possibility of producing low cost subunit vaccines that can be either parenterally or orally administered. Here we review data we obtained on the immunological response elicited by two recombinant versions of the glycoprotein S from the swine transmissible gastroenteritis coronavirus (TGEV) expressed in transgenic plants. Arabidopsis or potato plants were genetically transformed with cDNAs constructs encoding the N-terminal domain (aa residues 1–750) or the full-length glycoprotein S of TGEV, responsible for the neutralizing antibody induction against the virus, under the control of the cauliflower mosaic virus 35S (CaMV 35S) promoter. Genomic DNA and mRNA analysis of leave extracts from transformed plants demonstrated the incorporation of the foreign cDNA into the plant genomes as well as their transcription. Expression of recombinant polypeptides was observed in most transgenic plants by ELISA using specific antibodies. Mice immunized either parenterally with leave extracts from transgenic arabidopsis plants or, more interestingly, fed with potato tubers, developed antibodies that specifically reacted with TGEV in ELISA, immunoprecipitated the glycoprotein S and in some cases neutralized the virus infectivity. From the above results, we conclude that transgenic plants expressing glycoprotein S polypeptides may be potentially used as a source of recombinant antigen for vaccine production.

title: Metabolic Dysregulation in Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis
abstract: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) is a fibroproliferative disorder limited to the lung. New findings, starting from our proteomics studies on IPF, suggest that systemic involvement with altered molecular mechanisms and metabolic disorder is an underlying cause of fibrosis. The role of metabolic dysregulation in the pathogenesis of IPF has not been extensively studied, despite a recent surge of interest. In particular, our studies on bronchoalveolar lavage fluid have shown that the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system (RAAS), the hypoxia/oxidative stress response, and changes in iron and lipid metabolism are involved in onset of IPF. These processes appear to interact in an intricate manner and to be related to different fibrosing pathologies not directly linked to the lung environment. The disordered metabolism of carbohydrates, lipids, proteins and hormones has been documented in lung, liver, and kidney fibrosis. Correcting these metabolic alterations may offer a new strategy for treating fibrosis. This paper focuses on the role of metabolic dysregulation in the pathogenesis of IPF and is a continuation of our previous studies, investigating metabolic dysregulation as a new target for fibrosis therapy.

title: In Vitro and In Vivo Studies Identify Important Features of Dengue Virus pr-E Protein Interactions
abstract: This article presents an in-depth analysis of the interaction between prM and envelope proteins (pr-E) during replication of Dengue virus. Using a combination of in vitro and in vivo studies, researchers observed important features related to these interactions that are essential for successful infection. First, they determined that cleavage of the viral envelope protein precursor is dependent on host proteases. This was corroborated by testing different inhibitors with varying promiscuity profiles resulting in confirmation that subtiligase activity is required for successful pr-E cleavage and formation of mature virions. Additionally, genetic knockdown experiments revealed further insight into the interplay between viral polyproteins, demonstrating impacts to both function and location when individual gene products were removed from association networks. Furthermore observed differences in cell entry performance even among similar serotypes lead investigators to conclusively identify regions within pr-E’s fusion loop as misfolding hotspots which may influence recognition by target cell receptors leading to differential efficiency linked to virus infectivity potency across mutations targeting this element. Taken together these results establish a comprehensive understanding enabling more accurate modeling approaches for future drug design initiatives going forward against Dengue virus generated through structural elucidation efforts performed here at XYZ University laboratories

title: Nonspecific Proctitis: Association with Human Immunodeficiency Virus Infection in Homosexual Men
abstract: In a cross-sectional study of 140 homosexual men attending a sexually transmissible diseases clinic, the association between the presence of antibody to the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) and the presence of proctitis, as determined by histologic examination, as well as past or present exposure to other pathogens and details of sexual practices was analyzed. Significant associations with HIV seropositivity were found with the number of lifetime partners, positive treponemal serology, and evidence of previous infection with herpes simplex virus. However the major and unique finding was the strong and independent association between proctitis diagnosed by histologic criteria and seropositivity for HIV. Whether this is cause or effect awaits further elucidation.

title: Application of Epstein–Barr Virus for Optimization of Immortalized B-lymphocyte Production as a Positive Control in Genetic Studies
abstract: BACKGROUND: Infection of B-cells with Epstein–Barr virus (EBV) leads to more and subsequent immortalization. This is considered as the method of choice for generating lymphoblastoid cell lines (LCLs). Producing LCLs, although very useful but is very time consuming and troublesome, drives the requirement for quicker and more reliable methods for EBV-driven B-cell transformation. MATERIALS AND METHODS: After successfully production of LCLs, different parameters including temperature, serum concentration, type of culture medium, and CO(2) concentration were evaluated on EBV-transformed B-cells. In this study, we were able to produce LCLs and optimize condition. RESULTS: The best condition for generating LCLs was 37°C, 5% CO(2), 20% fasting blood sugar, and RPMI 1640. The study results were to establish a reliable method for producing LCLs that can be used to produce immortalized B-cells from almost any sources. CONCLUSION: This can help with tumorgenecity studies, as well as producing control material for rare genetic disorders and so on. The aim of this study was to determine optimized condition for reliable and reproducible LCLs from different sources.

title: Laboratory techniques of veterinary clinical immunology: A review
abstract: Laboratory tests currently used or easily applicable in veterinary clinical immunology were reviewed in the following three categories: (1) tests detecting disorders in humoral immune response: serum protein screening tests, gammaglobulin estimation and complement testing: (2) tests detecting disorders in cellular immune response: phagocyte function tests and lymphocyte function tests; (3) tests detecting autoimmune disorders: detection of antinuclear antibodies, rheumatoid factor, autoimmune hemolytic diseases, and autoimmune organ and tissue disorders. The principles of the tests and the interpretations of the results are presented with the appropriate references.

title: Computational inference of cancer-specific vulnerabilities in clinical samples
abstract: In this study, we investigate the potential for computationally inferring cancer-specific vulnerabilities in clinical samples. To do so, we leverage integrated genomics approaches such as existing functional annotation databases to harness insights into cancer biology while exploring novel signatures that can be observed at a molecular level. Through an analysis of genomic and transcriptomic data from multiple cancer types, we seek to identify generic pathways which may be exploited by therapeutic interventions. By examining large-scale transcriptomic profiles alongside known disease phenotypes in contemporary datasets, our aim is to develop a more nuanced understanding of how these processes interact at the cellular level and uncover putative oncogenic dependencies. We discuss the opportunities offered by computational inference of clinically relevant threats posed by individual cancers and its implications for personalized medicine strategies tailored to specific tumor subtypes.

title: Lead, a major environmental pollutant, is immunomodulatory by its differential effects on CD4(+) T cell subsets
abstract: This study investigates the potential immunomodulatory activity of lead, a major environmental pollutant, on CD4(+) T cell subsets. Lead exposure has long been linked to a variety of adverse health consequences and poses a serious public health threat. In recent years, however, research has pointed towards lead's ability to modulate immune responses in humans as well as animals. This phenomenon can be attributed to its capacity to induce changes in the circulating lymphocyte numbers and functions of CD4(+) T cells. The primary objective of this study is therefore to examine how lead alters key parameters related to both cytokine profi les and proliferation rates for each subset of CD4+T cells separately. Using an analytical approach combining flow cytometry analysis with functional assays such as CBA assay or ELSIA-based ELISpot assay we will assess differences between exposed groups vs unexposed cohorts controls at multiple levels before drawing logical inferences regarding mechanism effects affecting patients' health status upon chronic exposures. We hypothesise that our findings may suggest targeted interventions aimed at limiting susceptibility associated with chronic environmental exposure on diverse populations residing within contaminated areas from extensive industrial processes which are yet unregulated without suitable control measures implemented by international norms accepted across boarders worldwide.

title: Alterations in cell cycle dynamics in human endothelium cell culture infected with influenza virus
abstract: The cell cycle of endothelium EAhy 926 cell culture infected with influenza virus has been studied. Cytometric analysis of cell culture synchronized by contact inhibition revealed the elongation of the S phase of the cell cycle in EAhy 926 cells under the influence of influenza virus. This result was shown in an EAhy 926 culture infected with influenza virus and treated with nocodazole. Comparison of a lung carcinoma A549 cell line in which influenza virus causes G(0)/G(1) arrest and of an endothelial EAhy 926 cell line in which the same infection leads to S-phase elongation allows it to be suggested that different effects of influenza virus on cell cycle dynamics depend on the origin of infected cells.

title: Human Calicivirus-Associated Diarrhea In Children Attending Day Care Centers
abstract: The spread of human caliciviruses (HuCVs) is known to pose a threat to the health and well-being of children attending day care centers, yet the full scope of their associated symptoms among this vulnerable population remains largely unexplored. This study aims to evaluate HuCV-associated diarrhea in preschool-aged children receiving regular or occasional care at day care centers in a major metropolitan area. Data was gathered through questionnaires given to caregivers, observations by professionals, and stool sample analyses. Results were then compared between participants with different levels of exposure to HuCVs at participating day cares. Findings indicate that HuCV exposures can be linked directly with pre-diagnosed gastrointestinal problems resulting from recurrent bouts of acute diarrhea among those attending these facilities – providing important insight into evaluating potential policies for limiting outbreaks and illnesses amongst young students learning in close proximity.

title: Ricin and Shiga Toxins: Effects on Host Cell Signal Transduction
abstract: Shiga toxins and ricin are potent inhibitors of protein synthesis. In addition to causing inhibition of protein synthesis, these toxins activate proinflammatory signaling cascades that may contribute to the severe diseases associated with toxin exposure. Treatment of cells with Shiga toxins and ricin have been shown to activate a number of signaling pathways including those associated with the ribotoxic stress response, Nuclear factor kappa B activation, inflammasome activation, the unfolded protein response, mTOR signaling, hemostasis, and retrograde trafficking. In this chapter, we review our current understanding of these signaling pathways as they pertain to intoxication by Shiga toxins and ricin.

title: Pandemic influenza in Papua New Guinea: a modelling study comparison with pandemic spread in a developed country
abstract: This study investigates the discrepancies between pandemic influenza transmission dynamics in Papua New Guinea (PNG) compared to a developed country. Through epidemiological modelling, we examine the population-level effects of public health interventions for controlling and mitigating influenza within both settings. Simulated scenarios compare differences in social contact patterns, healthcare resources and socio-economic disparities on the spread of pandemic influenza. Results from the model highlight key implications for policy makers interested in understanding how social context impacts infectious disease control strategies; especially during outbreaks with global reach such as seasonal or avian influenza strains. With knowledge arising from this research, public health organizations are enabled to develop informed intervention mechanisms that effectively reduce morbidity and mortality related to epidemic waves of influenza virus infections among vulnerable populations worldwide.

With knowledge arising from this research, public health organizations are enabled to develop informed intervention mechanisms that effectively reduce morbidity and mortality related to epidemic waves of influenza virus infections among vulnerable populations worldwide.

title: The 2014–2015 Ebola outbreak in West Africa: Hands On
abstract:
The 2014–2015 Ebola Outbreak in West Africa: Hands On
This paper focuses on the vast effects of the 2014–2015 Ebola virus outbreak in West African nations. This was one of the most devastating and complex public health crises seen since modern records began. Through a combination of unprecedented challenges, from a lack of resources to inadequate political security, inadequate communication networks, and untrained health workers responsible for diagnosing and treating patients, this epidemic became an immense undertaking that demanded creative solutions with barely sufficient resources available. In addition to examining existing literature surrounding its longevity as well as treatment efficacy rates during this outbreak specifically analysis is made on innovative approaches developed by frontline actors throughout members’ states within the Mano River Union (MRU). Results suggest multi-level initiatives combining at both top-down state level decisions along with research into local programming grew increasingly successful over time while utilizing real time data gathering methods moved valuable information around quickly enabling faster response times across conflict ridden terrains . The collective voices provide advice regarding future pandemics drawing out conclusions advocating for comprehensive protocols expanding beyond merely medical personnel taking into account multiple societal sectors including education, agriculture & food security amongst others.

title: Estimating the age of Calliphora vicina eggs (Diptera: Calliphoridae): determination of embryonic morphological landmarks and preservation of egg samples
abstract: This study focuses on an important component in the field of forensic entomology: Estimating the age of Calliphora vicina eggs (Diptera: Calliphoridae). The importance of understanding development times for this species lies in its application to a variety of disciplines such as forensics and agriculture, with rapid aging methods significantly benefiting human resource management. To address this need, research was conducted on oviposition and resistance to dehydration, as well as morphological landmarks used for determining egg maturity. Additionally, preservation strategies were developed using glycerol-acetic acid buffers that improve storage life while preserving fertility potential. Results suggest that specific morphological landmarks correlate strongly to physiological staging during embryonic maturation and can be measured effectively within 1–3 days postoviposition. Furthermore, results also suggest a viable method for long-term storage if frozen at –20°C or lower; however care should be taken when applying preferential defrosting protocols due to the limited number of tests performed specifically regarding recombinant embryos from stored samples. Thus it appears glycerol-acetic acid buffering holds promise in terms of predictability when freezing C. vicina eggs over short time periods, providing valuable insights into extended sample survival capabilities necessary for certain species examination purposes such as criminal investigations related to corpse decomposition events where various insect stages are recovered from scene material during sequential sampling operations commonly referred by law enforcement practitioners.: 'Estimating the Age of Calliphora Vicina Eggs (Diptera: Calliphoridae): Determination Of Embryonic Morphological Landmarks And Preservation Of Egg Samples'.

title: Insights into the prognosis of lipidomic dysregulation for death risk in patients with coronary artery disease
abstract: BACKGROUND: Dyslipidaemia contributes to the progression of coronary artery disease (CAD) toward adverse outcomes. Plasma lipidomic measure may improve the prognostic performances of clinical endpoints of CAD. Our research is designed to identify the correlations between plasma lipid species and the risks of death, major adverse cardiovascular event (MACE) and left ventricular (LV) remodeling in patients with CAD. METHODS: A total of 1569 Chinese patients with CAD, 1011 single‐centre patients as internal training cohort, and 558 multicentre patients as external validation cohort, were enrolled. The concentration of plasma lipids in both cohorts was determined through widely targeted lipidomic profiling. Least absolute shrinkage and selection operator Cox and multivariate Cox regressions were used to develop prognostic models for death and MACE, respectively. RESULTS: Ten (Cer(d18:1/20:1), Cer(d18:1/24:1), PE(30:2), PE(32:0), PE(32:2), PC(O‐38:2), PC(O‐36:4), PC(16:1/22:2), LPC(18:2/0:0) and LPE(0:0/24:6)) and two (Cer(d18:1/20:1) and LPC(20:0/0:0)) lipid species were independently related to death and MACE, respectively. Cer(d18:1/20:1) and Cer(d18:1/24:1) were correlated with LV remodeling (P < .05). The lipidic panel incorporating 10 lipid species and two traditional biomarkers for predicting 5‐year death risk represented a remarkable higher discrimination than traditional model with increased area under the curve from 76.56 to 83.65%, continuous NRI of 0.634 and IDI of 0.131. Furthermore, the panel was successfully used in differentiating multicentre patients with low, middle, or high risks (P < .0001). Further analysis indicated that the number of double bonds of phosphatidyl choline and the content of carbon atoms of phosphatidyl ethanolamines were negatively associated with death risk. CONCLUSIONS: Improvement in the prediction of death confirms the effectiveness of plasma lipids as predictors to risk classification in patients with CAD. The association between the structural characteristics of long‐chain polyunsaturated fatty acids and death risk highlights the need for mechanistic research that characterizes the role of individual lipid species in disease pathogenesis.

title: The Respiratory Specimen Collection Trial (ReSpeCT): A Randomized Controlled Trial to Compare Quality and Timeliness of Respiratory Sample Collection in the Home by Parents and Healthcare Workers From Children Aged <2 Years
abstract: BACKGROUND: Most acute respiratory infection (ARI) research focuses on severe disease and overlooks the burden of community-managed illness. For community-based studies, home-based specimen collection by parents could be a resource-saving alternative to collection by healthcare workers (HCWs). In this study, we compared parent and HCW groups for their likelihood to collect specimens and the timeliness and quality of such collection. METHODS: In this unblinded randomized controlled trial, parents from Brisbane, Australia, were taught to identify new ARI episodes in their children aged <2 years. When their child had a new ARI, parents either collected a nasal swab from the child (P group) or contacted an HCW who visited to obtain a nasopharyngeal swab (HCW group). We compared the likelihood and timeliness of specimen collection and respiratory pathogen detection. A nested diagnostic study compared paired specimen collections from children in the HCW group. RESULTS: Included were 76 incident ARI episodes from 31 children and 102 episodes from 33 children in the P and HCW groups, respectively. The proportions of ARIs for which a specimen was collected were similar (P group, 69.7%; HCW group, 72.5%; P = .77), and pathogens were detected in 93.8% and 77.5% of the specimens, respectively (P = .03). The period between ARI onset and specimen collection was shorter in the P group than in the HCW group (mean difference, 1.9 days [95% confidence interval, 0.7–3.0 days]; P < .001). For the 69 paired specimens, viral loads were lower in the parent-collected swabs (mean cycle threshold difference, 4.5 [95% confidence interval, 3.1–5.9]; P < .001). CONCLUSIONS: Parents and HCWs obtained samples in similar proportions of ARI episodes, but the parents collected the samples fewer days after ARI onset and with a resulting higher likelihood of pathogen identification. This method can be used in population-based epidemiological studies of ARI as a resource-saving alternative. TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov identifier NCT00966069.

title: Coxsackievirus-cell interactions that initiate infection in porcine ileal explants
abstract: This study looks at how Coxsackievirus infection is initiated in porcine ileal explants. In recent years, the emergence of new enteric viruses has raised awareness regarding their virulence and replicative capacity. The aim of this study was to examine the interactions between Coxsackievirus (CV) strains and cells within porcine ileal explants using an electron microscope. Through these observations, we sought to gain an understanding as to which virus components interact with cells in order for CV infection initiation and establishment to occur. We discovered that while all CV serotypes tested have some ability to bind host IEC’s through unknown means, only a subset are able to sufficiently infect them at early stages post inoculation despite strain variability. Our findings illustrate differences between pathways employed by various strains during motoneuron attachment onto gut epithelia; noting that while adhesion molecules could be involved but need further investigation into specific ligand-receptor pairs responsible for viral binding events necessary for successful entry into gut cell junctions and thus initial replication of each strain throughout the intestine. Taken together our data suggest that distinct virus-cell attachment mechanisms mediate disease progression in pigs upon early exposure when compared with other species models such as humans, enabling us better understand treatment strategies unique for swine populations going forward [229 words]

title: Distinct Regulation of Host Responses by ERK and JNK MAP Kinases in Swine Macrophages Infected with Pandemic (H1N1) 2009 Influenza Virus
abstract: This paper investigates the distinct regulation of host responses in swine macrophages infected with pandemic (H1N1)-2009 influenza virus. Distinct but coordinated signalling pathways, comprised of extracellular signal-regulated kinases (ERK) and c-Jun N-terminal kinases (JNK), are important instigators of response to pathogenic insults. In this study, we highlighted how differentially regulated ERK and JNK MAP Kinase expression levels correlated with gene transcripts related to innate immune response within a population of swine macrophages challenged by H1N1 2009 Influenza Virus. Through qPCR analysis, immunofluorescence assays as well as inhibition studies using pharmacological LY294002 inhibitors for ERK/MAPKinase activation variation was determined. Results showed that both ERK and JNK likely have a pleotropic role in the remission or progression of sows’ macrophage immune responses to H1N12009 Infection by regulating cellular proliferation, cytokines production and apoptosis properties upon infection thereby presenting opportunities for functional health maintenance strategies targeting these two individual types of MAP Kinases  against other viral pathogens leading up to future promising treatments for diseases caused by such viruses including Swine Flu( HAN 1).

title: Enlightened Self-interest in Altruism (ESIA)
abstract: This paper addresses the surprisingly close relationship between enlightened self-interest and altruism, often assumed to oppose one another. By examining existing research in psychology, sociology, and economics, this study examines how motivated action driven by enlightened self-interest can lead to forms of unselfish behavior that might otherwise appear solely altruistic. Additionally, we uncover how a focus on both collective welfare via sociocultural dynamics as well as collaborative success derived from individual desires could generate more enduring outcomes than narrow self-preservation alone. Thus Enlightened Self-interest in Altruism (ESIA) is a primary consideration when viewing challenges within modern societies' complex socioecological landscapes. Through integration of behavioral science approaches including narrative coding and microlevel interview analysis with macrolevel system modeling strategies such as discrete event simulation models, we examine ESIA's associations with sustained communal activities related to environmental stewardship which have proved particularly resistant to traditional solo evaluations of prosociality or economic determinations alone.  Offering evidence for an integrated approach combining problem identification through varying viewpoints alongside investigative flexibility allows individuals—as well as organizations—to seize opportunities for meaningful causes affecting our shared future.

title: Complete Protection in Macaques Conferred by Purified Inactivated Zika Vaccine: Defining a Correlate of Protection
abstract: This study explores the immunologic protection against a Zika virus infection conferred by a purified, inactivated vaccine candidate in an animal model of human disease. The objective of this research is to define both the clinical and laboratory correlates of immunity against Zika Aedes-borne flavivirus after vaccination with Zanil, an attenuated live zika virus vaccine developed at PAHRC. In order to assess the breadth and strength of achievable protective responses in vaccinated macaques, several parameters were evaluated including neutralizing antibody titers determined by PRNT50 assay as well as histology and hematology tests. Results demonstrated complete protection against viremia and health symptoms associated with Vaccination with Zanil with no clinically significant safety outcomes following experimental challenge using 100xLD50 doses of ZIKV 180 days post vaccination; thereby providing support for further development as a means to protect people who are vulnerable to infection from ZIKV via mosquito transmission or other viruses belonging to this genus.

title: The Smartphone App haMSter for Tracking Patient-Reported Outcomes in People With Multiple Sclerosis: Protocol for a Pilot Study
abstract: BACKGROUND: Treatment and monitoring decisions in people with multiple sclerosis (MS) are based commonly on clinician-reported outcomes. These reflect physical and radiological disease activity and are the most relevant endpoints in clinical trials. Over the past few years, the number of studies evaluating so-called patient-reported outcomes (PROs) has been increasing. PROs are reports from patients concerning their own health perception. They are typically obtained by means of questionnaires and aim to quantify symptoms such as fatigue, depression, and sexual dysfunction. The emergence of PROs has made a tremendous contribution to understanding the individual impact of disease in people with MS and their health-related quality of life. However, the assessment of PROs consumes resources, including time and personnel. Thus, useful ways to conveniently introduce PROs into clinical practice are needed. OBJECTIVE: We aim to provide a rationale and pilot study protocol for a mobile health (mHealth) solution named “haMSter” that allows for remote monitoring of PROs in people with MS. METHODS: The core function of haMSter is to provide three scientifically validated PRO questionnaires relevant to MS for patients to fill out at home once a month. Thereby, longitudinal and remote documentation of PROs is enabled. A scoring algorithm graphically plots PRO scores over time and makes them available at the next visit. RESULTS: The pilot study is currently ongoing and will evaluate adherence to this mHealth solution in 50 patients over a period of 6 months. Results from the haMSter pilot study are expected in 2021. CONCLUSIONS: haMSter is a novel mHealth-based solution for modern PRO research, which may constitute the first step in achieving the ability to integrate PROs in clinical practice. This allows for a more problem-oriented approach in monitoring visits, which addresses patient needs and ultimately saves time. title: Applications of thiol-disulfide oxidoreductases for optimized in vivo production of functionally active proteins in Bacillus
abstract: This study focuses on the potential applications of thiol-disulfide oxidoreductases (Tsds) and their ability to optimize in vivo protein production in Bacillus. Recombinant expression of Tsds genes, fused with target proteins, have recently been proposed as an effective way to increase yields of a desired phenotype by decreasing unwanted posttranslational modifications. This approach has already demonstrated success in governing metabolism and redox balance, protein folding, assembly and secretion capacity but could also present novel means for producing more stable proteins in more complex systems such as whole cells or multi-enzyme pathways. Our aim is to evaluate the performance of this method within the context of improved functioning proteins at higher output when compared to conventional methods currently used for overproduciion of therapeutic proteins in bacteria. In order to pursue an analysis that incorporates all crucial aspects – from gene expression/regulation downstream product recovery results – comprehensive experiments will be needed: carried out using various organism models like gene knockouts or mutants combined with well characterized promoters operating via appropriate platforms depending on the application demands. The findings from these explorations should provide insights into how we can successfully exploit plant recombinant technology - relying upon Tsds enzymes - toward enhanced molecular end goals under prokaryotic constrained environments.

title: Host susceptibility to severe influenza A virus infection
abstract: The Influenza A virus (IAV) is one of the most important emerging infectious diseases, as it affects a wide range of hosts and can cause considerable morbidity and mortality. This study aimed to understand the host factors that contribute to severe IAV infections in humans. By comparing patient clinical histories, laboratory results and genetic data from more than 2000 individuals hospitalized with influenza across four continents over a five year period, we found specific genetic loci related to increased susceptibility of certain host populations to severe disease upon IAV infection. We also demonstrated that hereditary factors are linked with diverse severity outbreaks while accounting for age-stratified outcomes. Our findings are critical in determining high-risk subgroups for preventative or therapeutic interventions against severe IAV disease outcomes. title: Knowledge, Attitudes, and Interactions with Chaplains and Nursing Staff Outcomes: A Survey Study
abstract: We conducted a cross-sectional survey of nursing staff (n = 51) in an academic hospital finding a significant inverse relationship between the frequency of chaplaincy interaction and perceived stress (r = − 0.27, p = 0.05). We also found a significant positive relationship between rated importance of having a chaplain at the hospital and secondary trauma (r = 0.30, p = 0.03). There was a significant positive relationship between religiosity and rated importance for having a chaplain (r = 0.30, p = 0.03) and rated helpfulness of chaplains (r = 0.32, p = 0.02). Similarly, there was a significant positive relationship between spirituality and average length of conversations with a chaplain, rated importance for having a chaplain, and helpfulness of chaplains (r = 0.32, p = 0.03; r = 0.44, p = 0.001; and r = 0.52, p = 0.0001, respectively). Interaction with chaplains is associated with decreased employee perceived stress for nursing staff who provide care for severely ill patients.

title: Structural landscape of the complete genomes of dengue virus serotypes and other viral hemorrhagic fevers
abstract: BACKGROUND: With more than 300 million potentially infected people every year, and with the expanded habitat of mosquitoes due to climate change, Dengue virus (DENV) cannot be considered anymore only a tropical disease. The RNA secondary structure is a functional characteristic of RNA viruses, and together with the accumulated high-throughput sequencing data could provide general insights towards understanding virus biology. Here, we profiled the RNA secondary structure of > 7000 complete viral genomes from 11 different species focusing on viral hemorrhagic fevers, including DENV serotypes, EBOV, and YFV. RESULTS: In our work we demonstrated that the secondary structure and presence of protein-binding domains in the genomes can be used as intrinsic signature to further classify the viruses. With our predictive approach, we achieved high prediction scores of the secondary structure (AUC up to 0.85 with experimental data), and computed consensus secondary structure profiles using hundreds of in silico models. We observed that viruses show different structural patterns, where e.g., DENV-2 and Ebola virus tend to be less structured than the other viruses. Furthermore, we observed virus-specific correlations between secondary structure and the number of interaction sites with human proteins, reaching a correlation of 0.89 in the case of Zika virus. We also identified that helicases-encoding regions are more structured in several flaviviruses, while the regions encoding for the contact proteins exhibit virus-specific clusters in terms of RNA structure and potential protein-RNA interactions. We also used structural data to study the geographical distribution of DENV, finding a significant difference between DENV-3 from Asia and South-America, where the structure is also driving the clustering more than sequence identity, which could imply different evolutionary routes of this subtype. CONCLUSIONS: Our massive computational analysis provided novel results regarding the secondary structure and the interaction with human proteins, not only for DENV serotypes, but also for other flaviviruses and viral hemorrhagic fevers-associated viruses. We showed how the RNA secondary structure can be used to categorise viruses, and even to further classify them based on the interaction with proteins. We envision that these approaches can be used to further classify and characterise these complex viruses. SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1186/s12864-021-07638-7.

title: Diffusion in Dynamic Social Networks: Application in Epidemiology
abstract: This article provides an insight into the role of diffusion in dynamic social networks and its application to epidemiological models. We understand that there is a need for improved conceptualization in this field, particularly with respect to how dynamics shape and redirect the process of contagion through complex networks. This research seeks to explore the impacts on disease spread under different scenarios, while highlighting ways that epidemiological prediction could be enhanced by incorporating detailed observations on network movements. Our review examines established theories alongside contemporary empirical work using both computer simulations and real-world data sources. Bringing together disparate fields such as social epidemic theory, sociology, mathematics and health science, we show how our understanding of diffusion can assist in achieving timely identification of infectious outbreaks with potential implications across public health initiatives..

abstract: This study investigates the subversion of host innate immunity by Rickettsia australis, a bacterium closely related to Rickettsia rickettsii and vectors in some tick species. title: Psoas:lumbar vertebra index: central sarcopenia independently predicts morbidity in elderly trauma patients
abstract:
This article presents a study exploring the association between lower back vertebra index and sarcopenia, in relation to morbidity among elderly trauma patients. Growing evidence reveals that outcomes after traumatic injuries are further altered by age-related frailty conditions, including appetite decline, potential losses of muscle mass and strength referred to as sarcopenia. In particular, factors such as diminished psoas (hip flexor) size combined with increased lumbar vertebra sagittal index were observed in these individuals. The purpose of this investigation was therefore to examine if either central sarcopenia or changes in lower back shape could explain an elevated risk of morbidity following joint fractures encountered by geriatric individuals.

By utilizing data taken from medical records databases and anthropometric imaging software, we intended to measure the correlation between cumulative levels of hip flexor volume ratio or measures for lumbar vertebral curvature indices on clinical responses seen post-trauma amongst elderly patients discharged from hospital care during 2012-2015 period. Ultimately it was concluded that occurrences such as poor prognoses may be better understood when individual variations associated with both features are considered alongside one another; central sarcopenia could independently predict morbidity after broken bones experienced by aging persons admitted into hospitals; declined psoas muscle size unified with higher prevalence for vertebra angles provided key insights relating mortality gaps found within elderly individuals suffering similar traumas.

title: PKC promotes proliferation of airway smooth muscle cells by regulating cyclinD1 expression in asthmatic rats
abstract: AIM: To determine whether protein kinase C (PKC) has any effect on the expression of cyclinD1, a key regulator of growth control and G(1)/S transition, and to investigate the underlying molecular mechanisms of PKC involving the remodeling of the asthmatic airway smooth muscle (ASM). METHODS: The treatment of synchronized ASM cells from asthmatic rats with PKC-specific agonist phorbol 12-myristate 13-acetate (PMA) and antagonist 2-{1-[3-(amidinothio) propyl]-1H-indol-3-yl}-3-(1-methylindol-3-yl) maleimide methanesulfonate salt (Ro31-8220) was followed by the proliferation assay. PKCα and cyclinD1 expressions in ASM cells (ASMC) were detected by RT-PCR and Western blotting. The relation between PKCα and cyclinD1 was assessed by linear regression analysis. The effect of the construct recombinant plasmid pcDNA3.1-antisense cyclinD1 (pcDNA3.1-ascyclinD1) on the proliferation of ASMC was found to be induced by PMA. RESULTS: The data showed phorbol ester-dependent PKCα promoted the proliferation of ASMC. The closely-positive correlation existed between the expression of PKCα and cyclinD1 at the transcriptional (r=0.821, P<0.01) and transla-tional (r=0.940, P<0.01) levels. pcDNA3.1-ascyclinD1 could inhibit the proliferation of ASMC. pcDNA3.1-ascyclinD1 almost completely attenuated the PMA-induced proliferation effect as Ro31-8220+pcDNA3.1. CONCLUSION: The proliferation of ASMC by PKC might by regulated by the cyclinD1 expression in asthmatic rats.

title: Differential Regulation of Toll-Like Receptor-Mediated Cytokine Production by Unfolded Protein Response
abstract: This research paper explores the role of Unfolded Protein Response (UPR) on cytokine production through Toll-Like Receptor (TLR)-mediated pathways. To investigate the mechanistic relationship between UPR and TLRs in contributing to excessive proinflammatory cytokine secretion, cell culture experiments were performed under various conditions. Our results indicate differential regulation of TLR-mediated cytokine production by UPR, providing evidence for a complex host response to pathogen stimuli ultimately impacting inflammation levels.

title: The 2003 SARS Outbreak In Singapore: Epidemiological and Clinical Features, Containment Measures, and Lessons Learned
abstract:
The 2003 SARS Outbreak in Singapore: Epidemiological and Clinical Features, Containment Measures, and Lessons Learned 
In the winter of 2003, Singapore experienced a severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS) outbreak. This article examines the clinical epidemiology and containment measures taken during this event. Furthermore, it explores the lessons learned from the management of this transnational health threat to inform future preparedness efforts. By using published data sources such as official communicable disease reports, news articles, case definitions issued by global organizations like World Health Organization, we illustrate how international health surveillance and rapid response contributed to mitigating transmission of SARS in Singapore. Our findings conclude that an effective prevention strategy requires a holistic approach which takes into account public outreach for awareness raising, healthcare resources provision for timely diagnosis and treatment as well primary contact tracing efforts with support from local institutions such personnel quarantine facilities provided by various geographic zones across the country. We recommend policymakers apply the experience from managing SARS to ensure building societal resilience against infectious diseases in similar megacities around world now or then whether its via advanced digital technologies or other means available locally.

title: N-Myc expression enhances the oncolytic effects of vesicular stomatitis virus in human neuroblastoma cells
abstract: This study investigates the potential of N-Myc expression to enhance the oncolytic efficiency of vesicular stomatitis virus (VSV) in human neuroblastoma cells. Neuroblastoma is a common form of solid childhood cancer that presents a formidable therapeutic challenge, and therefore an improved anti-cancer approach is needed to manage it effectively. Upon infection with VSV, tumour-promoting genes such as N-Myc have been observed to induce greater cell death within the tumour owing to their cytotoxic effects. In this study we sought to explore how increasing expression levels of N-Myc affects VSV's efficacy in inducing tumorivorous effects against human neuroblastoma cells by utilizing both increases in viral replication and increased antigen presentation through direct cytolytic properties induced by elevated levels of N-Myc. Our findings suggest that high amounts of overstated N-Myc can significantly boost VSV’s oncolytic activity alongside other casein kinase 1α inhibitors, providing novel insight into adjuvant treatments for managing refractory forms of Neuroblastoma successfully.

title: Gene therapy for cystic fibrosis: an example for lung gene therapy
abstract: This paper examines the use of gene therapy for treating cystic fibrosis (CF) with a view to elucidating the potential efficacy of gene-based treatments for diseases that affect lung tissue. This review provides analysis of recent developments in the area, highlighting key issues faced in developing safe and efficacious therapies, such as target delivery and monitoring long-term outcomes. Emergent evidence from preclinical studies is discussed, together with stepwise approaches adopted by industrially funded clinical trials. Evidence supports the use of genetic medicines in treatment protocols; however, further investigations are required before it can be considered a reliable mode ofmanagementfor CF sufferers.It is hoped that this paper may provide insight into how combining therapeutic modalities can inform future strategies and encourage further research into advanced technologies to expand access to affordable personalized therapies

title: Therapeutic Vaccination in Chronic Hepatitis B: Preclinical Studies in the Woodchuck
abstract: The stillbirth of hepatitis B (HBV) remains a major global health concern driven by the lack of efficacious treatments. To address this challenge, our preclinical research explores the potential for therapeutic vaccination in chronic HBV as an approach to long-term control. In particular, we investigated and compared a recombinant woodchuck hepatitis virus nucleocapsid protein primed with DNA plus plasmid encodings HBsAg (D+P protocol) versus two other vaccine platforms, each alone or combinatorially used. Results indicate that D+P produced significant protective immunity on both humoral and cellular indictors relative to the other single approaches, thereby providing evidence of improved safety potential. Collectively our findings provide promising support towards development of therapeutic vaccinations against chronic HBV infection in humans warranting further investigation into clinical applications.
