title: An innovative approach to induce cross-protective immunity against porcine reproductive and respiratory syndrome virus in the lungs of pigs through adjuvanted nanotechnology-based vaccination
abstract: An innovative approach to induce cross-protective immunity against Porcine Reproductive and Respiratory Syndrome (PRRS) Virus in the lungs of pigs through Adjuvanted Nanotechnology-based Vaccination: An Examination of its Effects. This study examines how a novel nanotechnology vaccine delivery system affects the efficacy of vaccines for controlling PRRS virus infections in an animal model. Nanosized particles, such as DNA complexed with cationic lipids, have enhanced immunomodulatory properties, compared to conventional vaccination systems based on protein antigens or live viruses. With this method, successful antigen targeting is possible without requiring adjuvant stimulation or systemic activation of antibody production. By using these nanoformulations, the precise localization and controlled retention time of components within tissue sites can be achieved with superior control over traditional strategies which allow diffusion away from the target site after injection into circulation or other body cavities leading to reduced immune responses at desired sites. Thus it raises interest by providing an experimental means for fine tuning immunization protocols with higher reproducibility when required targeting specific subsets of immune cells attractive for combating viral diseases in multiple areas like lung carriers.

title: BRD4 inhibition exerts anti-viral activity through DNA damage-dependent innate immune responses
abstract: Chromatin dynamics regulated by epigenetic modification is crucial in genome stability and gene expression. Various epigenetic mechanisms have been identified in the pathogenesis of human diseases. Here, we examined the effects of ten epigenetic agents on pseudorabies virus (PRV) infection by using GFP-reporter assays. Inhibitors of bromodomain protein 4 (BRD4), which receives much more attention in cancer than viral infection, was found to exhibit substantial anti-viral activity against PRV as well as a range of DNA and RNA viruses. We further demonstrated that BRD4 inhibition boosted a robust innate immune response. BRD4 inhibition also de-compacted chromatin structure and induced the DNA damage response, thereby triggering the activation of cGAS-mediated innate immunity and increasing host resistance to viral infection both in vitro and in vivo. Mechanistically, the inhibitory effect of BRD4 inhibition on viral infection was mainly attributed to the attenuation of viral attachment. Our findings reveal a unique mechanism through which BRD4 inhibition restrains viral infection and points to its potent therapeutic value for viral infectious diseases.

title: Inclusion of Additional Unintended Consequences in Economic Evaluation: A Systematic Review of Immunization and Tuberculosis Cost-Effectiveness Analyses
abstract: This paper aims to examine the inclusion of additional unintended consequences in economic evaluation through a systematic review of immunization and tuberculosis cost-effectiveness analyses. Despite the use of health economic evaluations as tools for informed policy decisions, methodological limitations may hinder their effectiveness at capturing all relevant information related to impact on population health outcomes. These can include economically relevant effects not explicitly accounted for in reported estimates, such as indirect costs resulting from additional program activities and wider social impacts. In this study, an extensive search was conducted across four major databases to identify immune-mediated interventions that assessed both direct and indirect or secondary cost implications of interventions aimed at controlling TB designed with microsimulation models. The review focused on quantifiable aspects including disease incidence rate reduction; mortality rate changes; vaccination price settings; and specific populations considered within respective studies. As such, this systematic overview provides valuable insights for improving current practices of economic analysis methodologies used in evaluating large scale public health programs by ensuring consideration must be given to all elements associated with any program implementation offered for prolonged efficacy over time.

title: Rotavirus in infant-toddler day care centers: Epidemiology relevant to disease control strategies()
abstract:
Abstract 
A study on rotavirus and its incidence in infant-toddler day care centers was conducted to examine the epidemiology and disease control strategies for successful management of this gastrointestinal virus. We collected data from two cohorts, one consisting of 46 infants aged 4 weeks old to 12 months attending a university-affiliated daycare center in Seoul, South Korea over a four month period; while the other consisted of 2 extended families with 77 infants aged 4 weeks old to 11 Months during their homestay. Data analysis indicated that there were no overt clinical signs or symptoms among the children reviewed; however, fecal samples tested positive for rotavirus in 25% percent (n = 24) of cases across both cohorts. To provide protection against viruses circulating within child care contexts, preventative methods are recommended such as policies for exclusion and readmission criteria if applicable with special consideration given towards parents opting out of immunizations and sanitation practices including stringent handwashing guidelines as well as safe handling/preparation protocols for food products consumed by staff or children within close proximity settings.

title: A Novel Host-Proteome Signature for Distinguishing between Acute Bacterial and Viral Infections
abstract: Bacterial and viral infections are often clinically indistinguishable, leading to inappropriate patient management and antibiotic misuse. Bacterial-induced host proteins such as procalcitonin, C-reactive protein (CRP), and Interleukin-6, are routinely used to support diagnosis of infection. However, their performance is negatively affected by inter-patient variability, including time from symptom onset, clinical syndrome, and pathogens. Our aim was to identify novel viral-induced host proteins that can complement bacterial-induced proteins to increase diagnostic accuracy. Initially, we conducted a bioinformatic screen to identify putative circulating host immune response proteins. The resulting 600 candidates were then quantitatively screened for diagnostic potential using blood samples from 1002 prospectively recruited patients with suspected acute infectious disease and controls with no apparent infection. For each patient, three independent physicians assigned a diagnosis based on comprehensive clinical and laboratory investigation including PCR for 21 pathogens yielding 319 bacterial, 334 viral, 112 control and 98 indeterminate diagnoses; 139 patients were excluded based on predetermined criteria. The best performing host-protein was TNF-related apoptosis-inducing ligand (TRAIL) (area under the curve [AUC] of 0.89; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.86 to 0.91), which was consistently up-regulated in viral infected patients. We further developed a multi-protein signature using logistic-regression on half of the patients and validated it on the remaining half. The signature with the highest precision included both viral- and bacterial-induced proteins: TRAIL, Interferon gamma-induced protein-10, and CRP (AUC of 0.94; 95% CI, 0.92 to 0.96). The signature was superior to any of the individual proteins (P<0.001), as well as routinely used clinical parameters and their combinations (P<0.001). It remained robust across different physiological systems, times from symptom onset, and pathogens (AUCs 0.87-1.0). The accurate differential diagnosis provided by this novel combination of viral- and bacterial-induced proteins has the potential to improve management of patients with acute infections and reduce antibiotic misuse.

title: Molecular Detection, Phylogenetic Analysis, and Identification of Transcription Motifs in Feline Leukemia Virus from Naturally Infected Cats in Malaysia
abstract: A nested PCR assay was used to determine the viral RNA and proviral DNA status of naturally infected cats. Selected samples that were FeLV-positive by PCR were subjected to sequencing, phylogenetic analysis, and motifs search. Of the 39 samples that were positive for FeLV p27 antigen, 87.2% (34/39) were confirmed positive with nested PCR. FeLV proviral DNA was detected in 38 (97.3%) of p27-antigen negative samples. Malaysian FeLV isolates are found to be highly similar with a homology of 91% to 100%. Phylogenetic analysis revealed that Malaysian FeLV isolates divided into two clusters, with a majority (86.2%) sharing similarity with FeLV-K01803 and fewer isolates (13.8%) with FeLV-GM1 strain. Different enhancer motifs including NF-GMa, Krox-20/WT1I-del2, BAF1, AP-2, TBP, TFIIF-beta, TRF, and TFIID are found to occur either in single, duplicate, triplicate, or sets of 5 in different positions within the U3-LTR-gag region. The present result confirms the occurrence of FeLV viral RNA and provirus DNA in naturally infected cats. Malaysian FeLV isolates are highly similar, and a majority of them are closely related to a UK isolate. This study provides the first molecular based information on FeLV in Malaysia. Additionally, different enhancer motifs likely associated with FeLV related pathogenesis have been identified.

title: Community-setting pneumonia-associated hospitalizations by level of urbanization—New York City versus other areas of New York State, 2010–2014
abstract: BACKGROUND: New York City (NYC) reported a higher pneumonia and influenza death rate than the rest of New York State during 2010–2014. Most NYC pneumonia and influenza deaths are attributed to pneumonia caused by infection acquired in the community, and these deaths typically occur in hospitals. METHODS: We identified hospitalizations of New York State residents aged ≥20 years discharged from New York State hospitals during 2010–2014 with a principal diagnosis of community-setting pneumonia or a secondary diagnosis of community-setting pneumonia if the principal diagnosis was respiratory failure or sepsis. We examined mean annual age-adjusted community-setting pneumonia-associated hospitalization (CSPAH) rates and proportion of CSPAH with in-hospital death, overall and by sociodemographic group, and produced a multivariable negative binomial model to assess hospitalization rate ratios. RESULTS: Compared with non-NYC urban, suburban, and rural areas of New York State, NYC had the highest mean annual age-adjusted CSPAH rate at 475.3 per 100,000 population and the highest percentage of CSPAH with in-hospital death at 13.7%. NYC also had the highest proportion of CSPAH patients residing in higher-poverty-level areas. title: Lack of protection in vivo with neutralizing monoclonal antibodies to transmissible gastroenteritis virus
abstract: The threat of transmissible gastroenteritis virus (TGEV) continues to impact animal health and welfare worldwide. Despite the development of several neutralizing monoclonal antibodies that are seen to protect against TGEV in laboratory settings, their clinical efficacy remains largely unknown. The purpose of this study was to assess the protection conferred by these antibodies in vivo. Data was collected from a cohort of pigs infected with TGEV and given different dosages and formulations of antibody treatments prior to exposure. Results demonstrated that higher doses with optimal formulation reduced viral copy number, provided clearer lungs scores at necropsy, better overall body condition score and fewer alveolar macrophagocytes compared to untreated control animals. This suggests that whilst protective effects can be achieved ex vivo, further exploration is needed into developing optimal protocols for maximizing protective benefits via neutralizing monoclonal antibody therapy in an in vivo setting for TGEv.,

title: What We Think About When We Think About Triffids: The Monstrous Vegetal in Post-war British Science Fiction
abstract: In the face of continuing post-war reconstruction and the rising tide of urbanization, British science fiction writers such as John Wyndham (a pseudonym for John Beynon Harris) and John Christopher (Sam Youd) portrayed post-apocalyptic scenarios in which the vegetal directly determines the fate of human civilization. By destabilizing the relationship between plant and human, Wyndham and Christopher open up a space to reconsider the vegetal as a distinct life form itself, beyond its instrumental use-value, or as an anthropomorphized reflection of human thought. Although plant life is traditionally defined by its inability to move or to speak, both writers suggest that communication bound to the visual or oral is highly limited (for instance, human sight is confined to a limited spectrum). In Wyndham’s The Day of the Triffids (1951) plants become mobile and seemingly sentient, in the process becoming an invasive presence that exposes and challenges the limits of anthropocentric thought. By contrast, in Christopher’s The Death of Grass (1956), the absence of the vegetal renders manifest the subaltern status of plant life, while suggesting that plants are able to communicate through their materiality and posture. Both texts signal that what is conventionally understood as Other is actually a blank repository that ventriloquizes humans’ unconscious desire. Following the population’s sudden loss of sight in The Day of the Triffids, the characters begin to project their own thoughts and emotions onto the triffids, which highlights the indeterminate limits of anthropomorphic representation. The Death of Grass demonstrates that such anthropocentrism constitutes an act of metaphysical violence that, at the same time, under-imagines plant life and installs specialist terminology and botanical classification as a substitute. Presenting the relationship between plant life and human life as a contested space, these texts manifest the problem of anthropocentric certainties and the absolute alterity of plant-thought.

title: T-cell expression of Bruton’s tyrosine kinase promotes autoreactive T-cell activation and exacerbates aplastic anemia
abstract: The role of Bruton’s tyrosine kinase (BTK) in BCR signaling is well defined, and BTK is involved in B-cell development, differentiation, and malignancies. However, the expression of Btk in T cells and its role in T-cell function remain largely unknown. Here, we unexpectedly found high expression and activation of BTK in T cells. Deficiencies in BTK resulted in the impaired activation and proliferation of autoreactive T cells and ameliorated bone marrow failure (BMF) in aplastic anemia. Mechanistically, BTK is activated after TCR engagement and then phosphorylates PLCγ1, thus promoting T-cell activation. Treatment with acalabrutinib, a selective BTK inhibitor, decreased T-cell proliferation and ameliorated BMF in mice with aplastic anemia. Our results demonstrate an unexpected role of BTK in optimal T-cell activation and in the pathogenesis of autoimmune aplastic anemia, providing insights into the molecular regulation of T-cell activation and the pathogenesis of T-cell-mediated autoimmune disease.

title: A nationwide assessment of the burden of healthcare-associated infections and antimicrobial use among surgical patients: results from Serbian point prevalence survey, 2017
abstract: This abstract presents the findings of a nationwide point prevalence survey conducted in Serbia in 2017, which investigated the burden of healthcare-associated infections (HCAI) and associated antimicrobial use among surgical patients. The survey was part of an epidemiological project to better understand the magnitude and pattern of HCAIs and antimicrobial utilization in care settings across Serbian hospitals. Data from over 1500 surgical patient records were analyzed to estimate both the prevalence and complexity of HCAIs, as well as specific patterns precipitating their development or resolved with targeted interventions. Results suggest that around 11% of admitted patients had at least one active systemic infection at admission or did develop one during hospitalization. Bacterial etiologies predominated among them with Gram-negative bacteria being most prevalent (63%). Primary prophylaxis for infectious complications accounted for more than 18% all observed antimicrobial prescriptions nation wide while only 4% were designated for preoperative preventive antibiotics administration. This study highlights some important gaps between existing evidence base and best practice recommendations providing key indicators that can inform updated standards workable within Serbian health care context. Furthermore, it provides valuable groundwork on which future intervention efforts should focus to decrease adversities due to inappropriate antibiotic use along with reduction in morbidity related to HAI occurrence.

title: Anti-inflammatory effect of torilidis fructus ethanol extract through inhibition of Src
abstract:
This article introduces a new discovery of the anti-inflammatory effect Torilidis Fructus toxin by ethanol extract and Src inhibition. Traditionally, Torilidis Fructus has been used for its medical properties in East Asian cultures for centuries. Clinical trials have highlighted its efficacy in treating microbial infections as well as inflammation-related diseases. Recent studies funded by the National Key R&D Program of China evaluated this plant extract's potential effects against immune system disorders caused by excessive cytokine release from activated macrophages, such as rheumatoid arthritis (RA). Results show that ethanol extracts significantly reduced high levels of proinflammatory mediators through the inhibition of non-receptor tyrosine Src kinases – suggesting an effective therapeutic tool to treat RA and other related conditions. We aim to highlight these findings through discussing the effects of Torilidis Fructus on inflammatory response using specific cellular mechanisms and cleavage activity while providing further suggestions towards future research directions into establishing novel treatments against chronic illnesses. 

Abstract: This article describes experimental evidence demonstrating the effectiveness of Torilidis Fructus ethanol extract on reducing inflammation via inhibiting Tyr525/526 phosphorylation sites within Src proteins. Cell lines exposed to secretion histamines were treated with incremental concentrations of ethanolic extracts derived from Tlf which demonstrated a significant decrease in proinflammatory response when compared with untreated groups; showing potential clinical application for inflammatory illnesses including rheumatoid arthritis . These results support previous confirmation of antifungal activities linked to Tlf components whilst presenting new insights into potentially targeting src signalling pathways which suggest positive future outcomes into discovering alternative therapies where traditional medications may be unsuccessful or failed altogether.

title: Application of Epstein–Barr Virus for Optimization of Immortalized B-lymphocyte Production as a Positive Control in Genetic Studies
abstract: The Epstein–Barr virus (EBV) has long been utilized for the purpose of generating stable immortalized B-lymphocyte cell lines, however there is still unclear knowledge regarding their optimization as positive control material in genetic studies. This paper presents a study conducted to optimize EBV-immortalized B-lymphocytes production through understanding the interaction between cellular metabolism regulation and viral oncoproteins in order to create an optimized environment with consistent growth rates over a 5 month period. The findings of this research support that application of EBV can be used effectively as a reliable source of positive control towards implementation into genetic testing procedures suitable for modeling advanced bioprocesses or further analysis within the field.

title: Innate Immune Responses to Avian Influenza Viruses in Ducks and Chickens
abstract: Mallard ducks are important natural hosts of low pathogenic avian influenza (LPAI) viruses and many strains circulate in this reservoir and cause little harm. Some strains can be transmitted to other hosts, including chickens, and cause respiratory and systemic disease. Rarely, these highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) viruses cause disease in mallards, while chickens are highly susceptible. The long co-evolution of mallard ducks with influenza viruses has undoubtedly fine-tuned many immunological host–pathogen interactions to confer resistance to disease, which are poorly understood. Here, we compare innate responses to different avian influenza viruses in ducks and chickens to reveal differences that point to potential mechanisms of disease resistance. Mallard ducks are permissive to LPAI replication in their intestinal tissues without overtly compromising their fitness. In contrast, the mallard response to HPAI infection reflects an immediate and robust induction of type I interferon and antiviral interferon stimulated genes, highlighting the importance of the RIG-I pathway. Ducks also appear to limit the duration of the response, particularly of pro-inflammatory cytokine expression. Chickens lack RIG-I, and some modulators of the signaling pathway and may be compromised in initiating an early interferon response, allowing more viral replication and consequent damage. We review current knowledge about innate response mediators to influenza infection in mallard ducks compared to chickens to gain insight into protective immune responses, and open questions for future research.

title: An experience of subglottic airway foreign body removal in a patient under tracheal intubation: a case report
abstract: This case report presents a rare, complex procedure for the successful removal of a subglottic airway foreign body from an intubated patient. It offers insights into preoperative assessment and preparation, surgical technique and postoperative considerations in order to minimize potential complications while maximizing procedural outcomes. The authors provide details on the unique circumstances that demanded innovative techniques during this challenging management which could benefit other caregivers facing similar scenarios. This report illuminates how understanding of anatomy combined with effective problem-solving enabled a patient's successful recovery under what otherwise would have been an impossible situation.

title: Comparison of Influenza Epidemiological and Virological Characteristics between Outpatients and Inpatients in Zhejiang Province, China, March 2011–June 2015
abstract: This study examines the epidemiological and virological characteristics of Influenza in Zhejiang, China from March 2011 to June 2015. The comparison was conducted for outpatients and inpatients separately. Epidemiological characteristics such as seasonal trends, transmission rate, and age-group distribution were recorded for both groups. Additionally, isolates of influenza virus detected from these patients were collected during this period and analyzed to develop their genotypic diversity using reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) techniques along with a clade based phylogenetic tree analysis. Using chi square/Fisher exact testing, the results showed statistically significant differences between each group’s epidemic curve especially early November–January season which had more cultivable viruses being cultivated off the inpatient population than outpatient population (p<0.01). Furthermore, an implication drawn based on these findings indicated that there might be an effect present where Influenza virus is circulating faster among closed populations such as hospitals rather than open communities like outlying areas under same climate conditions .

title: Using Google Trends to Examine the Spatio-Temporal Incidence and Behavioral Patterns of Dengue Disease: A Case Study in Metropolitan Manila, Philippines
abstract:
This article demonstrates an innovative approach to exploring the spatio-temporal incidence and behavioral patterns of Dengue Disease using Google Trends in Metropolitan Manila, Philippines. This study provides an additional vantage point for understanding the spread of this medical condition both geographically and temporally through retrospective tracking of online search engine data. Secondly, it highlights how research findings can be utilized to inform relevant public health policies for dengue disease prevention and control on a city-wide scale. 

We adopt a mixed method approach by combining ecological analysis with keyword suggestions from online search history data generated from Google Trends. Our results demonstrate trends over time that suggests potential associations of geographic areas with peak seasonality as well as increasing levels of concern in pursuing related knowledge as shown by bouts of Dengue searches originating mainly during outbreaks periods. 

The implications drawn from our work serves twofold: (i) To bridge the gap between multiple disciplines such as geospatial analytics, epidemiology; and information science to enable better public health decision making through the integration and use of big data sources; (ii) To provide City Governments insight into informative traceable indicators when planning preventive strategies associated with communicable diseases given advances in technology like geospatial mapping tools coupled with big datasets derived from popular internet engines like Google ‘search'.   Finally, it establishes substantial evidence to suggest that using surrogate measures provided by online data systems can serve useful purposes within area contextually depending on targeted application domains

title: Synthesis, Characterization, and Anti-Cancer Activity of Some New N′-(2-Oxoindolin-3-ylidene)-2-propylpentane hydrazide-hydrazones Derivatives
abstract: Eight novel N′-(2-oxoindolin-3-ylidene)-2-propylpentane hydrazide-hydrazone derivatives 4a–h were synthesized and fully characterized by IR, NMR ((1)H-NMR and (13)C-NMR), elemental analysis, and X-ray crystallography. The cyto-toxicity and in vitro anti-cancer evaluation of the prepared compounds have been assessed against two different human tumour cell lines including human liver (HepG2) and leukaemia (Jurkat), as well as in normal cell lines derived from human embryonic kidney (HEK293) using MTT assay. The compounds 3e, 3f, 4a, 4c, and 4e revealed promising anti-cancer activities in tested human tumour cells lines (IC(50) values between 3 and 7 μM) as compared to the known anti-cancer drug 5-Fluorouracil (IC(50) 32–50 μM). Among the tested compounds, 4a showed specificity against leukaemia (Jurkat) cells, with an IC(50) value of 3.14 μM, but this compound was inactive in liver cancer and normal cell lines.

title: Genomic analysis of codon usage shows influence of mutation pressure, natural selection, and host features on Marburg virus evolution
abstract: BACKGROUND: The Marburg virus (MARV) has a negative-sense single-stranded RNA genome, belongs to the family Filoviridae, and is responsible for several outbreaks of highly fatal hemorrhagic fever. Codon usage patterns of viruses reflect a series of evolutionary changes that enable viruses to shape their survival rates and fitness toward the external environment and, most importantly, their hosts. To understand the evolution of MARV at the codon level, we report a comprehensive analysis of synonymous codon usage patterns in MARV genomes. Multiple codon analysis approaches and statistical methods were performed to determine overall codon usage patterns, biases in codon usage, and influence of various factors, including mutation pressure, natural selection, and its two hosts, Homo sapiens and Rousettus aegyptiacus. RESULTS: Nucleotide composition and relative synonymous codon usage (RSCU) analysis revealed that MARV shows mutation bias and prefers U- and A-ended codons to code amino acids. Effective number of codons analysis indicated that overall codon usage among MARV genomes is slightly biased. The Parity Rule 2 plot analysis showed that GC and AU nucleotides were not used proportionally which accounts for the presence of natural selection. Codon usage patterns of MARV were also found to be influenced by its hosts. This indicates that MARV have evolved codon usage patterns that are specific to both of its hosts. Moreover, selection pressure from R. aegyptiacus on the MARV RSCU patterns was found to be dominant compared with that from H. sapiens. Overall, mutation pressure was found to be the most important and dominant force that shapes codon usage patterns in MARV. CONCLUSIONS: To our knowledge, this is the first detailed codon usage analysis of MARV and extends our understanding of the mechanisms that contribute to codon usage and evolution of MARV. ELECTRONIC SUPPLEMENTARY MATERIAL: The online version of this article (doi:10.1186/s12862-015-0456-4) contains supplementary material, which is available to authorized users.

title: The Potential Neuroprotective Role of Free and Encapsulated Quercetin Mediated by miRNA against Neurological Diseases
abstract: Chronic neuroinflammation is a pathological condition of numerous central nervous system (CNS) diseases such as Parkinson’s disease, Alzheimer’s disease, multiple sclerosis, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and many others. Neuroinflammation is characterized by the microglia activation and concomitant production of pro-inflammatory cytokines leading to an increasing neuronal cell death. The decreased neuroinflammation could be obtained by using natural compounds, including flavonoids known to modulate the inflammatory responses. title: Structural landscape of the complete genomes of dengue virus serotypes and other viral hemorrhagic fevers
abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive analysis of the structural features of complete genome sequences of Dengue virus (DENV) and other viral hemorrhagic fevers. DENV serotypes, along with seven additional VHFs are characterized in terms of their genetic structure as well as nucleotide and amino acid compositions. A systematic comparison between the non-structural proteins (NSPs), against all 8 VHFs was conducted to gain insight into some common motifs or similar characteristics which exist amongst them. It was found that despite their individual differences, there were several consensus sites across NSPS including periodic cleavage signals and specific glycosylation system components from the various viruses studied. Furthermore, detailed statistics regarding CpG intron rich regions were reported for each sequence type allowing future studies to take on comparative investigations in relating gene expression levels to these positions where such high densities occur. In conclusion, this study offers greater understanding on how genomes sequencing can help elucidate effective epidemiological management strategies for dengue fever and related viral diseases

title: Estimating the age of Calliphora vicina eggs (Diptera: Calliphoridae): determination of embryonic morphological landmarks and preservation of egg samples
abstract: Blow fly eggs may sometimes be the only entomological evidence recovered in a forensic case, especially in cooler weather when hatching might take several days: hence, a method for estimating their age is greatly needed. However, developmental data on blow fly eggs are mainly limited to records of the time to larval hatching. The current paper describes the morphological changes occurring during embryogenesis of the blow fly Calliphora vicina Robineau-Desvoidy and their timing in relation to temperature, in order to determine those characters which can be used for simple egg age estimation using light microscopy. At 7.3 and 25 °C, 15 easily visualised morphological landmarks were determined in C. vicina living embryos, allowing for their age estimation with a resolution of 10–20 % of total egg developmental time. The observed age intervals were compared to the embryonic stages described for the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster Meigen, which are used as reference data in multiple developmental studies. Moreover, current guidelines for preservation of egg samples, which recommend the placement of living eggs directly into 80 % ethanol, were tested against the hot water killing (HWK) method prior to preservation in 80 % ethanol, recommended for larval and pupal specimens. Direct placement of eggs into 80 % ethanol caused marked decomposition of samples, and no morphological landmarks were discernible. On the other hand, HWK fixation prior to preservation in 80 % ethanol enabled visualisation of 11 of the 15 age-specific morphological landmarks that were discernible in living embryos. Therefore, HWK fixation prior to preservation in 80 % ethanol is recommended for egg samples, thus unifying the protocols for collecting entomological evidence.

title: Assessment of the ability of V920 recombinant vesicular stomatitis-Zaire ebolavirus vaccine to replicate in relevant arthropod cell cultures and vector species
abstract: This article examines the capacity of V920 recombinant vesicular stomatitis-Zaire ebolavirus (rVSV-ZEBOV) vaccine to replicate in relevant arthropod cell cultures and vector species. The ebola virus is a highly infectious, lethal pathogen that has caused numerous outbreaks in humans since its first discovery in 1976. With such high mortality rates associated with infection, there is an urgent need for a safe and effective vaccine solution against this deadly disease. Along these lines, the rVSV-ZEBOV vaccine was developed as an immunization tool specifically targeting the Zaire strain of Ebola virus. This study aimed to assess if vaccination leads to replication of the V920 recombinant reproductive form within arthropod cell cultures and vector species; thus giving insight into potential competence with regards to transmission by vectors. By understanding how suitably V920 peptides interact with mosquito or tick cells, critical information can be gained pertaining to both susceptibility profiles and development of candidate vaccines against future outbreaks involving those specific organisms or their kin.

title: Spontaneous repulsion in the [Formula: see text] reaction on coupled networks
abstract: This paper will examine a new phenomenon observed in the [Formula: see text] reaction on coupled networks. In particular, we demonstrate for the first time the spontaneous repulsion of components when a certain reaction threshold is reached. Our findings are based on an extensive laboratory study, which provides key insight into how repulsion can bring about significant changes in chemical reactions that are conducted between two or more units of a networked system. We explain our theoretical analysis and provide evidence to support its validity through simulation experiments performed over several cycles with increasing amounts of reactants as input parameters. The results show that beyond this critical threshold point, both forward and backward reactions expel their reactant sites until equilibrium is eventually restored again after some time lapse, leading to what appears to be macroscopic oscillations in properties. This effect could have remarkable implications for further research studies dealing with catalysis-related processes involving interfacial states and nano-structures, thus facilitating various new technological applications in dynamic energy conversion schemes.

title: Unified Theory of Bacterial Sialometabolism: How and Why Bacteria Metabolize Host Sialic Acids
abstract: This study presents a Unified Theory of Bacterial Sialometabolism – a comprehensive approach to elucidate the specific modes and biological functions behind how and why bacteria metabolize host sialic acids. Although previous research has outlined several candidates for bacterial sialidases, their exact roles remain unknown. By conducting both enzymatic assays and ectopic expression, we discovered that Type III Secretion System-secreted proteins can catalyze hydrolytic cleavage of these molecules in E. coli cells via trans-sialidase activity under physiological conditions. Our results further show an essential role for this enzyme family in nutrient scavenging during infection, with potential implications extending to other forms of limiting metabolic environments observed throughout nature. This novel theory provides important insight into bacterial nutrition strategies by highlighting both known and unanticipated utilization mechanisms involving predator–prey interactions between pathogenic microorganisms and their mammalian hosts.

title: AI-driven deep CNN approach for multi-label pathology classification using chest X-Rays
abstract: This paper presents an AI-driven deep Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) approach for multi-label pathology classification using chest X-Rays. In the last decade, advances in Artificial Intelligence (AI) and medical imaging technologies have enabled computer vision to make diagnosis from organs’ images with high accuracy. The development of strong machine learning models able to extract features diagnostically useful from Digital X-Rays allowing a differential diagnosis has been pioneered by researchers in Chest Imaging Analysis (CIA). However, a satisfactory performance on large datasets such as Multi Label BronchoPneumopaty Quantification Dataset is still lacking, motivating the research herein presented. Our work proposes a two steps CNNs architecture trained end-to-end that benefits from both higher level abstractions of convolutional layers as well as low level details extracted with deep residual blocks. Experiments reveal very encouraging results which attest this method competency to assign seven distinct subtle pathological labels pertaining to complex thorax anatomy according FIGO and WHO Classification Systems guidelines with promising scores measured through Cohen's Kappa coefficient metrics and precision/recall rates greater than 0.8 area under curves evaluation support our hypothesis and provide invaluable digital diagnostic assistance effectively incorporated into clinical practice workflow routines without compromising patient safety standards while greatly increasing healthcare delivery efficacy in remote facilities or challenges posed by time constraints providing global access to cost effective timely diagnoses accurately attained reducing human error risk factors prevention oriented better outcomes inevitably impacting millions of lifes worldwide eventually reaching UN Sustainable Development Goals 2030 target objectives

title: Adaptive social contact rates induce complex dynamics during epidemics
abstract: This paper examines the effects of adaptive social contact rates on epidemiological dynamics. Recent studies have demonstrated that dynamic changes in patterns of human behavior during pandemics can substantially influence disease spread. Using numerical simulation and mathematical analysis, we explore the impact of varying levels of contact rate adaptation strategies on epidemiology within a well-defined theoretical model framework. In particular, we focus on different types of contact rate adaptations - both random and strategic - in comparison to fixed baseline scenarios where social distancing measures are held constant throughout an epidemic outbreak. Our results suggest that this type of intervention has strong implications for disease control, vaccine efficacy and reach, as well as resource allocation optimization during pandemic management interventions. Furthermore, our findings provide valuable insight into how maximal public health benefits can be achieved through health policy implementation geared towards adapting behavioral networks according to changing transmission scenarios under realistic assumptions about population structure and individual decision making processes around social contacts behaviors such as handwashing practices or physical distance maintenance recommendations from authorities.

title: Inhibition of hepatitis C virus replication by Monascus pigment derivatives that interfere with viral RNA polymerase activity and the mevalonate biosynthesis pathway
abstract: OBJECTIVES: Hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection causes chronic liver disease and is a major public health problem worldwide. The aim of this study was to evaluate the potential of Monascus pigment derivatives, which were derived from a microbial secondary metabolite synthesized from polyketides by Monascus spp., as HCV antiviral agents. METHODS: We performed an in vitro RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp) assay to screen for HCV RdRp inhibitors. The anti-HCV activity of RdRp inhibitors in HCV-replicating cells was evaluated by quantification of the RNA viral genome. Molecular docking analysis was performed to predict the binding sites of the selected RdRp inhibitors. RESULTS: We have identified a Monascus pigment and its derivatives as inhibitors of the HCV NS5B RdRp. A group of Monascus orange pigment (MOP) amino acid derivatives, in which the reactive oxygen moiety was changed to amino acids, significantly inhibited HCV replication. Further, combination of the MOP derivatives (Phe, Val or Leu conjugates) with interferon (IFN)-α inhibited HCV replication more than IFN-α treatment alone. Lastly, molecular docking studies indicate the inhibitors may bind to a thumb subdomain allosteric site of NS5B. The antiviral activity of the MOP derivatives was related to a modulation of the mevalonate pathway, since the mevalonate-induced increase in HCV replication was suppressed by the MOP compounds. CONCLUSIONS: Our results identify amino acid derivatives of MOP as potential anti-HCV agents and suggest that their combination with IFN-α might offer an alternative strategy for the control of HCV replication.

title: A multi-center, randomized controlled trial by the Integrative Management in Japan for Epidemic Disease (IMJEDI study-RCT) on the use of Kampo medicine, kakkonto with shosaikotokakikyosekko, in mild-to-moderate COVID-19 patients for symptomatic relief and prevention of severe stage: a structured summary of a study protocol for a randomized controlled trial
abstract: OBJECTIVES: We aimed to test our hypothesis that additional administration of traditional Japanese (Kampo) medicine, kakkonto (kakkon-to: KT) and shosaikotokakikyosekko (sho-saiko-to-ka-kikyo-sekko: SSKKS), is more effective in relieving symptoms and preventing the onset of severe infection in mild-to-moderate COVID-19 patients compared to those treated only with conventional treatment. TRIAL DESIGN: The study is designed as a multi-center, interventional, parallel-group, randomized (1:1 ratio), investigator-sponsored, two-arm study. PARTICIPANTS: Patients and inpatients will be recruited from 8 Japanese academic and non-academic hospitals. The inclusion and exclusion criteria are as follows: Inclusion criteria 1. Diagnosed as positive for severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2). 2. Clinical stages of mild-to-moderate COVID-19. 3. Symptomatic; 4. ≥ 20 years of age. 5. Male or female. 6. Ability to communicate in Japanese. 7. Outpatients and inpatients. 8. Provided informed consent. Exclusion criteria 1. Difficulty in providing informed consent due to dementia, psychosis, or psychiatric symptoms. 2. Allergic to Kampo or Western medicines used in this study. 3. Pregnant and lactating. 4. Unable to follow up. 5. Participating in another clinical trial or interventional study. 6. Hypokalemic or taking oral furosemide or steroids. 7. Determined unsuitable for this study by the physician. INTERVENTION AND COMPARATOR: Patients in the control group will receive conventional treatment with antipyretics, painkillers, or antitussives for symptoms that occurred after they contracted the SARS-CoV-2 infection. Patients in the Kampo group will receive 2.5 g of KT (TJ-1@TSUMURA and Co.) and 2.5 g of SSKKS (TJ-109@TSUMURA and Co.) 3 times a day, orally, for 14 days in addition to the conventional treatment as mentioned above. MAIN OUTCOMES: The number of days till at least one of the symptoms (fever, cough, sputum, malaise, shortness of breath) improves in the first 14 days of treatment. To assess the cough, sputum, malaise, and shortness of breath, a numeric rating scale will be used to define improvement in terms of a 2-point decrease in the number of days from the start of treatment for at least 2 days. Fever will be defined as an improvement when the temperature is less than 37 °C. RANDOMIZATION: Patients are randomized (1:1 ratio) to each group using the minimization method, with balancing of the arms with severity of disease stage and patient age (< 65, 65 to < 75, or ≥ 75 years). Computer-generated random numbers will be used for the minimization method. BLINDING (MASKING): Open-label with no blinding NUMBERS TO BE RANDOMIZED (SAMPLE SIZE): The main research hypothesis of this study is that the combination of Kampo medicine and conventional treatment will significantly improve the patients’ symptoms (fever, fatigue, cough, sputum, and shortness of breath) during the first 14 days of treatment as compared with conventional treatment alone. Concerning the analysis of the primary endpoint, the duration of time before improvement of at least one of the common cold-like symptoms (fever, malaise, cough, sputum, and shortness of breath) will be estimated using the Kaplan-Meier method, and the survival curves will be compared between groups using the log-rank test. Assuming this method of analysis and based on previous studies reporting the efficacy of Kampo medicine for COVID-19 and H1N1 influenza patients, the median survival time in the Kampo medicine group is estimated as 3 days; this time will be 1.5 times longer in the control group. Assuming a one-sided significance level of 5%, a power of 70%, and an allocation ratio of 1:1, the required sample size is calculated as 126 cases. To compensate for a loss in follow-up, we plan to include 150 cases in both groups (Kampo group = 75, control group = 75). TRIAL STATUS: Protocol version 1.2 as of August 20, 2020 Recruitment start (expected): October 1, 2020 Recruitment finish (expected): October 31, 2023 TRIAL REGISTRATION: Japan Registry of Clinical Trials (jRCT) jRCTs021200020. Registered on August 25, 2020 FULL PROTOCOL: The full protocol is attached as an additional file and is accessible from the Trials website (Additional file 1). In the interest of expediting the dissemination of this material, the familiar formatting has been eliminated; this Letter serves as a summary of the key elements of the full protocol.

title: Enhanced infection control interventions reduced catheter-related bloodstream infections in the neonatal department of Hung Vuong Hospital, Vietnam, 2011–2012: a pre- and post-intervention study
abstract: BACKGROUND: Catheter-related bloodstream infections (CR-BSI) cause high neonatal mortality and are related to inadequate aseptic technique during the care and maintenance of a catheter. The incidence of CR-BSI among neonates in Hung Vuong Hospital was higher than that of other neonatal care centres in Vietnam. METHODS: An 18-month pre- and post-intervention study was conducted over three 6-month periods to evaluate the effectiveness of the intervention for CR-BSI and to identify risk factors associated with CR-BSI. During the intervention period, we trained all nurses in the Department of Neonatology on BSI preventive practices, provided auditing and feedback about aseptic technique during catheter care and maintenance, and reorganised preparation of total parenteral nutrition. All neonates with intravenous catheter insertion ≥48 h in the pre- and post-intervention period were enrolled. A standardised questionnaire was used to collect data. Blood samples were collected for cultures. We used Poisson regression to calculate rate ratio (RR) and 95% confidence interval (CI) for CR-BSI incidence rates and logistic regression to identify risk factors associated with CR-BSI. RESULTS: Of 2225 neonates enrolled, 1027 were enrolled in the pre-intervention period, of which 53 CR-BSI cases occurred in 8399 catheter-days, and 1198 were enrolled in the post-intervention period, of which 32 CR-BSI cases occurred in 8324 catheter-days. Incidence rates of CR-BSI significantly decreased after the intervention (RR = 0.61, 95% CI 0.39–0.94). Days of hospitalisation, episodes of non-catheter–related hospital-acquired infections, and the proportion of deaths significantly decreased after the intervention (p < 0.01). The CR-BSI was associated with days of intravenous catheter (odds ratio [OR] = 1.05, 95% CI 1.03–1.08), use of endotracheal intubation (OR = 2.27, 95% CI 1.27–4.06), and intravenous injection (OR = 8.50, 95% CI 1.14–63.4). CONCLUSIONS: The interventions significantly decreased the incidence rate of CR-BSI. Regular refresher training and auditing and feedback about aseptic technique during care and maintenance of catheters are critical to reducing CR-BSI.

Days of hospitalisation, episodes of non-catheter–related hospital-acquired infections, and the proportion of deaths significantly decreased after the intervention (p < 0.01). The CR-BSI was associated with days of intravenous catheter (odds ratio [OR] = 1.05, 95% CI 1.03–1.08), use of endotracheal intubation (OR = 2.27, 95% CI 1.27–4.06), and intravenous injection (OR = 8.50, 95% CI 1.14–63.4). CONCLUSIONS: The interventions significantly decreased the incidence rate of CR-BSI. Regular refresher training and auditing and feedback about aseptic technique during care and maintenance of catheters are critical to reducing CR-BSI.

title: Influence of positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) on histopathological and bacteriological aspects of pneumonia during low tidal volume mechanical ventilation
abstract: This study examines the influence of positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) on histopathological and bacteriological aspects of pneumonia during low tidal volume mechanical ventilation. Pneumonia, a common infection in intensive care units, carries high mortality rates when treated with traditional methods. The effects of different levels of PEEP during mechanical ventilation using low tidal volumes have not been thoroughly investigated yet. To better understand these effects, a rat model was used to observe histopathological and bacteriological changes upon exposure to PEEP at 10, 15 and 20 cmH2O following an intratracheal instillation of Pseudomonas aeruginosa bacteria for inducing experimental pneumonia. Results were compared between groups exposed to higher or lower Vt; main outcomes included bacterial load quantification within alveolar homogenates from lung tissue sample as well as qualitative assessments regarding inflammation according to specific cell types such as neutrophils, plasma cells and mononuclear cells present within the same tissue samples. Findings could be significant in better understanding how clinical decisions regarding different levels of ventilator support can help reduce mortality associated with pneumonia cases..

title: Contribution of Janus-Kinase/Signal Transduction Activator of Transcription Pathway in the Pathogenesis of Vasculitis: A Possible Treatment Target in the Upcoming Future
abstract: This study seeks to investigate the potential contribution of Janus-kinase/signal transduction activator of transcription (JAK/STAT) pathway in the pathogenesis of Vasculitis and its possible use as a treatment target. The medical community has so far relied on corticosteroids, chemotherapy, and other immunosuppressive agents to treat this condition even though exact mechanisms remain unclear. This article's goal is determine how JAK/STAT plays a role in promoting cytokine production, extracellular matrix remodelling and as well as causing endothelial damage - all key steps involved in vasculitis formation. Further research into understanding about the JAK/STAT mediators can lead to potential therapeutic strategies for targeting specific pathways implicated in this disease process. Thus by exploring its clinical utility, we could possibly improve outcomes from existing treatments with fewer side effects going forward that are tailored towards preventing or reversing vasculitic pathology concerning complications related to immune system dysfunction.

title: Protective Immunity against Respiratory Tract Challenge with Yersinia pestis in Mice Immunized with an Adenovirus-Based Vaccine Vector Expressing V Antigen
abstract: The title of this paper is ‘Protective Immunity against Respiratory Tract Challenge with Yersinia pestis in Mice Immunized with an Adenovirus-Based Vaccine Vector Expressing V Antigen’. Plague, caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis, remains a considerable public health threat despite centuries of control attempts. To ensure further protection and reduce disease outbreaks, development of effective vaccines are essential. In this study, we tested the use of adenovirus-based vector vaccine expressing virulence antigen (V antigen) for generation of protective immunity against respiratory challenge with wild type Y. pestis in mice. Results demonstrated that intranasal delivery route produced high levels of serum IgG antibodies as well as increased splenic lymphocytes population in immunized mice compared to placebo controls post vaccination. Ultimately, the results indicate that prophylactic immunization using our adenovirus vector can effectively protect rodent models from infection caused by virulent strain Y. pestis both systemically and locally within bronchoalveolar epitheliums.

title: Acute upper airway infections: Childhood respiratory infections
abstract: This article focuses on acute upper airway infections in children and the associated respiratory complications. In recent years, the global burden of childhood respiratory infections has increased significantly due to various factors such as overcrowding, urbanization and increasing antibiotic resistance. These infections can result in both short-term problems like bronchitis or exacerbations of existing conditions, as well as long-term disabilities. This paper reviews current evidence regarding key components of prevention and treatment for these common but often preventable childhood diseases including immunizations, nutrition status, symptom management and nebulizers for inhaled medication therapies. Additionally, this research details specific considerations for primary care physicians when it comes to recognizing a case requiring inpatient care versus one that can be effectively addressed with outpatient treatment. Finally, we discuss strategies that parents should consider to help manage their child’s symptoms outside of clinical settings while seeking guidance from trained medical professionals at all times. title: Willingness to pay for an early warning system for infectious diseases
abstract: This abstract reviews the key findings of a study examining the value individuals assign to early warning systems for infectious diseases. Titled “Willingness to Pay for an Early Warning System for Infectious Diseases”, this study employs discrete-choice experiments in 3 urban settings in 2 developing countries (Bangladesh and India) on adult participants aged 18-50. Our results show that willingness-to-pay values vary between country and setting, however overall there is a strong indication of public support for such early warning systems. Additionally, per capita income emerged as a significant predictor of willingness to pay while age was found not to have an effect on payments. Since these findings are highly optimistic and could shape future strategies towards health preparedness across low resource settings, we recommend further investigation and evaluation before policy application or interventions can be fully implemented with reduced risk at global level.

title: Chitin/Chitosan: Versatile Ecological, Industrial, and Biomedical Applications
abstract: This study examines the multiple applications of chitin/chitosan, a natural polymer found in abundance in nature. Chitin and its derivatives are used widely across various industries including ecological, industrial and biomedical sectors. This paper reveals how this readily available biopolymer is revolutionising modern technology with its numerous qualities such as sustainability, biocompatibility and enhanced solubility. Through detailed analysis on existing literature, we investigate the structural features that give rise to these properties, as well as examine future prospects for chitin/chitosan synthesis technologies. Our research aims to illustrate potential uses of this versatile material by standing at the forefront of topics concerning ecological stability, new product development and medical advancement. We hope this comprehensive review can further illuminate current understanding on relevant issues pertaining to chitin/chitosan-based devices and deliver constructive insights for industry professionals within ongoing debates surrounding biomaterials development.

title: Rapid Quantum Dot Nanobead-mAb Probe-Based Immunochromatographic Assay for Antibody Monitoring of Trichinella spiralis Infection
abstract: PURPOSE: Sensitive and selective point-of-care biosensor is an urgent pursuit of serological antibody detection to control parasite pathogen. For specific, quantitative and on-site screening of Trichinella spiralis infection in livestock, a quantum dot nanobead-monoclonal antibody (QB-mAb) probe-based immunochromatographic assay (ICA) was developed by introducing a competitive sandwich strategy (QB-CICA). METHODS: In the QB-CICA, QB-mAb probes competed with serum antibody for a particular epitope, followed by immunocomplexes binding to capture antibody on the test line. With the accumulation of target antibody, captured probes served as signal elements for fluorescent readout in a “turn off” mode, along with the fluorescence gradually weakened. The sensitivity and standard calibration curve of the QB-CICA were quantified using swine sera as negative control (n = 200) and artificial infected swine sera (n = 80) compared with a commercial ELISA kit. Besides, Trichinella spiralis-antibody targeting test ability of the QB-CICA, instead of other parasites or viruses antibodies (n = 10), was evaluated. RESULTS: The QB-CICA exhibited a good linear range, a low detection limit of 189.92 ng mL(−1) and 100% selectivity that was higher than commercial ELISA kit (90%), as well as the same serological positive rate (100%) with commercial ELISA kit in different infection dose models. CONCLUSION: Taking advantage of its simplicity, short response time (25 min), sensitivity and specificity, the proposed QB-CICA has potential applications for parasite-related antibody monitoring in food safety and clinical diagnosis fields.

title: NAD(+) homeostasis in renal health and disease
abstract: Renal function is an essential aspect of overall health and well-being. Despite its importance, very few studies have yet examined the role that NAD(+) homeostasis plays in renal health and disease. In this study, we aim to address this gap in knowledge by exploring the mechanism and pathways through which NAD+ metabolism, levels and activity are involved in normal kidney physiology as well as the possible implications of deregulated or imbalance NAD(+) homeostasis on diseases such as chronic kidney disease (CKD). Through analysis of existing literature combined with original research, our investigation may further elucidate NAD+’s involvement within a crucial organ system responsible for sustaining bodily balance. This article seeks to critically evaluate how alterations in key metabolites involved within the NAD(+) salvage pathway could lead to potential biomarkers for early diagnosis or therapeutic targets for Renal Disease pathology therefore contributing meaningful insights into Renal Health Research field.

title: Catalytic site studies on tuna (Thunnus albacares) pyloric caeca aminopeptidase
abstract: Tuna pyloric caeca aminopeptidase (tAP) is a glycosylated zinc-metalloenzyme containing apparently two identical subunits. The enzyme is reversibly inhibited in a time-dependent manner by amastatin. Slow development of tAP inhibition by this inhibitor could be demonstrated. Dissociation of the complex of tAP with amastatin is also slow. Two molar equivalents of the inhibitor are bound by the enzyme suggesting the presence of one catalytic site in each subunit. Chemical modification of tAP with 1-cyclohexyl-3-(2-morpholinoethyl)carbonyl-metho-p-toluene sulfonate and N-ethoxycarbonyl-2-ethoxy-1,2-dihydroquinone revealed the presence of essential acidic amino acid residues probably located at the active site. Compatible with the presence of arginine and tyrosine residues at the catalytic site of most metalloproteinases, tAP is reversibly inhibited by phenylglyoxal and inactivated by tetranitromethane in a time-dependent fashion. The rate of inhibition by these modifiers could be significantly decreased if the enzyme was previously treated with amastatin suggesting that the modified amino acid residues are located at the catalytic site. Diethylpyrocarbonate did not affect the activity of both native and zinc-depleted tAP suggesting that histidine is not involved in the zinc-ligand formation.

title: A Rationally Designed TNF-α Epitope-Scaffold Immunogen Induces Sustained Antibody Response and Alleviates Collagen-Induced Arthritis in Mice
abstract: This paper presents a novel strategy to ameliorate an inflammatory condition, Collagen-Induced Arthritis (CIA), through Vaccine Design with an Epitope-Scaffold Immunogen. By rational design of the immunogen, incorporating both TNF-α epitopes and a scaffold protein, the authors report achievement of sustained antibody production and reduced arthritic signs in CIA mice models. The data underpinning this study may provide evidence for developing reliable immune responses against different persistent antigens for therapeutic purposes using engineered vaccines containing epitopic peptides within carrier proteins.

title: INFECTION CONTROL CHALLENGES IN CHILD-CARE CENTERS

title: The social benefits of private infectious disease-risk mitigation
abstract: Does society benefit from private measures to mitigate infectious disease risks? Since mitigation reduces both peak prevalence and the number of people who fall ill, the answer might appear to be yes. But mitigation also prolongs epidemics and therefore the time susceptible people engage in activities to avoid infection. These avoidance activities come at a cost—in lost production or consumption, for example. Whether private mitigation yields net social benefits depends on the social weight given to the costs of illness and illness avoidance, now and into the future. We show that, for a large class of infectious diseases, private risk mitigation is socially beneficial. However, in cases where society discounts the future at either very low or very high rates relative to private individuals, or where it places a low weight on the private cost of illness, the social cost of illness under proportionate mixing (doing nothing) may be lower than the social cost of illness under preferential mixing (avoiding infectious individuals). That is, under some circumstances, society would prefer shorter, more intense epidemics without avoidance costs over longer, less intense epidemics with avoidance costs. A sobering (although not surprising) implication of this is that poorer societies should be expected to promote less private disease-risk mitigation than richer societies.

title: Epitope specificity and longevity of a vaccine-induced human T cell response against HPV18
abstract: Persistent human papillomavirus (HPV) type 16 and 18 infection can lead to pre-malignant and malignant diseases of the lower genital tract. Several lines of evidence suggest that T cell responses can control HPV infection. However, relative to other human viruses, strong effector memory T cell responses against HPV have been difficult to detect. We used an in vitro stimulation step prior to enzyme-linked immunospot assays to identify IFN-γ-secreting T cells specific for HPV16 and 18 E6/E7 peptides. This allowed the detection of HPV-specific CD4(+) T cells that were not evident in direct ex vivo assays. T cell responses against HPV16 or 18 peptides were detected in healthy volunteers (7/9) and patients with lower genital tract neoplasia (10/20). Importantly, this assay allowed tracking of vaccine-induced T cell responses in nine patients, following inoculation with a live recombinant vaccinia virus (HPV16 and 18 E6/E7, TA-HPV). Novel vaccine-induced T cell responses were demonstrated in five patients, but no clinical responses (lesion regressions) were seen. For one vaccinated patient, the T cell response was mapped to a single dominant HPV18 E7 epitope and this response was sustained for >3 years. Our data suggest that systemic memory T cells against HPV16 and 18, induced naturally or by TA-HPV vaccination, are relatively rare. Nevertheless, the assay system developed allowed estimation of magnitude, epitope specificity, and longevity of vaccine-induced CD4(+) T cell responses. This will be useful for vaccine design and measurement of immunological endpoints in clinical trials.

title: Metagenomic next-generation sequencing in the diagnosis of severe pneumonias caused by Chlamydia psittaci
abstract: This article presents a novel approach to diagnose severe pneumonias caused by Chlamydia psittaci through next-generation metagenomic sequencing (mNGS). To date, the standard medical practice for diagnosing this type of pneumonia has been limited, resulting in delayed management and poorer outcomes. Therefore, we sought to determine whether mNGS is applicable as an alternative diagnostic tool that provides information more accurately and at greater speed. As part of our systematic review, we conducted an observational study using a cohort of 40 patients aged ≥ 18 years with signs and symptoms suggestive of viral or bacterial pneumonia. Samples underwent both conventional pathogen diagnosis and metagenomics analysis for bacteria, viruses, fungi and parasites; results were analysed for sensitivity/specificity following a blinded impact assessment. Our retrospective case series demonstrated that mNGS was preferable over traditional methods to detect C.psittaci associated severe pneumonia with significantly increased sensitivity (p<0.005). Furthermore, compared to other available diagnoses known from history or previously done laboratory testing – such as antibiotic susceptibility assays – the potential saving in terms of turnaround time thanks to new NGS technologies proved immense. This preliminary investigation underscores that mNGS might be considered a promising test capable of expediting directed therapy with fewer adverse events due to improper treatments in managing cases concerning suspected Chlamydial infection associated severe pneumonias in adults due respects expected national regulatory approaches on clinical use application validation rules.

title: Ovine haemonchosis: a review
abstract: Ovine haemonchosis is an infectious disease of sheep caused by the gastrointestinal parasite Haemonchus contortus. The infection leads to a wide range of clinical conditions such as anaemia, malnutrition and eventual death from severe blood loss which has destructive implications for animal health and economic productivity. In this review, we examine the epidemiology, diagnosis, treatment strategies and control measures suggested for ovine haemonchosis in an effort to optimize cost effectiveness while improving animal welfare outcomes. Furthermore, based on recent advances in molecular engineering combined with classical epidemiological approaches, it may be possible to develop more preventative strategies against this parasitic malady among small ruminant animals. Therefore current research that seeks to employ alternative formulation drugs or new vaccine technology is discussed within the context of assessing their efficacy against ovine haemonchosis at a practical level across multiple regions worldwide.

Furthermore, based on recent advances in molecular engineering combined with classical epidemiological approaches, it may be possible to develop more preventative strategies against this parasitic malady among small ruminant animals. Therefore current research that seeks to employ alternative formulation drugs or new vaccine technology is discussed within the context of assessing their efficacy against ovine haemonchosis at a practical level across multiple regions worldwide.

title: Prevention of Human Rotavirus-Induced Diarrhea in Gnotobiotic Piglets using Bovine Antibody
abstract: The efficacy of passively administered bovine antibody for preventing human rotavirus (HRV)-induced diarrhea was investigated using a gnotobiotic pig model. Cows were immunized with inactivated HRV serotypes 1 (Wa) and 2 (S2) and simian rotavirus serotype 3 (SAIl), and immune colostrum and milk were collected. Antibody concentrates derived from these materials were fed to germ-free piglets that were subsequently inoculated with HRV Wa. Both viral shedding and diarrhea were effectively reduced or eliminated in a dose-dependent manner as a result of HRV immune antibody feeding. A quantitative virus-neutralizing (VN) antibody method permitted assessment of the functional antibody dose required to achieve a 50% reduction of disease (PD(50)) . PD(50) dose levels of 15.8 and 19.5 × 10(6) VN antibody units were determined for inhibition of diarrhea and viral shedding, respectively. Studies reported here provide new information on the quantitative relationship between protective antibody dose and diarrheal disease response.

title: Ecohydrogeochemical functioning of coastal freshwater herbaceous wetlands in the Protected Natural Area, Ciénaga del Fuerte (American tropics): Spatiotemporal behaviour
abstract: This abstract presents an exploration into the spatiotemporal behaviour of ecohydrogeochemical functioning within coastal freshwater herbaceous wetlands in the Protected Natural Area Ciénaga del Fuerte, located in the American tropics. Through multidisciplinary teams across physical sciences and engineering disciplines, initial sampling measurements have been conducted to evaluate prevailing water sources, hydrological regimes and environmental parameters contributing to their hydroecological characteristics over temporal scales. Statistical analysis is used to relate these ecohydrogeochemistry dynamics with sea level changes caused by El Niño Southern Oscillation events that influence open environment systems such as coral reefs and mangroves ecosystems. The results from this study will elucidate spatiotemporal trends that can assist natural resource managers in measuring effects caused by extreme weather conditions. Ultimately, a model for sound planning for aquifer management strategies aiming for reduced risk of ecological collapse may be established based on its results.

title: Public Roads as Places of Interspecies Conflict: A Study of Horse-Human Interactions on UK Roads and Impacts on Equine Exercise
abstract:
This research paper presents a study that investigates how the expansion of human traffic on UK roads has caused conflict between horses and humans, and examines the impacts this interspecies conflict has had on equine exercise. Exploring where the encounters have taken place, their frequency, severity level and intervention strategies used in response to said conflicts will enable an evaluation of their impact upon horse-human interactions and equine health. The results of this investigation could inform current understanding regarding best practices for safeguarding both species against such threats while minimising disruption to horse use of local roads as common areas across rural landscapes. 

Public Roads as Places of Interspecies Conflict: A Study of Horse-Human Interactions on UK Roads and Impacts On Equine Exercise

The growth in the number of vehicles accessing public roads across Britain has created a pressing issue for those who regularly ride horses along these shared routes – namely climate change mitigationists, private owners with fields running alongside public highways or bridleways, leisure riders or members from organised groups such as mounted police officers). Since British law provides access rights to most tarmacadamed pathways but offers no protection from motorised traffic formulae, there is increasing concern about injury risk posed mainly by heavy goods vehicles (HGVs) when coming into close contact with horses at high speeds. This paper undertakes an empirical analysis examining horse–vehicle conflict located throughout England’s road networks over three consecutive years focusing on its potential negative effects on welfare status through restricted levels natural movement inside these newly developed urban-style environments. Through interviews held cyclists; motorists; HGV operators ; equestrian influence groups (such as BHS), it is hoped that insights identifying solutions can be identified which could bring humane benefits without damaging existing user fees attached to certain private/public road access policies

title: A novel MSC-based immune induction strategy for ABO-incompatible liver transplantation: a phase I/II randomized, open-label, controlled trial
abstract: The paper titled A novel MSC-based immune induction strategy for ABO-incompatible liver transplantation: a phase I/II randomized, open-label, controlled trial examines the efficacy of using mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) to induce donor microchimerism in patients receiving an organ from an incompatible ABO blood group. As the demand for allogeneic livers is greater than supply, it is important to seek additional methods which could increase patient eligibility and decrease complications caused by incompatibility between donor and recipient. This randomized controlled trial evaluated the feasibility and safety compared with control predecessors of a newly developed approach that uses mesenchymal stem cell immunomodulation in combination with other preoperative treatments prior to ABOi liver transplantation. In this study 84 patients were enrolled following stringent criteria including biochemical parameters such as bilirubin level, prothrombin time activity and age at enrollment. Outcome measurements included graft acceptance rate, instances of rejection or re-transplant needed after one year follow up; outcome assessment was conducted over 6 months post procedure. The primary goal was to evaluate clinical improvement when comparing patients who received MSK immunomodulatory cells vs traditional treatment alone. This well designed trial holds vast potential implications on innovative therapeutic management strategies used prior to ABOi LTx procedures thus could be instrumental for successful 3rd party transplants among those ineligible due historic issues related to unrelated bodies' incompatibility problems.

title: A Mortality Analysis of the Cytomegalovirus (CMV) Infection Letermovir Prophylaxis Trial in CMV-Seropositive Recipients of Allogeneic Hematopoietic Cell Transplantation (HCT)
abstract: BACKGROUND: In a Phase III randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study of CMV-seropositive HCT recipients, letermovir prophylaxis significantly reduced the incidence of clinically significant CMV infections (CS-CMVi) through 24 weeks post-HCT. We investigated the impact of letermovir prophylaxis on mortality through Week 48 post-HCT. METHODS: Adult CMV-seropositive allogeneic HCT recipients with undetectable plasma CMV DNA at screening who could initiate treatment by Week 4 post-HCT were eligible. Subjects stratified by high or low CMV disease risk were randomized 2:1 to letermovir dosed at 480 mg/d (240 mg/d if on cyclosporine) or placebo PO or IV through Week 14 post-HCT. Time to all-cause mortality and non-relapse mortality (defined as death due to any reason other than the indication for HCT) through Week 48 post-HCT are presented using Kaplan–Meier (KM) plots censored at study discontinuation for reasons other than death/non-relapse death or upon study completion. Distribution of time to mortality endpoints was tested by stratified log-rank tests using two-sided P-values. RESULTS: This analysis included all 565 patients randomized and treated with ≥1 dose of study drug. Subjects began study drug a median of 9 days post-HCT; 36.5% started post-engraftment. The observed KM event rate for all-cause mortality was lower in the letermovir group (10.6%) than the placebo group (15.5%) at Week 24 post-HCT, and remained lower through Week 48 post-HCT (21.4% vs. 26.2%) (Figure 1). The observed K–M event rate for all-cause mortality in subjects who developed CS-CMVi was also lower in the letermovir group (4.6%) than the placebo group (17.1%) at Week 48 post-HCT. The observed KM event rate for non-relapse mortality was lower in the letermovir group (6.9%) vs. the placebo group (11.2%) at Week 24 post-HCT, and remained lower in the letermovir group (13.9%) than the placebo group (17.5%) through Week 48 post-HCT (Figure 2). CONCLUSION: All-cause and non-relapse mortality were reduced in the letermovir group compared with the placebo group through Week 48 post-HCT (relative risk reduction ~18% and ~21%, respectively). These results are consistent with a clinically meaningful survival benefit for letermovir prophylaxis. DISCLOSURES: J. title: Proximal femoral resection and Tensor Fascia Lata flap for recalcitrant trochanteric pressure ulcers
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Trochanteric pressure ulcers (PrUs) are difficult to treat and are often complicated by infection spreading to the hip joint. We review three cases from India where proximal femoral resection and pedicled Tensor Fascia Lata (TFL) flapping was used in the management of infected deep trochanteric ulcers communicating to the hip joint. CASE PRESENTATION: Three patients had a total of four trochanteric PrUs communicating to the hip joint. Proximal femoral resection along with radical debridement of the pressure ulcer (PrU) was the first step in our surgical protocol. Serial debridements were performed to make the resulting cavity healthier and ready for the subsequent flap surgery. TFL flapping was done to cover the raw area of the PrU and the donor site was closed either primarily or with a split skin graft. All patients were males with AIS A spinal cord injury (SCI) and stage 4 PrUs in the trochanteric region. One patient had bilateral trochanteric ulcers. There was complete healing of all PrUs with improvement in wheelchair mobility, and general health. DISCUSSION: PrUs are a common complication of patients with SCI and are often considered one of the most neglected issues of health care delivery in India. Proximal femoral resection with pedicled TFL muscle flap is a versatile and reliable procedure for the coverage of recalcitrant trochanteric PrU with hip joint involvement. Minimal donor site morbidity occurs.
